A SCIENTIST haS decided that fish are not neces- variV crazy when they are in seine.

A DLSPERSER.—In case of a riot, send a pick- pocket into the crowd, and it will very soon be is-pursed. WOMAN OF BUSINESS.—The ,wife of a Yankee, who had his life heavily insured, sot his death down to profit and loss. Ir. is said that nobody is broken on the wheel nowadays; but how is it with a bankrupt bicycle manufacturer?

WHEN a fop was trying to become the lion of a fashionable party, a wit remarked that he could never be anything but a dandy-lion. "PAPA, if three wheels• is a tricycle, and two wheels a bicycle, what is one wheel ?' "One wheel, my son? Well, let me see. One wheel must be a unicycle." "No, it aint, papa, it's a wheel- barrow."

_ "ARE you going to strike?" asked the boss boiler maker,,.as hc.met his men coming out of the yard with their coats on. "No," replied the leader, "we are going to stop striking until wages are raised."

THE fellow who wrote, "I now take my pen in my hand," was troubled with remorse when he discovered, after he had posted the letter, that he had been using a lead-pencil. THE great Junius said he never knew a rogue who was not unhappy. Of course not; it is the rogues who are not known who are the happy ones.

IT was said of an inveterate drunkard that he had met with great affliction, and drank to drown his grief. "Then," said a bystander, "his grief must know how to swim, for he has never been able to drown it."

AN old lady who had several unmarried daughters fed them largely on a fish diet, because, as she in- genuously observed, fish is rich in phosphorus, and phosphorus is the essential thing in making matches.

A BEAuriyub Boston girl fell overboard, and her lover, leaning over the side of the boat, as she rose to the surface, said: "Give me your hand!" "Please ask papa," responded the beautiful Boston _girl, as she gurglingly sank a second time. "TIME is money—that's a fact; and if you wish to know the value of time, just get a little speck of dirt in your pocket chronometer and take it round to a watch-tinker. He'll blow in it a couple of times, and charge you three dollars for repairs."

How can you hate him ?" "He didn't p.-arry you, don't you know; my love."

THE RULING PASSION. —A French paper points out that the passion for gambling is so !great in England that even in wedding notices it is neces- sary to state that there are "no cards," in order to put a check upon the national tendency to gamble on all occasions.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
Lord Tennyson, accompanied by the Hon. Hallam Tennyson, is at present almost daily seen driving through the picturesque district of flaslemere, in the neighhourhood of Aldworth, his Surrey seat.

I am able to state that the Prince and Princess of Wales have accepted an invitation of the German Emperor to pay a visit to Germany late in the autumn. Full State ceremonies will be observed during the stay in Berlin.

Acting under the direction of the Solicitor- General, the Public Prosecutor is still engaged in consideration of papers placed in his bands in con- nection with the case of Evelyn versus Hurlbert. It will probably be a fortnight or three weeks before he is able to arrive at a decision in the matter.

A member of the House of Commons, who in his capacity as magistrate recently visited Mr. Dillon in prison, was informed by the hon. member that as soon as he is released from confinement he intends to take a two months holiday. For that period of time, at least, he would not be willing to undertake the duties of leader of the Irish party in succession to Mr. McCarthy.

On Wednesday, at Mr. Stuart Rendel's house, a number of Welsh members met the members of the Church Disestablishment Campaign Committee. The meeting was unanimous in favour of pressing forward the campaign during the recess. It was resolved to appoint a joint finance committee, partly of members of the House of Commons and partly of Welshmen outside it. An appeal for funds will shortly be made.

Reports have appeared in various French news- papers announcing the intention of grateful French- men to subscribe for a testimonial worthy of Mr. Labouchere's acceptance, in recognition of his per- sistent advocacy.of the claims of the French Repub- lic upon the notice of the government of Lord Salisbury, suspected of proneness unduly to extol Germany. Mr. Labouchere tells us that he knows nothing of the undertaking except what he has read in the papers.

A Berlin Correspondent telegraphs that the Prussian Minister of Public Instruction has sum- moned Professor von Bergmann and Professor Hahn to send him within twenty-four hours an explana- tion regarding the accusations raised against them by Dr. Leidig. It will be remembered that this gentleman charged the Professors with having made experiments with patients suffering from cancer by inoculating healthy spots of their body with cancerous matter from the diseased parts in order to test the infectious character of the dis- ease.

There is a prospect of another .election in Ireland, which, should Mr. Parnell attempt to fight the seat, will supply fresh evidence of his position in the country. in March last the member for West Wicklow was adjudicated bankrupt. It was formerly the case that a member might in such circumstances retain his seat for twelve months. Under Mr. Chamberlain's Act of 1883, the term was reduced by one-half, and unless Mr. Bryne is, in the meanwhile, able to satisfy his creditors, a vacancy in Wicklow must ensue.

The Prince of Wales is no doubt sincerely glad that the,Emperor's visit is over. It has been long since the Prince has gone through so much labour as he has during the past week. The activity and energy of the Emperor—the amount of sight-seeing, visiting, and inspecting which he carried out—was not entirely agreeable to the disposition of his quieter and more plethoric uncle. The Prince was anxious that the visit should not be marred by any contretemps, and in this respect his wishes have been completely fulfilled.

If the Emperor had been as nervous as the Czar he must have quaked on Wimbledon Common on Saturday to find himself the object of batteries of cameras on all hands. It was a brilliant day, and the grand military combination brought thousands of amateur photographers on to the ground with all kinds of apparatus—big and little, old and new. It is no exaggeration to say that they were present in thousands; and it must have been a revelation to the Emperor of how the passion for photography has permeated all ranks in this country.

For the first time,"a lady has this year carried off the Cobden, Club sixty pound prize offered at the Universities' for the best essay on an economic sad- sect. The prize is competed for in successive years in rotation at Oxford. Cambridge, and Manchester. This year it is the turn of the Victoria University, and the winner is Miss Victorine Jeans, 8.A., of 10, Mayfield-road, Whalley Range, Manchester. The subject of the essay is "The Industrial and Com- mercial Effects, Actual and Prospective, of English Factory Act Legislation."

Lord and 'Lady Aberdeen leave England next month for Canada on a visit to their farm in the Rocky mountains. Struck, as all lovers of nature are, by the splendid scenery through which the Canadian Pacific Railway runs, and affected by the land hunger which seizes all travellers alike in those rcgions, Lord Aberdeen when there last year purchased a section, or square mile, of land, about 400 miles east of Vancouver. Thither he and the Countess intend to retire from time to time to ruralise, to study nature, and enjoy life quietly. '

Cardinal Manning entered, on Wednesday, on his 84th year. Though almost a prisoner to the house, his Eminence is activein body, and is as vigorous and receptive as ever in mind. Writing to Mrs. Gladstone a short time ago, the Cardinal, after say- ing, " You know how nearly I have agreed in Wil- liam's career, especially in his Irish policy, of the last 20 years," laments "how few of our old friends and companions now survive." A collection of letters written by his Eminence during the last five years has been published as a souvenir.

The decision of the Plymouth Trade Union case by the Judges of the Queen's Bench, on Tuesday, is among other tnings a personal triumph for Sir William Harcourt, who stated emphatically in the House of Commons during the debate on Mr. Robertson's Conspiracy Bill that the judgment of Mr. Bompas, now reserved, was bad law. It will be remembered that• Sir William, who is a far better lawyer than nine-tenths. of his critics, was equtilly right in the great licensing case of Sharp v. Wake- field, when his view was upheld against the Solici- tor-General by the Court of Appeal and the House of Lords.

The Czar and Czarina are still cruising about in Finnish waters. They constantly change from one place to another, generally seeking the secluded districts in order to be entirely undisturbed.. The Czarina dresses in plain cottons. Here, far away from the aristocracy, the military, and the police, the Czar appears to attend only to the. most urgent business. He is kept acquainted,6with events in the outer World by the daily despatch of couriers and constant telegrams. Every day a cook brings provisions all the way from St. Petersburg. As in previous cruises, there is a band on board the Im- perial yacht. The weather is beautiful, and it is hoped the Czarina will derive a great deal of good from the voyage.

The jubilee number of "Punch," gives double the usual quantity of matter, pictorial and literary, at the ordinarylprice of 3d. There is the usual number complete in itself, and a sort of supplement forming the jubilee number. It is largely reminiscent in its character, and is therefore doubly fnteresting. Mr. ," Punch " himself,intervieweelty Anno Domini 1891 relates to his visitor, in rapid narrative form, the history of his fifty years. There are reproduced several pictures from the earliest mumbers. There is one of Dizzy in r 1847, doubtidse drawn with the same fidelity with "which his lineaments were por- trayed in more recent years. It is a wonderful thing, with the curie and frill, the .cuffs, the tight trousers, and the pointed shoes. A .companion pic- ture is one af Mr. GleAstone drawn in 1860, which bears a striking resemblance to his latesOn when he was l&st seen in the House of Commons.

"A BLEG-Bt RN DICK- SHONARY:" This is the title of a little work of 78 pages by "Tum-o'-Dick o' Bob's," with whose " Sayin's " our readers are more or less familar through contribu- tions to this journal. The style is lively, and the comments are for the most part as pertinent as they are humorous. The writer is thoroughly acquainted with Lancashire idioms; and he has an apt method of illustrating a word by an appropriate story. In his own way he announces that his books are sold at " fippence apiece." They are well worth the money. We give a specimen of— A TOOATHRI WORDS O'ERLOOKT. ABACK° (Behind; at the back of). " Ged the abacko me, Owd Lad." Aw towd th' payfon this were a Scripture :quotation, but he dudn'd know ' id. ANGRY (vexed). This meeans infleeamed, sooa when yo're towd nod to anger a sooar place yo'll understand as id doesn'd meean vexin' id. ARRA.ND (errand). That's plain to be sin bi ony leatherheyd. BULL-BEEF (a fall on a slide). There wodn'd be mich gam on a slor iv id worn'd forth' bull-beefs as some o'th' stiff uns ged. BLOWER (a screen of tin or zinc). A blower is one o' th' gret inventions o' this inventive age, an' unvallyable to a werkin' mon wi' no time for blowin' th' fire wi' th' ballies in a mornin'. BOWT BREAD (Loaves bought at a shop—some- times also called shop-bread). Aw tell yo' wod, fooak, there's some weary rubbish among bowt- bread, for beawt reclenin th' alum, etsette.ra, it's a varry common thing to find buttons an' cockroaches, an oddments o' o' soorts in id. - BEVERAGE (a pourboire). Th' payson's showin' off his Greek an Latin ageean, though aw keep tellin' him to stick to summat n'ar hooam—say French or Welsh. When a youngster hes a new suit on id relations nip id for new, an' tell id as id mon pay beverage—thad is, " wet " 'em—thad is, gi' them summat to wet 'em wi' th' shape o' brass; but at th' finish up they gi' th' youngster coppers to buy toffy wi'. Ov coorse, pour boire may meean this, for aw dorn'd understand th' deead lang- widges. BRAWL (to bowl, a hoop). That's moore sensible, iv yo' like. CHEEK (impudence). Nowt o' t' soort. Ph' door- pooasts is co'd door-cheeks. See JOAIL forther on. CHARLEY (a corruption of Charles). Wrang agean. It's a hump on one's back. CADGE (to beg). Reight. CHUCKIES (hens). Factory lads dorn'd know at they're givin' utterance to a jooak as coom eawt o' th' Ark wi' Adam when they tawk abeawt tekkin' their lasses to see th' chuckles dance. It's abeawt time some new jooaks were invented. DUDS (Clothes). See wod aw say abeawt CLOOA.S. DRINK (Used as a noun as well as a verb). " Wod'll ta hey a gill o' cowd Drink on" meeans ayther beer or pooarther. DUCKSToOAN ( ). A game played bi' childer we stooans, an' iv there' nooan handy then wi' haif' bricks. "Dm" (Dividend).. "Everything comes to him as waits," said some wise mon or other, but aw think " diyis " is excepshuns to thad rule i' mooast cases. DRAKEN-HEN (The landrail). This is a brid. • FLARE-UP (a quarrel or disturbance). Ay, or a row, or a feight. GATE (way). Ged eawt o' mi gate meeans ged eawt o' mi way or rooad; an' tekkin' onybody a-gate is tekkin 'em on thi* way they're gooin.' -See AGATE, besides this. GOOIN'S-ON (proceedings). That's abeawt as n'ar as id con be put. IlAms (the berries of the hawthorn). Iv everybody as is so fond o' pooin' blossom—an chuckin' id away—wod nobbut think on as th' berries comes in handy for the brids durin' th' winter time when there's little else to eyt, they'd happen stop sich thowtless werk. JOAK (jamb, a support, pillar, or post). Ther'es door-joams, window joams, an' cornish joams. JOOAN (John). This is a Kristian name. JUD (George). An' sooa is this. JOLLOP (jalap). Yo' need no knocker-up, or %rum, to ged yo' up soon i' th' mornin' after tekkin' a penn'oth o' this fine oVvd slmmer beverage. POoRLY (sick; indisposed). There's two things wanted afoore a chap con fairly enjoy bein' poorly as he owt to enjoy id, an' them is (fostly) bein' on stannin' wage, an' (lastly) hevin' no pain or dangerous ailment. Under Lhese circumstances , mooast on us could stan' hein' poorly for two month ey'ry year—nay, 'appen as long as three month. SnaLIN (sinned). There's nooan so mich difference ;between us here.

WHAT PHOTOGRAPHY CAN DO.

M. Marey, who has been lecturing before the College of France, has showir that it is possible to photograph an insect's wing movements without blurring. The exposure in this case is not more than the 1-25,000t,h part of a second. He has even re- duced this period of exposure,and has photographed the blood globules flowing in a vein. An invention has been made at Georgetown Observatory, district of Columbia, called the photo-chronograph. The instrument causes a star to record the time of its own transit across the meridian, climb abating the risk of personal errors:
(Continued from last week.) THE WEATHER AND WORK ON THE FARM.

March Bth : The first thing I have to growl about is the weather of the past month. It was about the worst we have had for the year, and you will re- memner that it was in February last year that we had the flood. We have had some rain and frost, we have had snow and rain and frost, and the river has been up some ten or twelve feet, but not nearly so high as the flood, so that we have not been nerv- ous. The toads have been very muddy, and in fact nearly impassable, but are now drying up and almost dusty. We are busy just now getting our seed in. and I am very anxious to get through before the dry weather, as 1 do not want another poor season like last year. I have another man helping me to dig out large stumps.; everyone got out is one less, and it makes the land all the better. A SCHOOL MEETING.-OBJECTIONS OF A LEGAL

div.head: MUSICIAL MILLIONAIRES.
div.p: MUSICIAL MILLIONAIRES.

Many New York millionaires are adept performers on musical instruments. John D. Rockefeller is an enthusiast on the flute, and William Astor plays classical melodies on the piano and organ. Erastus Wiman, Creighton, Webb, and the Standard Oil magnate, Henry M. Flagler, prefer the organ. Fre- derick Vanderbilt finds charm in the banjo and Colonel De Lancey Kane is one of the best amateur cornet players in the country.

div.head: WONDERFUL-BICYCLE RIDE.
div.p: A WONDERFUL-BICYCLE RIDE.
160 MILES IN TWELVE HOURS.

H.E. Joly, of the Dublin Wanderers C.C. and the Irish Road Club, has succeeded in covering 160 miles in twelve hours, the previous record-133 miles—being held by B. Turney, Balbriggan C.C. Joly left the Leinster Arms Hotel, Maynooth, on Saturday, and rode via Edenderry, Clonbologue, Tullamere, to Clare, where he was turned by P. J. M'Grlyan, Wanderers C.C., repeating the same course. Reaching Maynooth-144i miles—at 7.40 p.m., he continued on to Straffan„Sallins, and Clare, finishing at Baberstown cross roads at 10 o'clock p.m., being ,checked by Delaney, National C.C. Joly is twenty-five years of age, weighs 13 stone, and is 5 feet 11 inches in height.

div.head: TILE LINCOLN MURDER.
div.p: TILE LINCOLN MURDER.

At the Lincoln. Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Jus- tice Vaughan Williams, Arthur Spencer, aged 22, pork butcher, was indicted for the murder of Mar?, Ann Garner, at Lincoln, on the 31st March. Mr. Lindsell, for the defence, asked the jury to return a verdict of manslaughter. He referred to the provocation the pri- soner had received, and said he did not seem to have shot ,the woman with intent to kill her.—His Lordship, in summing up, said it did not matter whether the prisoner committed this deed after long reflection., or whether he did it on the impulse of the moment; in the eye of the Law in either case it was wilful murder.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, and the Judge passed sentence of dekbh. The prisoner seemed very indifferent.

div.head: ORANGE CELEBRATIONS.
div.p: THE ORANGE CELEBRATIONS.

The 12th.of July Orange celebrations took place on Monday at a great number of centres throughout Ulster. Early in the morning a huge procession left Belfast for Ballyriienoch, ,five miles distant, where a meeting was held, presided over by the Rev. W. Kane. Resolutions were passed recording thankfulness for the improved state of the 'country, declaring unabated hostility to Home Rule, ,and expressing the determination to resist to the last extremity any attempt to substitute any other authority for that of the Imperial Parliament. A riot occurred at Keady, county Armagh, on Monday. On an Orange procession Passing that town, shots were fired and one man was wounded. His injuries, how- ever, are riot serious. On Monday afternoon the Orangemen of Liverpool and district demonstrated about 5,000 strong in Knows- ley Park, placed at their disposal by Lord Derby. They were erinveyed to the park by four special trains from Liverpool. At a meeting which was held Bro. Faram, Prov. Grand Master, presided. A vote of confidence in the Government was passed.

div.head: LUMINARY.
div.p: LUMINARY.

On last Monday the annual school meeting was held for the election of directors. We had two to elect this year, and we had five candidates. I can tell you there was some fun. The retiring director vacated the chair, and I had to take it. You have no idea how there old" Mossbacks "of farmers will haggle about a point of law. Just to show you: One old man was nominated for the office and had no opponent, and yet he declared he could not be elected unless he was balloted for, so to please him I asked some one else to propose another, and the second man ran him very close. However, I man- aged to keep them in a good humom, and when we were through some of them said they never had a more agreeable meeting. I guess we shall have about a thousand dollars to Spend on our school this year. We get so much per head from Government. Edith will teach some of the juniors this year if I can arrange it.
TOO -MANY SQUIRRELS AND RABBITS : A FAT GROUSE.

March 22nd: I canno*,-, help thinking what a change has come over my lite, and you would think so too if you could only just see us out here this evening. This morning I made a trip round the land with some poison, to poison squirrels and rabbits. I used to think they were pretty little things. but now I sincerely wish they were all poisoned. They are a perfect nuisance, eating up everything we plant out, both grain and vegetables. The boys, John and NI alter, took the colt over to pasture, and, having their guns with them, they shot a fine grouse. They are big fellows these grouse—quite as big as chickens. A DISAPPOINTING " EXAM" : NATURE'S RESUR- RECTION.

There has been a teachers' examination all along this State, and here at Salem the passes have been remarkably few. One only attained a " 8.A.," two a "first-class," and the next only "second class," or no certificate at all. There has been some bitter disappointment over it, I can tell you. We are having some splendid weather just now. Spring is just bursting on us; the trees are budding, and the swallows and blue birds are building round the house. It is resurrection again with all nature, We are just running our seed into the ground as fast as we can get the ground ready.

div.head: SWINDLING AGENT IN ARCADIA.
div.p: A SWINDLING AGENT IN ARCADIA.

April sth; Spring is on us, and it is grand. The strawberries are in flower, and in about three weeks, or about the time you get this, we shall be looking for berries, and we have lots of cream. Our cows give plenty of milk, and we sell ten or twelve pounds of butter in the week, besides what we use, so I guess we shall soon be having our "strawberries and cream." Of course they are sour' to you, but just come over once and try them ; I will undertake to find you all you can eat even though you can eat your way through a train load of them. Now there is a challenge for you. I was swindled a few weeks ago by an agent from San Francisco. He represented a club called the "Fidelity," and he told us all such a.lot of lies that he induced six of us to join. Finally a Scotchman at our works got down on him and made him return the entrance fees of five dollars, and had him arrested. The Sheriff let him out on bail, and he cleared out to California taking with him all our fees except those of the Scotchman who was too smart for him.

div.head: VALUE OF LAND.
div.p: THE VALUE OF LAND.

Since I last wrote to you the Oregon Land Com- pany have been asking if I will sell them ten acres of woodland to lay out in town lots. They have already sold some fourteen thousand dollars' worth of land half a mile below our place. If the lots they have sold are ever occupied, I can sell my land at 800 dollars per acre just as they have done. That will do a trifle better for me, and it will certainly come to that some day.

div.head: BEST TIME OF THE YEAR.
div.p: THE BEST TIME OF THE YEAR.

April 19th : How cruel about the weather! Why don't you live in a proper country where you can grow good weather? Since we left February behind we have had it beautiful. The fruit trees are the loveliest sights I ever saw—just one mass of bloom. If there is only one half the quantity of fruit that there is blossom there will be abundance. This, to my mind, is the finest time of the year. I lave to wander round the fields and orchards and watch everything grow. And, again, it is not too hot and the flies do not disturb one so much. You speak about the poets' make-believe about spring. I wish you could see it out here ; I guess you would believe it was spring, with the swallows and bluebirds bill- ing and cooing under the eaves. I tell you it is lovely.

div.head: GRIPPE.
div.p: LA GRIPPE.

If we could only stop at that! But alas, even here there is something. We have had that dread- ful la grippe here again, and it is far more deadly this time than last year. Every day they are tak- ing some one to the grave-yard on the hill side, carried off with that dreadful lull; fever. After all, .this is a hard place on lungs, and no sooner does la grippe lay hold of you than lung fever bets in and it is all up in a ft..V days. However, lam thank- ful to say, we have ail pulled through so far. I have had the "grip 'but I am better now.
HIGH PRICE OF GRAIN.-A PLEASANT ANTICIPATION.

We had finished our ploughing this last week, and the spring wheat is looking very good. I ex- pect a much better crop than last year. The result of last year's poor crop is being felt now in the price price of oats and horses' food. I sold ten bushels of oats at sixty cents per bushel, a fear- fully high price, as I have bought at twenty-five cents before now. I wish I had a thousand bushels to sell, but we have only about twenty to spare from my own horses' food. As far as ploughing is concerned, I have never yet had to do it. I can get a man for a dollar a day, and I can earn 3i dollars, so you see it does not pay me to do all the hard work. There has been one excursion up the stream, but we do not have time for cheap trips here: it is all rush. However, I have promised if I sell ten acres of land in town lots at the same rate land around here has been sold at, I may see Old Warrington again before another three years have gone. (To be continued.)

div.head: CRIME IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: CRIME IN CHESHIRE.

Colonel J. 11. Hamersley (Chief Constable of Cheshire) has issued his quarterly report of crime in the .co unty, which states that the total number of person s apprehended and summoned was 2,746, of whom 33 were committed for trial, 2,400 sum- marily ,convicted, and 313 discharged. In compari- son with the corresponding quarter of 1890 there is a decrease of 38 apprehended and 514 summoned, the former caused by fewer persons being appre- hended for drunkenness,and the latter by a decrease in the number of prosecutions under the Rabies (Muzzling of Dogs) Order. 1890. When compared with the same period of 1886 there was an increase of 282 apprehended and 528 summoned, the former arising from offences of drunkenness and persons sleeping out without visible means of subsistence, and the latter by proceedings under the Education Act, Highway Act, and Rabies (Muzzling of Dogs) Order. Seven hundred and forty males and 82 females were proceeded against for drunkenness, a decrease of '3O males and 43 females, or a total de- crease of 73 persons when compared with the May quarter, 1890. Comparing this with the correspond- ing quarter of 1886, there was an increase of 215 males and 11 females. Thirty-two licensed houses were proceeded against, 18 being convicted and 14 dismissed as against 28 proceeded against, 13 con- victed. and 15 dismissed in the May quarter, 1890; and 17 proceeded against, 11 convicted, and 6 dis- missed in the corresponding quarter of 1886. Dur- ing the year ended 31st March,1891,53,597 vagrants have been admitted to the IVorkhouses of the unions within the county, which gives a decrease of 5,196 as compared with the year 1890, and an increase of 12,218 over 1886.

div.head: LiETITIA THORNTON.
div.p: LiETITIA THORNTON.
BY LOUISA BIGG. 4.13T110R OF "CLARE WELSMAN," ETC.
CHAPTER IV.
Robert left the next morning, but before he went he had promised to come down again early in the new year.... . .

"We will try and get up some more skating," said lawtitia. "Parties you must not expect, but you may be asked out to tea as you have made witch a favourable impression." "Are there no parties here, then ?" asked Dillon laughing. "There are no balls, for we have only one young man in the place and he cannot dance." " Lretitia," cried Miss Priscy, "what nonsense. There are Dick Grayson, and the Bletsoes and the Tomsons."

"Oh, I call them boys," said Lmtitia. "There is Mr. Delatield," said Dillon, to see what she would say. "He does not care for parties; he amuses him- self sufficiently with philanthropy." "You are not fond of philanthropists, then?" "Oh, yes' I am; at least I am fond of Mr. Delafield. She is certainly heart-whole—in that direction at any rate, thought Robert. As her coysin he felt that he had a right to be inquisi- tive and interested in Laatitio.'s affairs.

The two ladies drove him to the station, and as they had some purchases to make, at the county town which lay midway between Hampton and London, they accompanied him for some miles on his journey. "I suppose you are going to be very busy in London said Miss Priscy on the way. "I expe3t I shall find plenty to do.' "What sort of things I wonder," Lmtitia. . .

"Weighty matters" of the law," he answered, enigmatically; "probably if I explained them to you, you would wither me with sarcasm and say that I was amusing myself.'" "I cant say till I hear what they are." , .. . . . .

The train slopped at their statiOn, so there was no time for any more talk, and with a hurried adieu they parted. . Miss Prisey and Lmtitia tramped from *shop to shop and did their business, and finally with a stock of parcels found themselves once more in the train. They were just sitting down for a solitary journey when the door was flung open, and a florid middle-aed lady and two daughters got in. They, too, had evidently been shopping and were full of their adventures.

"I declare we seem to know everybody," said the eldest girl, "to think of our meeting those Bartons, of all people." "Yes," said the mother, "I thought we should never get away from them." "It is such a bore to meet people when you want to shop, an d that woman ! ' said the younger girl, who had coarse thick lips, and a spiteful expression of countenance. "Did you hear her ask us to go over?"

"No, dear," answered her mother, "what did you say 2" "Oh, we had to be delighted ' " said the elder; "we could not get out of it." "I do not dislike Mrs. Barton at all," said the jovial mother, " they give capital dinners." "Well, I suppose we must go and listen to their prosisg," said the yr:linger girl, "but don't gush .to them too much, mother, if it's all the same to you:" _

The conversation went on in the same strain till the two got out of the carriage." " What dreadful women " said L.Ptitia,, "I cannot imagine why one's fellow-creatures were made so disagreeable. "Some are less disagreeable than others, my dear," said Miss Priscy. "But how few people's lives are worth anything," said Izetitio. ; "how stupid and greedy and selfish we all are. I wonder what Robert meant by what he said about being busy." ;" Writing for his paper, most likely," answered Miss Priscy ; "you know he has only the two hundred a year that your Uncle Thornton left him, and he evidently likes to have things nice about him, so it is necessary for him to earn something." "Is that all he meant ? " said Lvtitia with s melancholy, scornful face, and she looked silently at the passing landscape till they reached Hampton station.

div.head: Off AP'IIIR V.
div.p: Off AP'IIIR V.

oust at this time Mr. Delafield was throwing himself with persistent ardour into a new project which had occurred to him during the autumn. He had made up his mind to found a reading-room and coffee-house in Hampton, and had already acquired one of the most roomy cottages in the village, with a view to throwing it open at Christmas. At present it was undergoing extensive repairs, and bade fair to fully satisfy the expectations-of its owner. It was not a very large building, and the rooms were all low-pitched, but they were such as the inhabitants of Hampton were accustomed to, and were being decorated in a neat and artistic manner, the reading-room actually aspiring to a dado and blue-tinted walls.

The weather had been dry and open, and the alterations had gone on apace. The wh'ole affair, from the first rough plan down to the papering and painting, had been of absorbing interest to Mr. Delafield, and had made the early winter pass easily and pleasantly. It was now the first week in December, and the preparations for opening were nearly completed; fortunately there were no new walls to dry, the mason's work having consisted in the demolition of two old partitions, and•the carpenters had stuck to their work in a manner beyond all praise. The whole village was in a state of expectation with regard to "The Institute," as after many Internal arguments Mr. Delafield had decided that his new hobby should be called. Miss Priscy, who who was a great ally of his, often looked in, and so did other ladies of the village, but Lxtitia declined to be drawn into the excitement after.the first few weeks. _ _

•w "I wonder, my love, that you are not more interested about the Institute,' said Miss Priscy, after she had failed in persuading Lmtitia to accom- pany her on one of her frequent visits of inspection. "I am interested, cousin," answered Miss Thom-

div.head: ton.
div.p: ton.

"I do not think you are; I declare it seems to me quite unnatural when there is little going on in the village, that you should not want to see the alterations, and Mr. Delafield such a friend of ours. He looked quite hurt when you began laughing at it the other night." "But I have often heard you say how well people did without such things in your time." "Nevertheless, my dear, I think it is a very good thing for them to have such things now that there is so much drinking; and it is so good of Mr. Delafield to take all this trouble about it.
"The fact is, I should like the Institute a great deal better if there was not a general election coming off." _
"Bat what connection can there be between the two?" asked Miss Priscy, opening her mild blue eyes very wide. "I wish, my dear, you were not so fond of. politics; I can't understand what you mean."
Letitia did not vouchsafe any explanation, but sat looking into the fire. . . . . .
wai; beginning to recognise the fact that some day Mr. Delafield would ask her to be his wife, and she was doubtful and troub.ed. As she had told Robert Dillon, she was fond of Mr. Dela- field.

She had known him now for ten years, and he had always shown her kindness. His father and hers had been close friends, and when he succeeded to the family estate, he had also become trustee for her property in old Mr. Delafield's room. This had of necessity brought about a close intimacy, for as the other trustee lived in the North of Eng. land, he was the one upon whom she chiefly relied while a minor, and now to rely upon him had be- come a habit with her.

He was a good-looking, clear-headed man at five- and-forty, just the kind of man to make a good husband for her, only she did not want to marry him, and would have preferred his friendship to his love. She was angry with herself that it was so, and there were times when his standing in the world, his attention to herself, and a natural desire to settle her fate in life, made her strongly inclined to accept him, but she was always conscious that these were her lower moments, and that in them she sank to the level of those she most despised. After Miss Priscy, in her velvet mantle and grey bonnet trimmed with soft, curling feathers, had disappeared on her errand, LaAitia, again set her- self to seriously consider what she should do. "It may be," she argued, "that after all this is the path marked out for me; I may do wrong if I refuse the gifts laid at my feet." Then she tried to picture what her life with Mr. Delafield would be; how she must receive his company, and flatter his constituents, for he was ambitious of a seat for the county, and measure out the: hours in an unvarying round, and bring every thought into bondage to tbe-Landed interest;

she pictured it, and her whole soul revolted against it. Something, she scarcely knew what, held her bag: from entering that path; a vague aspiration after an imagined good higher and more subtle; a longing for some way, steep and thorny, perhaps, but where grew flowers of unutterable sweetness. It had been many times so with her; again and again she had bent her unruly will, and reasoned down ner transcendental longings, and, on a sud- den, a strain of music—a printed line—a painted canvass—had thrilled her like a trumpet call, and she had burst the bonds that were beginning to oppress her, and rejoined her invisible spiritual kindred. Had Mr. Delafield been unfortunate or poor, or in trouble, I think she would have married him, but he was rich and comfortable, and the luxurious smoothness of his life repelled her. Miss. Priscy returned in an hour's time in a con- siderable flurry and excitement of a pleasing character.

"What do you think, Ltetitia " she cried; "the Institute will be opened the Monday before Christ- mas day, and the new door is finished, and the cof- fee-room is papered. Mr. Delafield wants some of us to meet together and see about engaging a matron and buying the tea cloths and things. He was there when I went in, and I promised to invite the other ladies to go there on Thursday afternoon and consult as to what is wanted." "Who are the other ladies ?" asked Lmtitia.
"You, Sand Jessie Grayson, and Mrs. Grayson, and the Jenkinsons. You will come, won't you, dear ?"

"Oh, yes, if I can be of any use," said Izetitia, who was feeling weary with her inward struggle, and inclined to drift with the stream an see what might come of it. , "Jessie throws herself into the Institute with the greatest energy and is going to have a dozen dusters."
"Jessie ?" said LEctitia; laughing, " why she hates needlework; what has come over her ?'
CHAPTER. VT.

The Institute was gatisfactorily opened, and when Dillon came down to the Firs for a few days' visit according to his promise, a series of fortnightly entertainments was in prospect. . " We must have a few lectures," said Mr. Dela- field, who was lunching at the Firs the day after Dillon's arrival.
"Robert," said Miss Priscy, "you had better begin the series by relating your adventures at the seat of war."
"I am sure we should be very grateful to Mr. Dillon," said the founder of the Institute, rather stiffly.

Aii'd to Lmtitia's surprise, Dillon accepted the proposal, Saying- -" When should you want to have it? I have got nothing ready yet." "11 you could .give us the first week in March, we might begin with a couple of concerts,". said Mr. Deiaficld.

"My cousins will find me a regular bore, and rue' the day when the. let me come here first." " We will try and endure you," said Lwtitia, "jr you amuse us and make yourself useful. We shall consider the March visit a continuation of this."

"That will be a comfort to my mind; three visits per quarter is too muuh, but as you put it in that light, I will certainly come." They were all invited to spend the next evening at Mr. Grayson s at the vicarage, and when they arrived they found a considerable party invited to meet them. Jessie, in a black net dress, was nod- ding from one group to another and from time to time glancing anxiously towards the door. Her sister-in-law, Mrs. Grayson, was a young woman with light hair and pale eyes who always listened to your conversation with an arriere pensee to the nursery. She was usually pervaded by two or three children, especially in the morn- ing, and as they were allowed to roam the house at their own will there was not much peace to be found in it. Jessie, who was one of many sisters, lived at the vicarage for three parts of the year and was not very content with her lot, but being a good girl she made the best of it. Mr. Grayson, her brother, was as Miss Priscy had said, much absorbed in collections and parish machinery generally, and looked worn and driven, from the constant strain upon his energies. The dominant spirit of the household was Jessie, but her kingdom was too limited to suit her taste, and she was oppressed by an unreasonable longing for wealth and station.

"Jack," she said to her brother one day, "how I envy Letitia Thornton. Why are not we rich? I do not believe she cares whether she is or not, and I do, oh so much !" and she looked down discon- tentedly at her shabby morning dress. "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's goods," replied John Grayson, with his sweet tempered smile.

"Oh, no, I don't, only I wish that I had some like them. I cannot imagine why I want so to be rich, for we never had any chance of it, and yet I feel as if T was being kept out of my rihts. Is it not old, Jack ?"

"You mast try and be patient, little woman, and if it is good for you you will have riches," said poor Jack, with a sigh: He was none too rich himself, and at times found patience difficult. To-night no one would have guessed what longings and anxieties gnawed at Jessie's heart, and. she .greeted the different guests with her brightest smiles' her coolest reception being accorded to Mr. Delafield, who came rather later than the rest. or Delafield was an incarn- ation of all the good things she longed for; the prestige, the wealth, the power, and the grace that all these bring with them, and she had an irrepres- sible inclination to try to charm him and hated herself for it.

One young lady after another took her seat at the piano, and Mr. Tom Jedkinson patronised the entertainment so far as to sing a song about an individual who "always came home to tea." It was probably intended to be comic, but Mr. Jenkinson's manner of singing it, added to a went of point in the words, caused the company to listen to it with a serious attention embarrassing to the singer. He remarked to Miss Grayson afterwards, that it appeared to him that the inhabitants of Hampton had no sense of humour.
"Ladies never have," he added with a bland smile.
"Pardon me, Mr. Jenkinson, you are quite mis- taken," said Letitia, who was standing by, "We always know when anyone makes himself ridicu- lous."

After trying in vain to think of a suitable repar- tee he turned away and began talking to Mr. Gray- son, while Luatitia whispered to Jessie, "I am afraid I was very rude, dear, but he is such a conceited horror that I never know how to be civil to him!"

"Hit him hard, he has no friend here; shall we ask your cousin to sing ?" Miss Thornton signed to Dillon, and he crossed the room and joined them near the piano. "Will you sing something Robert? One of your German Folkslieder, please. "I believe I promised to be useful, to Tobey," he said, seating himself at the instrument; and striking a few bold chords he began a melody beloved of German soldiers, with his clear, full tenor. It was a description of the fatal march to Moscow, and told how the great army with its "viele lanwlert tausend Malan," young and beautiful, perished of cold and hunger. There was a roll of drums at the end of each verse, and the air kept time with the swing of a marching army. It brought to Lzetitia's mind a picture she had seen of the wastes of Russian snows, and the gaunt fail-. ing horses, and the men.,with death in their faces struggling hopelessly with the horrible wind and sleet ; she could fancy that she saw them fall out, one after another, to perish, and shuddered. "It is a lovely air," she said, "but how dread- ful ! "
"1 did not understand it," said Jessie," but I like it exceedingly ; it is so weird."

There was a general buzz of approval from the listening circle round the piano, and Dillon was obliged to sing several more songs, and was voted a decided acquisition. "If I were Mr. Delafield, I should not encourage that cousin of Miss Thornton's,' said the wife of a neighbouring curate to Mrs. Gray.ori ; "he is hardly a safe relation for a rich young lady." "Rut why should Mr. Delafield mind?" asked Mrs. Grayson; "I should have thought he would like to have her well married, as he has taken so much interest in her affairs."
"No doubt he would, but I imagine he thinks the best thing for her would be to marry her him- self."
"Do you really think so? It would he very suitable, but I did not know he intended it."
"Oh, my dear, it is town talk; everyone has settled that it will he a match."
"There is always so much gossip. You do not know what to believe."

" Well, you will see," said the curate's wife, oracularly. Soon after this conversation supper was an- nounced, and they all went into the dining-room, which Jessie had decorated very tastefully with green bunches from, the shrubbery. The old oal;

sideboard was wreathed with holly and laurel, the polished leaves shining and glistening in the fire- light, and from the picture frames drooped gar- lands of ivy. She was too busy at first taking care of her brother's guests to think of the final effect of her work, but presently Mr. Delafield began admiring it, and she flushed with pleasure in spite of her:3elf, and felt that she was rewarded for all her trouble.

"it does look pretty," she thought, "and, after all, being poor has its advantages; it teaches one to make the most of things. I daresa.y when lie gives a party he has a decorator down and. knows nothing about it all till it is done. I wonder if he ever could get as dirty and dusty as I do." And she glanced with pathetic amusement at Mr. Delafield's spotless linen, with the.plain diamond studs, and at his perfectly-fashioned black suit.

"What do you think Mrs. Stubbs told me last night, Jessie V cried Mrs. Grayson the next morn- ing, from the depth of a cupboard in which she was storing the extra glasses used last evening. "Some nonsense, I daresay," answered Jessie, handing up three tumblers and two wine-glasses with dexterous fingers, "she is a dreadful gossip.' "I know • but she says it is in everyone's mouth that Mr. Delafield is going to marry Lzetitia Thorn- ton."
Jessie was conscious of a sudden shock, as if a, cold hand had been laid upon her, but site angrily ignored it, and said coolly— "I do not know why he should not, they are very intimate."

The langour and weariness that follow excite- ment were upon her, and after that little conver- sation, the work of settling the house in order grew suddenly heavy and dreary. When she had done her tasks she went upstairs to dress for the early dinner, and sitting down at her white covered table she looked in the glass scornfully. "I ought to be ashamed of myself," she said, gazing at her own image with tears in her eyes; "it is dreadful that I should care anything at all about it; bad to care about the money, but a hundred times worse to care about the man. I did not know I did, and I cannot imagine how it hap- pened. I must work myself out of it." And after dinner she began the cure of her weary thoughts by tramping round among the most dis- agreeable of her brother's cottage 3. I imagine that a good deal of the willing drudgery of the world is done for some such reason as this of Jessie's, and there are worse ways of curing a sore heart. What a curious and pathetic history would be that of our good works; how many have for their mainspring some secret pain or hidden despair that stings sympathy into life, and makes inaction unbearable. (To be continued.)
TWO MEN WRONG----ONE MAN ItIGHT,.
".You will be in kingdons-conte in less than twelve months?" "You can't live three years!"
"You are not going to die!"

These three prophecies were addressed to the same man. The last one had the most comfort in it, yet he couldn't tell which had the most inspiration. Here's the story. It isn't pleasant reading at first,but. it "comes out" all right, as the children say. Perhaps it's better to let our friend tell it himself. We all like the pronoun" I," that's why an autobiography is never dull. This relator is a butcher of Auckland,. N.Z., and his style is so clear and good, it needs no- editing. He says: "Some five years ago, when lifting a quarter- of beef, I noticed a remarkable soreness in the small of my back. I called a doctor, gave up bdsiness, and took to my bed. He prescribed a lotion to be rubbed in arounwl the region of the kidneys. This was done,and I remained in bed several days,suffering excruciating agony. At last,. having examined the kidney secretions, the doctor said, You have Bright's disease, and will be in kingdom-come in less than twelve months.'

"Never believing I had Bright's disease, I thought, however, it would be as well to insure my life. On ex- amination, the company's physician refused to pass me for life insurance, saying, You can't live three years.' "About three months afterwards I was again seized with a severe attack, and went about more dead than alive. Finally I broke down and again took to my bed, as was supposed, for the last time. I sold one of my businesses so as not to leave too many affairs for my wife to supervise, made my will, and explained to my wife what to do in case of my death. I can well remember her listening with tears in her eyes to what she believed were my last instructions. I then lingered for some weeks, waiting for death to free me from my suffer- ings—taking whatever medicines were prescribed, but deriving little or no relief.
"One evening a friend called, and we talked over my case, and the very serious turn it had taken. Presently he said, 'You are not going to die. Have you tried Seigel's Syrup yet?'

1j coniess-edwthat I had not. In fact I had religiously followed the instructions of my medical advisers. My friend persuaded me to try Seigel's Syrup, and I began at once, taking twenty-drop doses according to the direc- tions. In about a week Heft a little more life in me, and after having finished ihe seccnd bottle I was convinced that improvement hac: fairly set in. I continued taking the Syrup until I had consumed ten bottles, then went downstairs to work again, still using the Syrup. After having taken from eighteen to twenty bottles altogether, Hound myself entirely well. It is now four years since I took my last dose of Mother Seigel's Syrup for Bright's disease of,the kidneys, and I have suffered no symptoms of kidney complaint since.
"(Signed) ROBERT HuTczaNsoN, Butcher

Wellington-Street, Auckland,New Zealand." We print Mr. Flutchinson's statement as he wrote it, yet it is not probable that his malady was actually Bright's disease, as that is a degeneration or destruction of the substance of the kidneys, and difficult, if not im- possible, to cure. What he really suffered from was, no doubt, a debilitated state of the system, originating in indigestion and dyspepsia, with severe kidney symptoms as is often the case. When we remember that nearly all maladies, including rheumatism, gout, consumption, liver complaint, heart disease, &c., are due to poisons in the blood, arising from fermented food in the digestive tract, we can see why Mother Seigel's Syrup is victorious over so great a variety of apparently diverse diseases. And because of the one source of these complaints, serious and often fatal mistakes are made in the diagnosis and in the treatment. The point to emphasise is this: Heart disease, consumption, and Brigut's disease are much rarer than they are supposed to be. Generally what seems like them is a group of symptoms of indigestion and dyspepsia. It is always best to take the advice of Mr. Hutchinson's friend when he said, " You are not going 0 die ; try Seigel's Syrup."

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. The Manchester Corporation Bill was read a second time. The Earl of Abermarle (Lord Bury) took the oath and his seat in succession. TIM FACTORIES Bitr...—On the motion to go into Com- mittee on the Factories and Workshops Bill, the Earl of DIINRAVEN protested against the superseding of the Government inspectors by the local governing bodies. Lord DE RAMSEY said it would be impossible for the Government to supply inspection on the scale demanded, and it was better that each local authority should be responsible for the supervision of the factories under its Jurisdiction. In Committee, a considerable number of amendments were proposed by Lord Thring, the Earl of Dunraven, and other peers; but the only one accepted !IY the Government was that proposed by Lord Derby Imposing a penalty not exceeding £lO upon employes Who, receiving particulars of their work from their em- ployers for their own information, made fraudulent use cf such information. The Bill passed through Commit- tee.
The House adjourned at 8.35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. MR. DR COBAIN.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, in the absence of the First Lord of the Treasury, stated that evidence had been procured of Mr. De Cobain's knowledge of the charges against him, and he moved that he be asked to appear in his place on July 23. The motion was agreed to unanimously. THE POST OFFICE AND ITS PENCILS.—It was admitted that the telegraph department of the Post Office is sup- plied with German-made pencils, and the reason given ZS, not that the foreign pencils are cheaper, but that they answer the purpose better. FOREIGN MARRIAGES.-In the absence of Sir James Fergusson, Mr. JACKSON brought in a Bill to amend and explain the Foreign Marriages Acts, which was read a third time. The House then went into Committee of Supply. Baron HENRY DE WORMS had to reply to charges and accusations in regard to Newfoundland, South Africa in general, and Zululand, Natal, &c. MISCELLANEOUS.—Subsequently the Fisheries Bill Passed through Committee. The Highways and Bridges Bill was read a third time. The Statutory Rules Proce- dure (re-committed) Bill passed through Committee. The Betting and Loans (Infants) Bill was considered in Com- mittee, but was opposed by Mr. E. Robertson, on whose Motion progress was reported. The House adjourned at 12.25. HOUSE OF LORDS---TursnAv. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past five o'clock. THE IRISH LAND BILL, &c.—On the motion for the third reading of the Purchase of band and Congested Districts Ireland Bill, Earl SPENCER expressed satisfac- tion that the Government had passed such.a measure, though he objected to its extreme complication. Earl Forteseue congratulated the Government, and the bill Was read a third time. The report of amendments to the Brine Pumping (Compensation for Subsidence) Bill Was received, and the Earl of Belmore reported that the joint committee of both Houses on railway bill were of Opinion that the London and North-Western Bill should be allowed to proceed. Their lordships rose at five minutes to seven o'clock.

div.head: HOUt.:3E OF COMMONS.--TuEsney.
div.p: HOUt.:3E OF COMMONS.--TuEsney.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QuEsTioNs.—Mr. CHAPLIN said he did not expect to pass this session the bill dealing with the adulteration of artificial manures and feeding stuffs, but probably the Criticisms it had called forth would facilitate its passing next session. The Attorney-General informed Dr. Tanner that the police had been directed to ascertain Whether the evidence against the person who had warned Mr. De Cobain was sufficient to justify a prosecution.— Mr. STANHOPE, in answer to Mr. Rentoul and Mr. Byron Reed, said the Commander-in-Chief had given orders that an Orange Lodge which had been formed in a regiment should be dissolved, as a contravention of the Queen's Regulations. Mr. 'GOSCHEN, answering Mr. Lees, said the trustees and directors of the National Gallery were of opinion that it would not be expedient to give any general sanction to the periodical exchange Of pictures lent by them to provincial institutions. Mr. GOSCHEN informed Major Basch that the bill for the regulation of the cattle trade, would not be proceeded With this session, but the President of the Board of Agriculture proposed to draw up rules and regula- tions. SUPPLY.—In Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, Dr. TANNER made some strong allegations as to the sanitary defects of the Liverpool steamers Celtic and Servia, but Sir M. HICKS BEACH replied that Dr. Tanner had delivered the same speech last year, and that nothing had been found to justify his statements. Progress was reported at twelve o'clock. The Fisheries Bill was read a third time and past. The Cathedral Churches Bill was withdrawn. The house adjourned at five minutes past twelve eclock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. , CIVIL SERVICE ESTIMATES.—The House again went into Committee of Supply, and the Civil Service Esti- mates were once more taken up, and Sir J. Swin- borne and Mr. Cobb criticised the proceedings of the Charity Commissioners of England and Wales. The vote was ultimatOy agreed to, as was also that of £26,411 for the Civil Service Commissioners, after some criticism by Sir G. Campbell, Mr. Roby, and Mr. Summers. On the vote of £111,704 for the Local Government Board, Mr. SAMUEL SMITH Warmly advocated an extension of the scheme for the emigration of pauper children to Canada, and in the Course of his remarks asserted that in some cases the emigration of workhouse children was opposed because the contractors and officials who were interested in keeping up the establishments were personal friends of the Guardians. Mr. RrrcuiE agreed with Mr. Smith as to the value of emigration but deprecated his remarks as to Guardians and their friends. The vote was agreed to. Mr. RITCHIE, replying to Mr. Thomas Ellis, said the decision to refuse Corwen a local board would be re- viewed if the sanitary administration did not improve. Leave was given to Mr. A. Thomas to introduce a bill to _al:Point a Secretary for Wales, to constitute a Welsh Education Department, to introduce further provisions for local government, and to create a National Council for Wales. The House adjourned at 6 o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MITESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. The EARL of DERBY reported from the Select Committee on the Children's Life Assurance Bill that in their opinion, it 'was not expedient to proceed further with the measure this session: THE ELEMENTARY EDUCATION BILL.---Lord CRINBROGY Moved the second reading of the Education Bill, and in the course of his remarks, dealing with the reports cur- rent that the bill was that of Mr. Chamberlain, said Mr. Chamberlain so far, as he was aware, never saw it until it was introduced in the House of Commons. The Government had had their attention called to the vast rise in the rate for education in various 1 Places, and it was their intention to consider the ques- tion next year with a view to the mitigation of the bur- den. Earl Spencer thought the passing of the bill would Probably lead to the increase of a million children in average attendance. The Archbishop of Canterbury looked upon the various provisions of the bill as well considered. The Duke of Argyll believed it was a good thing to maintain the responsibility of parents for the education of their children. After some remarks from the Bishop of London and the Marquis of Ripon, the bill was read a second time. The Penal Servitude Bill passed through committee, and the Brine Pumping and Compensation for Subsi- denre Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at five minutes to eight o'clook. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THEMSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. JACKSON, replying to Mr. Cross, said arrangements had been made for acquiring a site for the new Liverpool Post Office in Victoria-st. Mr. RAixv.s Informed Mr. Barclay that power should be given to the local authorities to give guarantees for the extension of the telegraph service. Mr. MAT- TaEws, replying to Mr. Mundella, said he would take an early opportunity of conferring with the Educa- tion Department as to the raising of the standard for • full timers under the -Factories and Workshops Act of 1878. Sir :TAMES FERGUSSON informed Sir G. Campbell that the importation of spirits on the West Coast of Africa would be regulated by • the Brussels Act When ratified. Other questions were in reference to Preserving the ancient monuments of Egypt, an „.alleged scheme for constructing a dam across the oile at the top of the first cataract, the order °f Public business and trade disputes. Mr. Chaplin informed Mr. T. E. Ellis that in 1880-91 ?1,840 was expended in grants for agricultural educa- tion, of which £5OO was awarded to the University Col- lege of North Wales at Bangor, the highest sum awarded .?.sy the board to any institution in Great Britain. Mr. .11a almond took the oath and his seat for County Carlow. SUPPLY -...The House went into Committee of Supply c?u the Civil Service Estimates, and Dr. Tanner arguing 4tom the large number of suicides and 'injuries in luna- tic asylums thought they pointed to insufficient care. ;82 discussion afterwards took place regarding alleged u-rezularities in the taking of the Welsh census. _ Afterwards a motion to report progress was agreed to, and the House adjourned at one o'clock.
AN EXCURSION TRAIN WRECKED.
7 PERSONS KILLED

A Central News telegram from New York on Sunday night states :—A disastrous collision occurred to-night on the Midland Colorado Line at Aspen, Colorado. An excursion train was run into by a detached locomotive, seven passengers in the former being killed and six injured.

div.head: EMPEROR'S DEPARTURE.
div.p: THE EMPEROR'S DEPARTURE.

The German Emperor and Empress and the Prince and Princess of Wales concluded their visit to Lord Salis- bury at Hatfield on Wednesday afternoon, and their Im- perial Majesties subsequently went to Windsor to take farewell of the Queen. On their return to London the Empress at once left by special train for Felixstowe, on the Suffolk coast, where her children are staying. On uesday morning the German Emperor arrived at Leith, and embarked on board the Imperial yacht, which, after passing under the Forth Bridge so as to afford His Majesty and his attendants an opportunity of viewing the magnificent structure, proceeded to Nor- way.

div.head: WISBECH ELECTION.
div.p: THE WISBECH ELECTION.

Thr contest in the Wisbech division is now in full swing, and will be one of the shortest on record. It was only Thursday week that it was announced that Captain Selwyn's ill-health had compelled him to resign his seat, and already the polling is fixed for Thursday next. Al- though the Liberals have long been preparing for the contest—the Hon. Arthur Brand having for two years actively canvassed the constituency—their advantage over the Conservatives is more apparent than real, for the latter, although now suffering the disad-1 vantage of having an unknown candidate, had been able secretly to mobilize their forces. Mr. Surr William Duncan, of Horsforth Hall, near Leeds, is the Conserva- tive candidate, and addressed two meetings on the day the vacancy was made known.
LORD SALISBURY AT ST. JAMES'S HALL.

Lord Salisbury. speaking at the United Club dinner at St. James's Hall, on Wednesday night, said he could not tell when the general election would be. All he knew was that the Septennial Act would come into operation in August, 1893. He would not deal with political meteorology, but he had no fear. They must defend to the utmost the established churches of the country. The question of disestablishment in Wales was being agitated, but he considered that the final attack on the English Church was more remote now than it was five years ago. It was proposed to deal with the electorate. Again the cry of one man one vote was being raised. He considered that unfair, because it would interfere with the oldest franchise in the country. The Conservative party had no reason to fear the result. He noted that agrarian speculation in Ireland had given way to cleri- cal conspiracy. In the course of further remarks, Lord Salisbury dealt with female suffrage, and several items of the Tory programme.
nHESHIRE REGISTERED ELECTORS.

From a return issued on Thursday, giving the number of electors on-the register in ,every Parlia- mentary constituency in the United Kingdom, the following is the return for the Chester County Divi- sion : Wirral Division 11,709 Eddisbury „ Macclesfield ~

INTERNATIONAL -CONU REGA.TIONAL
COUNCIL.

A number of American and Colonial delegates to the International Congregational Council were on Monday entertained at breakfast by the Liberation Society. Mr. Alfred Illingworth, M.P., who presided, said the Liberal party was pledged to the dises- tablishment of the Scotch and Welsh Churches, and when that had been accomplished the Church of England would be attacked on all sides. On Tuesday Dr. Dale presided, and delivered an address on "The Divine Life in Man." The repre- sentatives of various bodies were then received, including the Presbyterian Church of England, Baptist Churches, Free Church of Scotland, United. Presbyterian Church, Wesleyan Methodist, Primi- tive Methodist, Calvinistic Methodist, Bible Chris- tians, Methodist New Connexion, and others. At the afternoon meeting the Rev. H. Arnold Thomas read a paper urging the obligation of personal ser- vice in Christian work. The Rev. A. E. Dunning, of Boston, read a paper on the training and service of the young, and the Rev. R. F. Horton a paper on guilds. The Rev. Nehemiah Boynton, of Boston (Massachusetts), read a paper describing the Society of Christian Endeavour. -

_ On Wednesday the subject for discussion was the present direction of theological thought. In the afternoon the economy of Congregationalism was the subject for discussion. The Rev. Thomas Green, Ashton-under-Lyne, read a paper on doctrinal papers in trust deeds.

VIADUCT INSTITUTE BOWLING CLUB V. IiIsIOTTY ASII VILLAGE.—The return match between these clubs was played at Earlestown on Saturday afternoon. The green was in splendid condition, and the home club completely outplayed the visitors, finally winning by 117 points. After the match the players adjourned to the Viaduct Inn, where a capital tea was partaken of and thoroughly en- joyed. A convivial evening was afterwards spent. RIFLF MEETIgiI AT BISLEY. The National Rifle Association's annual meeting was opened at Bisley, on Monday. In the Alexandra com- petition, at 500 and 600 yards, Colour-Sergeant Orr, of the Argyle and Sutherland Highlanders, was first with a best 66 points; while Sapper Bratherton, 2nd Cheshire Engineers, and Private Robb, Queen's Edinburgh, were second and third with a like number of points. The Humphrey Cup, shot for by teams from the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge, with small-bore rifles at the three long ranges' was won by Cambridge with 791 points, against 723; and in a match under similar con- ditions a team of Volunteer officers beat a team of Regu- lar officers by 1,661 points, against 1.620. The chief event on Tuesday was 'the opening of the competition for the Queen's Prize. The day was bright, but a shifty wind affected the shooting, and the average scoring was lower than that of last year. No highest possible was reached, but Private Moore, Ist V.B. Somer- set Light Infantry, put oh 34. Scores of 33 were made by Sergeant Young, Ist V.8.H.L.1., Private W. H. Trask, H.A.C., Sergeant Todhunter, 4th East Surrey, and Ser- geant Barrett, 2nd Norfolk. , On Wednesday theshooting at the Five Hundred Yards Range in the first stage of the Queen's was begun and completed. Aggregates of 64 points were reached by Private Gawatkin, 3rd Welsh ; Private C. F. Green, 2nd Gloucester ; Sergeant H. Gibbons, sth Middlesex; Ser- geant Redpath. Ist Northumberland Fusiliers; Sergeant Barratt, 2nd Norfolk ; and Corporal Roscamp, 2nd Nor- thumberland. The average is thus lower than last year when there were several highest aggregates. Sergeant Larway, 2nd Gloucester Engineers, was declared the winner of the" Daily Graphic" Cup. On Thursday the first stage of the Queen's Prize was completed with firing at 600 yards. A changing wind at the ranges proved disastrous to many well-known marksmen, and consequently the average scoring was low compared with last year. Corporal Pape, Ist V.B. Border Regiment took the bronze medal with an aggre- gate of 93. There were three aggregates of 92 and five of 91. The makers of 82 will compete for the silver medal to-day (Saturday), with theexception of Private Gaudin, 2nd Jersey Militia, and Lieutenant Glen, sth V.B. Scots Regiment, who are counted out.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. ALGERNON EGERTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. ALGERNON EGERTON.

The death of the Hon. Algernon Fulke Egerton,of the Old Hall, Worsley, took place at Be'grave- place, London, on Tuesday night, following on a paralytic seizure ten days ago. Mr. Egerton, who was a son of the first Earl of Ellesmere, was born in 1825, and educated at Harrow and Christ Church. Oxford, where he took the degree of D.C.L. in 1853. In 1863 he married Alice Louisa, eldest daughter of the late Lord Geo. Cavendish,M.P.,and cousin to the Marquis of Hartington. He leaves six daughters and one son, who is at present at a military school near London. The late Mr. Egerton was a justice of the peace, and deputy lieutenant of Lancashire, honorary 'colonel of the 4th Volunteer Battalion Manchester Regiment, and formerly honorary colonel of the Duke of Lancaster's Own Yeo- manry Cavalry. He had a long experience of political life, first entering Parliament as a Con- servative representative of South Lancashire in 1859. On the constitnency being split up Mr. Egerton was returned for the South-eastern divi- sion. Again, at the election of 1874, Mr. Egerton was once more returned at the head of the poll. This seat he retainel up to 1880, but at the election in that year Mr. Robert Leake and Mr. William Agnew were returned in the place of Messrs. Eger- ton and Hardcastle. For two years afterwards Mr. Egerton did not seek to obtain a seat in Parliament, hut in December, 1882, on the occasion of Mr. F. S. Powell being unseated as member fol. Wigan, the Conservatives of the borough invited Mr. Egerton to become their candidate. He aid so on the under- standing that he should be relieved from parlia- mentary duty at the next general election,and,after a contest with Mr. Walter Wren,he was returned by a majority 0f.624 votes. He continued to represent Wigan until 1885, and although pressed to become candidate at the general election in that year he declined to do so. On the death, in October, 1890, of the Hon. Alfred Egerton, his nephew, who repre- sented Eccles, the Hon. Algernon Egerton contested the seat against Mr. Roby. but the latter was elected.

div.head: TERRIBLE MURDERS IN TEXAS.
div.p: TERRIBLE MURDERS IN TEXAS.

NEW ORLEiNS, WEDNESDAY.—The "Picayune" gives an account of a terrible case of murder by robbers at Joshua, Texas. The men went to the home of a man darned George Newbeary, situated near that town, and demanded admittance. Newberry's mother, 65 years of age, thinking it was her son who had returned, opened the door to the men, who demanded money. They were told there was none in the house, whereupon they took the woman outside, tied her to a post, and inflicted a terrible gash upon her throat. One of the ruffians then entered the house, awakened a child seven years old who was in bed, and asked where her father's money was. As the child refused to tell, she was taken into the yard, where her throat was cut. Another little girl of five and a baby boy of two were killed in a similar manner. The woman, although much injured. is still alive, and was able to give an.account of the affair.

div.head: CENSUS RETURNS.
div.p: THE CENSUS RETURNS.
LOCAL POPULATIONS
We are enabled to furnish the totals of the population, &c., for 1891, showing the increase or decrease since 1881, of the following towns : _ _ _ _
Inhabited Popula- houses. tion.

There has been a remarkable increase in the popula- tion of St. Helens. There has been a large growth, too, at Warrington during the last ten years, for whilst in 1881 the total was 42,552, in 1891 it is 52,742, being as many as 10,190 more. This is as much as a fourth of what was the total population in the first of those years. This growth was, however, a little less than what it was n 1871-81. for then it was 10,408. Thus in the last 20 years the increase was as much, 20,600. Runcorn has also very greatly developed. In 1881 the inhabitants numbered 12,443, but in 1881 the total was 15,126, the increase being 2,633. In 1881-91 it was as much as 4,924—the number in the last year being placed at 20,050.

div.head: TOTAL POPULATION OF THE COUNTRY.
div.p: TOTAL POPULATION OF THE COUNTRY.

The figures of the recent census have now keen re- vised, and it appears that the total number of persons I returned as living in England and Wales at midnight on tne sth April was 29,001,018. This shows an increase during the preceding ten years of 3,026,572, or 11.65 per cent. This is a less per centage than that disclosed by any census since the first enumeration in 1801. The actual number added to the population during the last ten years is, moreover, not only proportionately less,but is absolutely less than the addition during the previous decade, which, considering the difference between the initial figures of the two periods, reveals a remarkable arrestment ol the previous national increase. While the population has increased 115 per cent., the number of inhabited houses has increased no less than 12.5, pointing apparently to an increase of material comfort amongst the people. The total number of inhabited houses returned in the present census is 5,452,802. The average number of occupants to each inhabited house was 532 in 1891, 538 in 1881, and 5.33 in 1871. There are 62 towns with more than 50,000 inhabit- ants. They are :-London, which is returned at 4,211,056, as against 3,815,544 ten years ago,sho wing an increase per cent. of 10.4. Liverpool comes next, with the only decrease, from 552,508 persons ten years ago to 517,951. The rest of the 60 all show an increase more or less substantial.
