div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
DOUBLE COLLAPSE OF EMBANKMENT AT ELLESMERE.
OPENING OF EASTHAM SECTION DELAYED
TILL THURSDAY.

Owing to the collapse of the embankment at Elles- mere Port the interesting event fixed by the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company to take place on Monday—the opening of that section of the canal extend- ing from Eastham to Ellesmere Port—had to be post- poned. There is always a great rush of water at high tide through the" gap," as the opening into the wide basin forming the Port of Ellesmere is called. The engineer- ing staff of the Ship Canal Company brought all their strength to bear at the ebb of the tide on Saturday with, the view of filling up a gap and forming a hugeembank- ment to prevent the water from breaking through. They had only about eight hours in which to do this work, but it was confidently believed that it would be satis- factorily accomplished in that time. Had such been the case a line of 1-4 oats belonging to the Shropshire' Union Canal Company would have passed through the canal for the first time on Monday instead cf proceeding through the usual course into the Mersey. Unhappily the forces of nature were too powerful for the officials ; rather should it be said that the engineers had taken upon themselves a task too heavy to be carried out effectually in the time they had at their disposal. It was of course desirable to keep the " gap " open as long as possible in order not to interfere with the Shropshire Union traffic, for under their Act, the Ship Canal Company would be liable to a penalty of £4OO a day so long as the traffic was delayed. The " gap " was filled up with all expedition, and a huge embankment was formed which looked like resist- ing any Pressure on the part of the tide. But the engineers were still rather apprehensive as to the result. About four o'clock on Sunday morning, to the deep regret of all beholders the tide forced down a portion of the embankment, and in spite of the efforts made to repair the breach it gradually extended, and finally the hundreds of thousands of tons of earth which had been piled up were swept away, and the" gap" resumed its normal condition. THE SECOND COLLAPSE.

When the tide receded the engineers set to work again, and another embankment was constructed on Sunday afternoon. Again the work proved fruitless. At half- past one o'clock on Monday morning the tide, in its ever-increasing volume,beat uptmthe mass of earth with a force that was irresistible, and, an opening once made in the embankment, it gradually widened, until the whole of the works were washed away, or nearly so. It was then determined by the engineers to fill up the gap in layers of material at low tide, and to carry out the work gradually. That science will triumph in the end goes without saying.

div.head: DIRECTORS AND GUESTS AT EASTHAM.
div.p: DIRECTORS AND GUESTS AT EASTHAM.

In anticipation of the opening of the section—which. by the way, is three miles in length—some thousands of persons visited Eastham and Ellesmere Port on Monday. The weather was glolionsly fine. The majority of the directors and a few friends proceeded by special steamer from the Prince's Landing Stage at one o'clock to East- ham. It had been arranged that a tug should take a number of trade boats from Eastham to Ellesmere Port at high tide, but, as already stated, this could not be done. Thousands of sightseers collected round the huge locks opening into the canal, and on the high bank on the Cheshire side of the works. In one of the locks was the splendid pleasure yacht Norseman, belonging to Mr. S. R. Platt,of Oldham,which had been placed at the disposal of the directors and their chief officials and friends. She was dressed rainbow fashion, a streamer of flags of various bright colours extending from the boom over the main topmast and down to the jib-boom end. Very bright, graceful. and picturesque did she look; and the crew presented a smart appearance in their white uniforms. In the main lock the tug-Fanny, also gay with flags and bunting, was stationed in readiness to take privileged persons down the canal. At three o'clock the directors and their friends went on board the Norseman, and amid ringing cheers from the spectators they started on their first trip along the canal. Amongst those on board were Sir J. C. Lee, deputy-chairman of the board of directors; Mr. C. .T. Galloway, Mr. J. K. Bythell, Mr. S. R. Platt, the Mayor of Manchester (Alder- man J. Mark), the Mayor of &Ilford, the Mayor of Oldham, Councillor W. H. Bailey, (Salford), Sir E. Jenkinson, Mr. W. J. Crossley, Mr. Saxon (solicitor), Mr. J. Leigh (Stockport),Mr. W. H. Talbot (Town Clerk of Manchester), Captain Pearson (assessor of the Liver- pool Court of Passage), Mr. Abernethy (consulting en- gineer), Mr. H. Boddington, Mr. Leader Williams (chief engineer); Mr. W. H. Topham (works managerN, Mr. J. H. Manisty, Mr. W. A. Mathison, Mr. W. Elliott (resid- ent engineer), Mr. A. H. Whitworth (secretary). Mr. Marshall Stevens, Mr. J. Price, Mr. C, J. Wills, Mr. T. J. Reeves, Mr. J. Hales (general manager of the Shrop- shire Union), Mr. J. Platt, Mr. Fitz Gibbon, Mr. W. H. Collier, Mr. W. Grundy, and Mr. Potts. At intervals along the course of the canal the navvies engaged upon the banks gave hearty cheers, and waved their hats and handkerchiefs, as the Norseman passed on its way to the Ellesmere Port end of the section. arrived there the visitors were greeted with loud cheers by the crowd up- on the bank, and they had a view of the " gap " which had caused so much trouble and annoyance. The Norse- man' which is 168! t. long over all, was swung round with the greatest ease,and in the course of a few minutes she started on the return journey.

div.head: BRIDGIG THEE GAP.
div.p: BRIDGIG THEE GAP.

The chief topic of conversation on board the Norse- man was the two successive breaches made in the wall bridging the gap. It was said that in many instances undertakings of that kind had been attempted, but very rarely had they been successful. The engineers of the Ship Canal never for a moment relished the idea of " dumping " down sand and clay to stop up the great rush of water at the Ellesmere gap, but they were com- pelled against their better judgment to attempt it as the , only alternative in the circumstances. Loud complaint was made of the stringency of the Act of Parliament, and the galling restrictions with which the promoters were,hampered in every way. A high official stated that the amount of debris which had, been swept away from the embankment was overstated. According to his ver- sion, the gap at Ellesmere Port, which is the only en- trancl from the Mersey to the port. was 300 feet wide. It was estimated that 5,000 cubic yards of excavation would be necessary to fill up the open space. Of this quantity 3,500 cubic yards were put in on Saturday afternoon, and of these 1,500 cubic yards were carried away, leaving 2,500 yards remaining. On Sunday 3,000 more cubic yards were put in,of which 2,500 yards gave way. All the debris was washed into Ellesmere Pool,and none of it into the estuary. It was also stated that at Barry, in South Wales, similar attempts had been made to stop the tidal water, but they were fruitless, and had to be given up, after several trials, in favour of another mode of procedure. THE GAP CLOSED. TRAFFIC ON THE EASTHAM SECTION.

The Eastham section of the Ship Canal was on Thurs- day night opened for traffic. There was no prepared de- monstration in honour of the event, which, however,was not allowed to pass without some recognition. On Wed- nesday the Mersey " gap " at Ellesmere Port had I:een successfully closed. The early part of Thursday was spent in strengtheeing:the bank, no less than three hun- dred waggon loads of clay adding to its stability. At 11 o'clock in the morning the work was begun of removing the barrier of earth which separated the two now com- pleted portions of the Eastham section. This was no light task, and could not be completely effected till the evening tide, entering through the gateway at Eastham, reached its full height. Then it was, at twenty-five minutes past seven, that the small but powerful tug called the Rocket steamed through the opening which the dredgers had made andovith its trailof seven barges, made its way to Eastham. It was rather a happy thing that a boat with a name so historically associated with commerce between Manchester and Liverpool should have have had this distinction. It was not, however, a thing which was premeditated, and indeed there was just a suggestion of sharp practice on the part of the skipper. The steamer Fanny, a handsome I little pleasure boat, had sailed up from Eastham with the special design of taking a select company on board, and it was the Fanny which was to have been first in passing through the opening in the elem. The favou red passengers had got aboard her, and the experimental cruise was just about to begin, when the Rocket was seen to bend round the steam dredger Barry and to dart towards the gap. Having such a formidable tail, it was impossible to check the progress of the little craft. The Rocket went on its triumphant way. As the procession safely cleared the point of difficulty, about a thousand people, who had lined the banks of the canal in expecta- tion of the event, gave a very cordial cheer. Mr. Leader Williams, the chief engineer of the canal, was on board the dredger Manchester during these few critical ' moments, and with his colleagues, Mr. Price, Mr. Man- isty, Mr. A. H. Whitworth (secretary), and others, re- ceived cordial congratulations. Ihe whole scene was very interesting. On the high banks of the canal the peoplestretched away in a long thin line. Within the Ellesmere Port embayment—the wide upper portion of the section which till the last few days was open to the • Mersey—there were about twenty coasters and barges,all of them flying colours. In another direction there was a more unique display, for on the top of the Ship'Canal mountain ran a long line of streamers which could be seen miles away. After the Rocket had sped on its way down the canal towards Eastham a considerable num- ber of other boats took the same course. One of these was the Ellesmere Port "packet," which had not missed a tide for fifty years till the Ship Canal makers suffered their disappointment on Monday last. The work of clearing the dam on liOtursday occupied, owing to one or two accidents of a minor sort, !ether more time than was calculated. Mr. Leader Williams gave the word to begin work at eleven o'clock. One of the most formidable pieces of work was the uprooting of some heavy timbers which had been driven firmly into the bed of the canal, and which were the chief bulwarks of the damn. By seven o'clock at night the timber had been so undermined that their removal became an easier matter. They were the very last obstacles to be overcome.

div.head: WEAVER SECTION.
div.p: THE WEAVER SECTION.

The chief attention of th engine,rs will now be centred on the Weaver portion. This is practically complete at ready, and the important matter is to connect it with the Eastliam section, so making a complete length of about ten miles, or nearly a third of the entire waterway. It is expected that a month will be sufficient time in which to carry out the work. There are no troublesome "gaps "in the estuary to be contended with, simply be- cause there is no important place of traffic like Ellesmere Port. In order to flood the six miles from the Port to the mouth of the Weaver a series of 4ft. pipes will be run through the earth which at the end of the embayment separates the two lower sections of the canal. By a gradual process, coverlna, some five days, the full depth of water will be obtained. Already it should be said, the greater portion of the section is under water to the depth of five or six feet. What then remains to be done is• simply the clearance of the dividing bank of 'earth. A demonstration of some dignity will be held when the first salt boats make their entrance from the Weaver Naviga- tion into the canal.

div.head: A. BRIEF MARRIED EXPERIENCE AT
div.p: A. BRIEF MARRIED EXPERIENCE AT
RUNCORN.
AN ILL-ASSORTED PAIR.

David Foster,,a labourer on the Ship Canal, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting his wife, Mary Jane. Mr. E. W. Humphreys appeared for the complainant, and said both parties were 22 years of age, and had only been married eight weeks. He should desire to give the devil his due, and he was bound to say that for fourteen whole days the de- fendant behaved somewhat as a civilized and rational human being. After that he appeared to have got it into his head that his wife was a ct.attel to do what he liked with. He proceeded periodically to inflict castigation upon her. If the Bench believed the woman's story there was no justification and no provo- cation for the assault, and he (Mr. Humphreys) should ask the Bench to relieve her of the responsibility of liv- ing with hirn. A fortniOit after they were married the defendant struck his wife on the face with his fist, and almost knocked her into the fire. On the following Sunday he took out his knife, opened it, and threatened to cut her throat and his own afterwards. On an aver- age of twice a week since he had abused her and thrashed her. On Saturday night, the 4th inst, the defendant was led home from his work blind drunk, by his brother. The defendant made a disgusting exhibition of himself and vomited all over the place. His wife remonstrated with him, whereupon he struck her several times with his fist, knocking her to the floor, and while she was lying there he kicked her several times, making her "black and blue." Although the brother-in-law, and ' sister and two others were in the room they did not raise a finger to prevent the defendant thrashing his wife. The defendant went out and did not return until Sunday morning, when he said he, had lost his money, and as there had been no provisions obtained on Saturday, there was only a little bread and butter to eat during the day. There were a few flukes, but these the defendant had eaten. On the next morning the poor woman had to send to her father's house for food to sustain her, and in the evening the defendant assaulted her again, strik- ing her on the faze twice. Next morning he told her to get a good breakfast, as he was not going to keep her any longer.—The complainant corroborated this state- ment. and Henry Aspic', of Parker-st., her father, and her mother spoke to seeing the assault on Monday night from the roadway.—The defendant said he had a " sap " of drink on Saturday night, but he had his senses. He lay on the sofa and she started scandalizing, him, threatened to smash his face with a poker, and as she would not be quiet, he " shoved " her clown with his hand. She got up, picked up a fire iron, but his brother-in-law stepped in between them and prevented her striking him. He just gave her one " clout " with his open hand on the face. He then put on his hat and walked home to hi S mother's. He denied that he had threatened to cut her throat. On the Monday he knocked her down nicely on the sofa, but did not hit her. He was in danger of his life from her people, who "put on him" something scandalous. He would live with her if she would only behave herself.—Samuel Wor- rall, brother-in-law to defendant, in whose house the couple lived, said the defendant only gave her boo blow across the shoulder, and the defendant's brother, Joseph Foster, made a similar statement.—Mr. Brun.drit said he was sorry to see such a case brought before them. That they both wished to be separated did not speak well for one or the other. There was, no doubt, fault on both sides; she had been ready with her tongue, and he had been ready with his fist. As they both wished to be separated, the magistrates thought it about the best thing to do, and they granted a separation order,a,nd de- fendant must pay 10s. per week towards his wife's maintenance. He would be fined is. and costs for the assault. The costs amounted to £1 12s.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CHILD.
div.p: THE FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CHILD.

An inquest was held on Monday at the Golden Lion, Latchford, by gr. IL C. Yates, coroner, con- cerning the death of Oswald Cook, aged nearly four year, son of Alfred Cook, greengrocer, 2:25, Mints- ford-road, previously recorded by Us. The deceased's father said on -Fri Jay afternoon he was coming from Grappenhall with his cart,loaded with hampers of potatoes. Witness was leading the horse, and the deceased was sitting between his two elder brothers, aged 11 and 14. near to the horse. When they had got about a mile frozn.Grappenhall witness looked round— he did not know why—and saw the deceased lying on the ground in front of the right wheel, fie tried to stop the horse, but could not in time, and the wheel went over the child's body. Witness picked him up and took him to Dr. Ronald's surgery. The child died in his arms there about five minutes later.—Thomas Cook, aged 14, thedeceased's brother, said the child was sitting side- ways on the hamper with hislegs upon it. Witness had . . . _ . .

hold of the reins, but did not notice the deceased fall. In his opinion he must have fallen backwards.—Alfred Cook, aged 11, said the deceased had his fate to the horse and his legs hanging over the front of the cart. Witness did not see him tumble, but noticed that he seemed drowsy.—The Coroner remarked that it wts an indiscreet thing to place a child where he was bat he did not think the father thought what he was doing at the time.—A juryman mentioned that die father.was man who was very indulgent to his children.—.A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: BETTWS-Y-COED OUTRAGE.
div.p: THE BETTWS-Y-COED OUTRAGE.
DUNCAN INSANE.

At Carriarvon Assizes on Tuesday, Richard Coolidge Duncan, aged 26, an American citizen, was tried on a charge of feloniously attempting to kill and murder his wife, Kate Duncan, on the 12th May last, in the parish of Bettws-y-Coed. Mr. Eldon Bankes and Mr. E. H. Lloyd (instructed by the solicitor to the Treasury) ap- peared for the prosecution, and Mr. Kemp, Q.C., and Mr. Bryan Roberts, M. P., were council for the defence. Evidence was then given as to the prisoner's move- ments on the 12th May, and by Evans as to Ending Mrs. Duncan lying wounded with the prisoner bending over her..

One or two of the medical witnesses stated that pri- soner told them his wife had been injured by falling from a rock, but Dr. Jone 3, of Festiniog, informed the Court that when he closely questioned the prisoner on the matter, the latter replied, "I did it myself," adding in a low voice that, having lost 30,000d015. after marriage, he was penniless, and that he had intended to drown his wife at Llandudno.

Other evidence was given, and for the defence Mr. Kemp urged that the prisoner was not responsible for his actions, haring always suffered from insomnia and depression. His loss of money was a myth. Prisoner was committed on the ground of temporary insanity, and was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure.
SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A STEAMER.

The main steampipe on the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Rohilla burst on Thursday morning as the vessel was leaving the Royal Albert Docks, and six Lasear firemen were scalded, three of them so seriously that they had to be removed to the Seamen's Hospital, where faint hopes are entertained of their recovery. The de- parture of the Rohilla will be delayed two days.
THE CHARGE AGAINST MR. CHARLES.
A. TYFFE.

Mr. Justice Matthews, charging the grand jury at Guildford Assizes, on Tuesday morning, referred to the charge again Mr. Chas. Allan Fyffe, the eminent historian and Liberal candidate for Devizes, of indecent conduct with a boy. Everything 'must depend upon the trust. worthiness of the prosecution, and the cardinal feature was whether the boy was a consenting party. The jury founad there was no bill.

Some time ago we gay°, an historical account of the origin and growth of the wire trade in Warrington. and now we hart° before us an important volume which deals with wire as manufactured the world over. It is {role the pen of Mr. J. BUOKNALL SMITH, C.E., and it is entitled "A Treatise upon Wire and its mann' facture and uses,embracing comprehensive descrir tions of the constructions and applications of wire ropes." Mr. SMITH is well qualified for the task he has undertaken; he is the author of works oil "Cable Traction," "Rope Haulage," &c., and hes had extensive experience in various parts of the globe. In the preface it is stated that the object of the treatise is" to convey to the average reader intelligible and practical discriptions of the history', manufacture, and uses of various kinds of plain and worked wire as occurent in, or applir able to, innumcrable industries and purpose: in daily service to all classes of the community. This object, it is satisfactory to state, is admirabli accomplished. A large body of information ha° been got together and carefully classified, the author having spared no pains in his endeavout to produce what may be regarded as a standal4 work. Wire being a manufactured article car not be spoken of as being as old as the hills; but its origin is far back into the dim region of misty tradition. Like many other ancient things, it is supposed to have had a beginning in Egypt. It formed part of the decoration of AARON'S robe 91 high priest; and there is a specimen of wire in On Kensington Museum which was made by till Ninevites 800 years before the Christian era. Wit' regard to the present mode of drawing wire, it stated that it was practised in the Lenne districv 3f Germany during the fourteenth century. 0° more delicate productions of the article are mann: factured in copper, bronze, brass, platinum exT silver and gold. IN Ireland, under the Coercion What is Act, the magistrates have a rough Intimidation ? and ready method of determining what is intimidation—a method which results in the peasantry who venture to combine seeing plenty of law, but very little justice. It is other- wise in this country ; Trades Unionists have fought their way in Parliament and in the law courts until they may be said to have got such a footing as ensures justice being done to them. Still, there has been some uncertainty during the past few months as to what was intimidation in the eye of the law; and it was felt that, if Mr. BOMPAS, Q.C., was right, in a conviction recorded by him at Plymouth, it would be necessary to obtain an amendment of the law. The cake, with two others, was referred to the Court of Appeal, and judg- ment was delivered, on Tuesday, by the Lord Chief Justice. Briefly stated, the facts seem to be that the defendants who were pronounced guilty, at Plymouth, of intimidation were secretaries of Trades Unions. Acting on behalf of their Socie- ties, they sought to prevent Mr. TREVELYAN em- ploying non-union men side by side with union men in unloading ships. They threatened to bring out the union men if Mr. TREVELYAN persisted in his conduct; and, as he paid no attention to these threats, the men were brought out. When the case came before the Recorder, it was contended that the action of the secretaries amounted to intimidation; Mr. BOXPAS took the same view, although there was no suggestion of personal violence, and the three doiendants were convicted of a breach of the law. The case has naturally excited considerable attention. Various members of Parliament have spoken strongly on the matter; and Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT did not hesitate to express his opinion as a lawyer that the conviction was founded upon a wong interpretation of the law. Sir WILLIAM proves to be right; ior the judgment of the court is that the conviction can- not be upheld, and must therefore be set aside. • In another case, proceedings had been taken be- cause a workman was discharged on the threat being held out that the rest of the workmen in the employ of the firm would decline to work with Nin, if he did Apt: igin a particular union. This, it - -- wag Argued, was intimidation, notwithstanding the absence of violence. The magistrates, homer. I refused to convict; and the highercourt supported their refusal, ruling that there was no proof of intimidation as defined by the Act of 1875. The Trades Unionists thus won a victory in each case ; and, by obtaining an authoritative interpretation of the law, they may be said to secare themselves for the future. Nobody would deny the right of an individual workman to refuse to work with someone who was objectionable to him; and if the right holds good of one it cannot surely be said to be unreasonable that it should hold good of 100 or 1,000 men, when they think fit to act in Concert, always assuming that there is no personal violence, Or threat of violence. An employer is held to be perfectly at liberty to say he will no longer employ a particular workniatVot) for that matter, to say he will discharge &try workman, giving each, of course, due notteb. If we are to be fair as between man and nn the converse must hold good; a 'workmext, or a whole body of workmen, must be at liberty to leave their employment—notice being • given—without any question being raised as to conspiracy or intimidation. it has taken many years of agitation to establish this common-sense view of the matter as the law in this country' but there can be no doubt as to its being established, especially after the judgment which was delivered, on Tuesday, by Chief Justice Coleridge.

ON Monday the inquest was re- The Haydock sumed and concluded on the Disaster. Haydock disaster, whick resulted in four workmen losing their lives. They were engaged in sinking a shaft at King Pit, and were being let down when they were thrown ot% of the hoppet in which they were descending, ana were killed. It would seem from the evidence that the accident happened through the hoppet striking against a bearer, after it had been set swinging; and according to the statement of JONATHAN FLOYD who was in the hoppet, and had a marvel- lous escape, it was set swinging through the break being put on suddenly. It would appear that the men were being let down at a rapid rate; and if the speed was suddenly checked it is obvious that it would have a disturbing effect Upon the hoppet. HARDMAN, the engineman, stated that he applied the brake gradually; but on the other hand he pleaded that he had been grum- bled at by the Then for lowering them down too slowly through the smoke. It was suggested that the men might have set the hoppet swinging themselves: but there was no evidence to support this theory. On the contrary, evidence was given that HARDMAN was in the habit of letting the sinkers down too quickly, and, further, it was actually stated that one of the men who Was -killed remarked, as he was descending on this particular occasion, that they were" going at a mile a minute." The conclusion of the jury was that "when•the men were descending,the hoppet caught on the bearer and upset, this being caused by the swinging, but they were unable to say what was the cause of the hoppet swinging, as there was no evidence to show. They believed the engineman did let them down too fast, and he should be cau- tioned, and they thought that the bearer should be taken out if not in use, or .that facing boards should be put upon it." The verdict was therefore one of "Accidental Death." It is suggestive that Mr. HALL, her Majesty's Inspector, said he had noticed recently that the winders for sinkers in the whole country wound very rapidly. This is a matter that should be seen to. 'There should be some means of regulating the speed. It is appalling to think that reducing the time of descent by a quarter of a minute may mean all the difference between life and death.

The work of—c-OnStructing the new railway from Iplvton to St. Helens is now i in progress. Quan- tities of materials, which nclade iron girders, &c. are now constantly arriving at .St Mary's Station for the work at this end of the line.

WORTHY OF IMITATIOW. The "Liverpool Journal of Commerce" says that Messrs. Lewis and Mounsey have issued a circular that Mr. T 1101910.8 Snape, whose firm some years ago Was unable to meet their engagements, had in- structed them to pay the balance with 50 per cent. added on the outstanding debit. It appears that the firm failed upwards of twenty years ago, but Mr. Snape resolved if ever he was able to pay the creditors in full he would. About 5,000 of the miners of Messrs. K. Evans and Co., Limited, had a lively time at Blackpool on Saturday. It was a case of. Haydock-on-the- Sea. It is believed that the collier was amongst the number who said—" Aw get a wesh all o'er once a year, an that's when aw go to Blackpool."

Some 300 or 400 females are,it appears, employed in the binding of cheap bibles; and it is admitted by the sedretary of the Women's Book Binding Society that lower prices are paid for binding bibles than for other works. Doesn't this look very much like " sweating " ? And why should the worst price be paid for binding the best book?

The week has been one of ups and downs on the Eastham section of the Ship Canal. At the beginning of the week, things looked bad—with the tide sweeping away the Ellesmere embankment. At the end of it, they look well—with the embank- ment solid, the section open for traffic, and excursions actually advertised between Eastham and Ellesmere.

Of fooling with firearms there is no end. A youth named Poole, son of a postmaster, was examining a gun the other night at Rosenallis, Queen's County, when the weapon exploded, and the charge entered his sister's head, killing her. That youth will have learnt a lesson for life ; and it is to be hoped the tragedy will have made an impression on a few others.

Things are getting lively at Dundee. On Sun- day, the Barbers' Association opened a free shaving shop in Ann-st., in opposition to a barber there who refused to shut his shop on Sunday. In the course of the day they shaved 500 persons free of charge.

Tliere is a story told of rival barbers who com- peted with each other in reducing charges until one put out a notice saying—" I shave for nothing." The other instantly responded with—" I shave for nothing, and give something to drink ?" His shop was soon full; but, as he demanded one penny from each person who had the benefit of his razor, his customers pointed to his sign, and demanded what he meant. His reply was that if they would read carefully they would see that he put a ques- tion. His answer to that question wan—" No; my charge is one penny."

In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, atten- tion was drawn to a matter commented on in these columns last week, namely, the necessity of reducing the fees of the Patent Office. Mr. L eng and Sir William Harcourt pressed the matter home; and drew from Sir Michael Hicks-Beach an Omission not only that something should be done, but that the whole subject should receive careful conshlQllttin with a, view to doing that something.

--- the Emperor of Germany has been delighted with his reception by the people of England, and the people of England have been delighted with him. He leads the way as a monarch ; and seems to have early learnt the wholesome lesson that kings have their duties as well as their privileges. The note of peace, which he struck at the Guild- hall, appears to have been as sincere as it was clear. All Sovereigns say they are for peace; but some, unfortunately, are too ready to fight for it.

According to the evidence given at the Carnar- von Assizes, on Tuesday, Mr. R. C. Duncan, the American, was insane when he all but murdered his wife, in Wales, in May last. It seems that his talk about the money he had lost was the result of hallucination. He reasoned rationally from irra- tional bases, as many lunatics do. He is certainly not fit to be at large; and is to be "detained dur, ing her Majesty's pleasure,"

Mr.. W. T. Stbad has been on the hunt again. This time he announces in the "Review of Re- views "that the whole story a the Prince of Wales beiug in debt, in the hand's of money-lenders, and about to appeal to the Queen or Parliament is a " series of falsehoods." He states" on the high- es't authority "that the Prince is "not in debt." "Glad to hear it," everybody will say, and particu- larly to find that it is not true—to quote a line from Byron that— His cash comes from, his wealth goes to a Jew.

The outcast Jews of Russia are not to be allowed to possess Palestine in peace. The Turks, who are masters of the situation, object, and have made it known that they will allow those only to disem- bark who are on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. The outcasts must, however, be taken in somewhere; and there is talk of their brethren in the United States assisting them to settle in America. If they can take to agriculture, there will be room for them in several States ; but the Jewish plough- man is as yet a rare creature.

The total population of England and Wales is 29,001,018; less by nearly three quarters of a million than was estimated on the basis of the growth of the previous decade. it is not a matter to cry about that the population is not increasing quite so fast as it did. Was it not John Stuart Mill who said the time would come when it would be regarded as a sin against society for a father to bring more children into the world than he could possibly maintain? There is a decrease in the birth rate. Cali it be that fathers are beginning to think of these things ?

What have Orangemen to say to this "The Commander-in-Chief has recently issued instruc- tions to the Commander-in-Chief in India directing that steps should be immediately taken to close an Orange Lodge which has lately been formed in an infantry battalion in that country,and like instruc- tions have been given in regard to similar lodges in other regiments, some of which are quartered at home." What are:Orangemen to do? Exclaim with the poet Cowper— Oh for a lodge in some vast wilderness? Perhaps the best thing for them to do would be to join the Primrose League; there is only a shade of difference.

There is a suspicious paragraph going the rounds announcing the discovery of a mammoth cave in Oregon. We are told that—" It has two open- ings, and contains many passages of great beauty. There are numbers of semi-transparent stalactites, several giant milk-white pillars, and a number of pools and streams of clear, cool water. A week was spent in exploring the cavern, and innumer- able passages and chambers were discovered. On penetrating one of these passages for a distance of several miles the exploring party came across a lake of clear water and a waterfall 30ft. high." This is pretty, very pretty, if true. But if the mammoth cave cannot be found, there is certainly a mammoth liar somewhere about. •

There is every prospect of a Women's Liberal Association being formed in Warrington; and there is no denying that there is a fair field, seeing that social and temperance questions are coming to the front. Lord Salisbury intimated in his speech in London, on Wednesday, that next time the franchise was dealt with by Parliament, the question of removing the restrictions on the female franchise would have to be considered. The Tories will move in the matter if they think they have anything to gain as a party; but it is for Liberals to take action because they think it will be best for the nation. Justice cannot be said to be done until woman, in her relation to the law, is on a footing of equality with man.

PICNICS FROM CULCHETH, On Saturday, Oil annual picnic in connection with the Twiss Green Independent Methodist Chapel took place, when about 50 journeyed to Eastham. The party went by train from Kenyon to Liverpool, when they sailed .over to Eastham. On' the same day the annual picnic in connection with Newchurch Parish Church was held, the place selected this year being Blaekpool. The party,on arriving at the" Brighton of the North,"visited the various places of interest, and arrived at Kenyon on the return journey about 9.30. A pleasant day wirs spent in both cases, the weather being all that Could be desired.

CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, SIMMS CROS3, WIDNES,

. , ... The Rev. R. G. Hughes, pastor of this church, preached special sermons on Sunday. In the morning he dealt with the subject of" Good manner," and in the evening "The use and abuse of life." Good congregations listened to these discourses.

div.head: VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES,
div.p: VICTORIA-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES,

The Rev. C. E. Norman of Didsburi College and of Runcorn, occupied the pulpit of this place of worship on Sunday. There was a large congregation at both the morning and evening service, and the collections on be- half of the Tract Society amounted to £4.

WIDNES ORANGEMEN ,LAT KNOWSLEY. About 150 of the members or the Widnes branch of Orangemen took part in the Orange Demonstration at Knowsley Park on Monday. They were carried in conveyances from Mr. Lea's establishment. On return- ing they had tea at the Conservative Club. WIDNES AND:DISTRICT PERFECT THRIFT B viLDING SOCIETY.

In connection with this --s-o-ciW3; a public meeting was held in the Conservative Club Assembly Room, on Mon- day evening when Mr. Horsley. the founder of the Society, delivered a lecture on "How to live rent free." Musical selections were given. RIINCORN PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS. The annual sermons in aid of Runcorn Parish Church day and Sunday Schools were preached in All Saints' Church, on Sunday, by the Yen. Arthur Gore, D.D., Vicar of Bowden, and Archdeacon of Macclesfield, to large congregations. In the afternoon a children's ser- vice was held. Specially selected music was sung during the day. The collections realised £lB.

THEFT BY DOMESTIC SERVA.NT AT RUNCORN. Yesterday, at Rnncorn Police Court, Charlotte Hoare, aged 17, a domestic servant to George Duckett, fish dealer, Church-st., was charged with stealing £3 belong- ing to Michael McGrath, a fish salesman. McGrath lodged at Duckett's, but was away for the week, and when he returned be found that £3 had been taken from his box. The police ascertained that the prisoner had been spending money freely and arrested her, whereupon She admitted her guilt. She had £2 10s. in her posses- sion. e Vvat remanded until to-day.
RUNCORN _GIRLS _FRIENDLY SOCIEyy.

The members of this society had their annual treat on Thursday. Over 200 girls were driven from St. Michael's Church to Aston in waggonettes supplied by Mr. Jackson, and as the weather was beautifully fine, the drive was much enjoyed. On arrival at Aston the member* were met by the members from Halton and Aston, and altogether they entered Aston Church where thq Bev. n. Marsden preached an appropriate sermofi Mt Wards an excellent tea was provided in the Schoolroom and the evening was spent in the charming grounds of Aston Hall. The party arrived home in good time.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES. Yesterday morning, at the Widnes Police Court, before Mr. V. H. Gossage, an old man, named Richard Boyce,' residing at 5, Farrant-st., seventy-five years of age, who has been in the employ of the Widneg Local Board for a number of years, was charged with attempting to com- mit suicide on Thursday evening, by jumping into the river Mersey. The prisoner's wife died in January last, and since that time he has been very depressed in spirits. He has been drinking heavily for the last few weeks, and on Thursday evening while under the influence of drink r the prisoner went down to the river and jumped in. He was rescued by two bystanders, and handed over to Police-constable Holcroft. When he was taken out of the water, he exclaimed, "Why didn't you let me alone—my life is a burden to me ?" On the application of Superin- tendent Noblett, the prisoner was sent to the workhouse.
BOWLING AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday afternoon a main of bowls was played on the green Of the Bridge Hotel, Runcorn. The green was in good condition, the entries were numerous and the prizes well worth winning, the proprietor, Mr. Jas. Woods, having added £2 to the entrance fees. Some good games were witnessed and the result was that Tom Dean carried off the first prize, Sam Johnson the second. and Wm. White the third. The next three prize win- ners were Robt. Wright, Tess Taylor (Tyldesley), and Wm. Baines (Liverpool). Yesterday morning a series of matches were played on the same green. Tom Woods gave " Toss " Taylor 2 points,in a game of 31, and won by 31 to 27. The game was called 27 all. The stakes were £lO. James Woods, the proprietzr, played Henry Rutter two games of 15s. for aside and the latter won both games. The victor then played to similar games with Robt. Wright,who vanquished his opponent 15-14 and 15-5.

div.head: FREEMASONRY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FREEMASONRY AT RUNCORN.

The members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and ac- cepted Nasons (758) celebrated the festival of St. John, on Thursday evening, at the Masonic Hall, Devonshire- square. The lodge was opened in due and solemn form by Bro. J. Cooper, W.M. The W.M. elect was then pre- sented for installation by ttro.W.Mellor,P.M ,P.P.G.J.D., supported by Bro. Annett, P.M., and the retiring W.M. Bro. Cooper in an impressive manner proceeded to instal Bro.J.Littler, S.W.,as W.M. for the ensuing year. The newly-elected W.M. then invested the following breth- ren as officers:—J. Cooper, 1.P.M., C.W.D. Phillips, S.W., T. S. Burgess, J.W., T. Sharrock, S.E. W. Han- kinson, J.D., A. Linaker, I.G. W. R. Wass. P.M. treas. (re-elected), T. H. Annett, P.M. secretary, J. Coxhill, P.M., D. of C., P.P.G.A.D. of C. W. E. Lancaster, or- ganist, J. Le Couteur, almoner, T. Lydiate, tyler. At the conclusion of the form!l business, the members sat down to a banquet, at which the customary loyal and masonic toasts were proposed and honoured. An in- teresting event was the presentation of a P.M. jewel anda life governorship in the Cheshire Masonic Educa- tional Institute to Bro. Cooper, The jewel was a very handsome one of chaste design, supplied by Bro. Rooker, of Birmingham. The visitors present .were Bros. Woo!rich (Liverpool), Taylor and Silcock (War- rington), and F.,Wilkinson (Widnes). EXTRAORDINARY CASE *LLEOED CRUELTY TO A HORSE A 17NCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst, a boy named John Johnson was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state. John Moore, con- taactor and carter, was charged with causing the horse to be worked. Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., said on the 23rd June he was in Bridge-st., and saw a black horse belonging to Mr. Moore attached in chains to a cart laden with coal. The animal had a large deep wound between each fore leg,matter was oozing from them and thefriction upon them when the horse was walking must have caused it much pain. The animal had warts on almost every part of its body and many of them were bleeding. The tendons of both hind legs and of one fore leg were contracted and only the toes of the hoof could the animal put to the ground. The horse was not fit to work.—Inspector Bowyer corroborated. Since the summons was taken out Mn Moore had destroyed the animal.—Mr. Henry Taylor, R.S.V.S., of St. Helens,said he examined the horse on the 26th. In his opinion it was an act of cruelty to work the animal. There were suppurating wounds under each foreleg and the tendons of three legs were contracted. The animal was totally unfit for work.—For the defence Mr. Moore called Mr. James Sturrar, jun., R.S.V.S., of Chester. He said Mr. Moore telegraphed for him on the 23rd, and he arrived in the evening. The horse was in very good health and in very good condition. It had warts all over its body more or less. There might have been a little discharge from the warts on the elbows and breast, but there were no suppurating wounds whatever. The animal would suffer no pain from the contracted limbs or from the warts which were not sensitive.—By Inspector Dowtv The horse would not be saleable in the market. The horse was not destroyed on his instructions. Had Mr. Moore followed his instructions he would have continued to work the horse, but Mr. Moore was rather slack of work.—Mr. Brundzit : Do you want us to believe that because Mr. Moore gets slack of work he destroys his horses P—Witness said the horse was not valuable and not worth keeping idle.—Mr. Brundrlt said the case against the boy was dismissed. They had had two qualified veterinary surgeons, one saying the horse was quite un- fit and the other that it was quite fit to work; and how on earth the magistrates were to arrive at a conclusion he could hardly say. The horse had been destroyed and there was an end to the matter and the magistrates thought that met the case. The summons against Mr. Moore would therefore be dismissed.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J ULY 18, 1891.
PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.

The teachers and children of Mill Brow Baird School have presented Miss Kennan, headmistress, with a hand- some jewel case on the occasion of her leaving the school to undertake a similar position at British Higher Grade Schools, Wrexham. WIDNES CASES AT LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS.

At these sessions on Wednesday, the following sen- tences were passed :—Michael Costello (50), labourer, month's imprisonment, for having, at Widnes, on the 14th June, wounded Brian Evers; Brian Evers (40), labourer, one month, for having, at Widnes, on the 14th June, wounded Mary Costello ; Ann Crank (39), no occu- pation, one month, for having, at Widnes, on the 4th July, obtained by false pretences certain articles of clothing, the property of John Williamson ; William Walmsley (62). labourer, one month, for having, at Widnes, on the 22nd June, wounded Mary M'Dermott ; Thomas O'Brien (27), labourer, two months, for having, at Widnes, on the 13th June, stolen two hens and a chicken, the property of Martin Rourke. BODY OF A BoY FOUND IN THE MERSEY.

Two flatmen sailing from Liverpool TO—Run- corn, on Thursday afternoon, found the body of a boy about 12 years of age in the Garston deep and towed it to Runcorn. The body now lies at the mortuary awaiting identification. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT PENNINGTON., George Parkes, 46, plumber, pleaded guilty on Tuesday, at Liverpool County Quarter Sessions, to having, at Pennington, on the 22nd June attempted to commit suicide by throwing himself into the Manchester Ship Canal, and was sentenced to one day's imprisonment. J. & W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warriugton.—Adrt.
A BOY DROWNED AT EA.RLESTOWN.

Yesterday afternoon a lad, named David Thomas Jones, 11, Grafton-street, Earlestown, was drowned in what is known as Pritchard's pit, off Wargrave- road. He was fishing, along with some other chil- dren, when the accident happened. SHOCKING MUTILATION ON THE RAILWAY.

As a goods train was passing Childwall Station about four o'clock yesterday morning the driver noticed the body of a man lying in the six foot. He was terribly mutilated, having been evidently run over by a passing train, one side of his face being literally cutoff. There was nothing to establish iden- tity,and the body was removed to the Childwall Abbey Hotel. He is apparently a working-man about 35 years of age. THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES. _ _

It was confidently expected by the people of Wid- nes that the charter of incorporation would be re- ceivedin time to allow the first municipal election to take place in November, and keen disappoint- ment will be felt on learning that such an event will not be possible. In answer to the inquiries of Mr. H. S. Oppenheim, acting clerk to the Local Board, the officials of the Privy Council inform him that the charter cannot be prepared early enough to permit the election of councillors to be held on the first November. The charter is,however,expeeted be- fore the end of the year, but for the present the efforts being made for a keen election contest are paralysed.
ROYAL MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL, AND NORTH
LANCASHIRE AGRICULTURAL 'SOCIETY.

The annual show at Bury, on Thursday, Friday, and Saturday next promises to be one of the most .successful the society has held. We understand thakthe entries in the various classes are unusually large, and are of a very high character, and fully representative of the agricultural interests of the kingdom. The opening ceremony, and the public dinner, at which the Right Hon. the Earl of Derby, K.G., will preside, will add considerable interest to the proceedings of the first day, and the numerous other attractions provided for this and the follow- ing days, amongst them the working dairy and the leaping and other competitions, presage an un- doubted success up to the close of the show. The works at the show ground, which are already pre- pared for the reception of the exhibits, have been carefully arranged, and are of a very extensive nature, owing to the unusual number of entries in implements, horses, and cattle, and in fact in all classes without exception. Leadin-4 prize bands of the district have been engaged for each day, and music of the highest class will be presented.
_...".,...-. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. F. H. Gossage (chairman) presided, and there were also present Messrs. G. I. Niel, H. S. Timmis, B. Brown, D. Wright, J. Taylor, F. Hayes, S. Sadler, J. Tilley, R. Cook, J. Midwood, Dr. O'Keeffe, J. Houghton; H. S. Oppenbeim (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), and J. Sinclair (surveyor).
RESIGNATION OF DR. COOPER.

The'Chairman read a letter he had received from Dr. Cooper, in which he stated he greatly regretted that, in consequence of his failing health, he should be obliged to resign his appointment as Medical Officer of Health. He thanked the Board for their kind consideration dur- ing the 18 years he had held the post.—Mr. Wright, in moving that the letter be referred to the Health Com- mittee, regretted the cause of Dr. Cooper's resignation, and said lie had no doubt that gentleman had the sym- pathy of the Board. (Hear, her.)—The letter was then referred to the Health Committe4.

div.head: VYRNWT WATER SCHEME.
div.p: THE VYRNWT WATER SCHEME.

It was stated on Thursday that the flow of Vyrnwy water into the Prescot reservoir had been satisfactory during the last few days,and on Thurs- day night the stock in the storage reservoir had reached to within about a foot of the top of the embankment. The quantity was estimated at about' 40,000,000 gallons. No information could be ob- tained as to when the water would be sent on to Liverpool. J. L. W. Durros s SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: RISLEY INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHURCH.
div.p: RISLEY INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHURCH.

In connection with the above place of worship the anniversary services were conducted on Sun-. day. Sermons were preached. afternoon and even- ing by Mr. R. Henshall, of Warrington, to large and appreciative congregations. An augmented choir and part orchestra led the singing, the organ being presided over by Mr. Arthur Mounfield, of Warring- ton. At the evening service, Sir J: Stanlees "What are these ?" was rendered with good effect by the choir. The collections and donation:, amounted to about £lO.
PRENtiFR,S4ITTIES, Cash or ifiro,— GAM, A.ND. Warrington. —Advt.

STACK FMK AT EIALTON. On Monday midnight, a fire was discovered to have broken out in a stack of straw belonging to William Parry, Brow Farm, Halton. The fire was first discovered by a man named Thomas Newport, of Halton, who immediately gave information to P.C.Fryer and the Runcorn Fire Brigade was soon on the spot under the command of Mr. R. Wright. It is believed the stack caught fire by some one lying near it, and probably smoking. The damage, which is estimated at £4B, is fully covered in the Alliance Assurance Company.

div.head: VOLUNTEERS FINED.
div.p: VOLUNTEERS FINED.

At the St. Helens Police_r Court, on Friday, Wm,. Lawrensonwand Arthur Lawreuson, brothers, of West Derby, members of the 2nd Lancashire Engi- neer Volunteers, were summoned by Sergt.-Major Burns for having failed to make themselves effi- cient. The defendants had failed to put iu the required 15 drills, and, in consequence of their non- efficiency, the corps lost tne capitation graut of 30s in each case. The defendants had also rendered themselves liable to a subscription of is. per mouth for the last twelve months. The Bench made an order for each defendant to pay £2 2s. an I costs. BAssixgrrEg.—J. div.p: The hopes entertained last week that a settle- ment of the dispute in the building trade at St, Helens would be early arrived at, have not been realised, and there are at present no prospects of its immediate termination. At an informal meet- ing of the master builders' and men's representa- tives, Alderman 111‘Kechnie was asked to act as arbi- trator, but he cannot act owing to absence in Scot- land. No other arbitrator has been selected. The contractor for the internal fittings of the Thatto Heath branch library has been unable to commence work owing to the dispute. _ _
J. &W. DUTrows SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.
ROSE QUEEN FESTIVAL AT GLAZEBURY.

On Saturday the • second annual rose queen festi- val which is got up solely by children, was held under favourable circumstances. A procession which represented various trades and characters was formed, and marched through the village. The queen was a charming girl, aged five years, named Mary Elizabeth Shaw, daughter of Mr. George Shaw. After calling at several places, the party adjourned to a field which had been lent by Mr. S. Bent, where Mr. Joseph Boardman performed the ceremony of crownink the queen. Tea waspartaken of, after which the party went to a field lent by Mr. Spencer Barlow, where the remainder of the evening was pleasantly spent in games. J. &W. Durros's SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Ativt. MR. MAYBRICK'S INSURANCE POLICY.

In the Queen's Bench, on Monday, an action was partly heard respecting an insurance effected in October, 1888, by the late James Maybrick, in favour of Florence Maybrick, who was afterwards convicted of poisoning him. The Mutual Life As- sociation have paid £2OO, out.of £2,000, the amount of the policy, but refused to pay the remainder. The case for Mrs. Maybrick is that the sentence was commuted on the ground that it was not estab- lished that she caused her husband's death, and that even assuming she did, it was no answer to the claim. The case was not concluded, but will not be taken again till Monday next, the judge having consented not to resume till then to suit the con- venience of counsel. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51. Bridge-st.. Warrington. and at Barleatown.—Advt. ILECOGNIZANCES &TREATED AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. Stapleton-Bretherton and Mr. A. R. Glad- stone, Timothy Conroy, described as of Runcorn, should have surrendered to his bail to answer a charge of having on.the Bth inst., obtained by means of menaces and threats .£5 from Mrs. Ann Taylor, licensee of the Clapgate Hotel, Halebank. Conroy failed to put in an appearance, and Superintendent Noblett asked that the recoguizances of his sureties should be estreated. The sureties were John Proffit carter of 2, Ellis-st., Widnes, and George Houghton, general dealer of Post Office Row, Halebank, who had each been bound over in the sum of 1.30. Houghton said he had kept his eye on Conroy until Wednesday morning when he gave him a sovereign to engage a barrister and he had never seen him since.—Mr. Bretherton said the Bench had no course but to make the order for the recognizances to be estreated.—Mrs. Taylor applied for a warrant for the apprehension of Conroy and it was granted.
J. 1: iv. Burrores SUMMER 54. LE now on. Sankey Street. Warrington.—Advt. NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

The annual election of the Newton Improvement Commissioners has been fixed for Wednesday next, the 22nd inst. The retiring members on this occa- sion are Messrs. George McCorquodale, T. J. Gilles- pie, and G. Ratcliffe, all of whom are eligible for re-election. It was at one time thought there would be a stiff contest for the vacant seats, but better c.unsels have prevailed, and the three retir- ing members will this year be returned unopposed. The last day for sending in nominations was Tues- day, and when the day closed it was found that Messrs. McCorquodale, Gillespie, and Ratcliffe had been nominated by Mr. F: A. Frost, and Mr. J. Lip- trott, of Newton. In addition to these Mr. J. Barr, jeweller, Bridge-st., and Mr. P. Thompson, provision dealer, Bridge-st., Earlestown, had been nominated by Messrs. T. Molyneux, T.A. Pimblett, F. A. Brown. J. Woods, R. Toft, J. Cawley, W. Gilmour, W. Ral- son, and others. A meeting of some of the princi- pal movers in the affair was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, on Monday night, at which it was de- cided to avoid a contest if possible. but that if any others were nominated from the Newton district, in addition to those named above, the election would be contested. Should no others be nomi- nated, it was perfectly understood that Mr. Barr and Mr. Thompson would withdraw, and a deputa- tion was appointed to wait upon Mr. McCorquodale and Gillespie to explain this. Messrs. Thompson and Barr have now withdrawn, and thus the three retiring Commissioners will be formally re-elected on Wednesday next.

div.head: OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that the gas tests on the 23rd and 29th ult. resulted as follows: Illuminating power equal to leB7 and 18-35 candles, free from sul- phuratted hydrogen. The average illuminating power of the gas during the month had been 18.19 candles. It was recommended that the following tenders be ac- cepted for the period ending 30th June, 1892, viz : ' Simpson, Davies, and Co., 4,500 tons, Pearson and Knowles, Arley slack, 7s. 11d, per ton; J. and W. Richardson, 3,000 tons Cross Tetley's slack, 7s. Bd. per ton ; Mass Hall Co., 2000, tons screened nuts, Bs. 6d. per ton ; Abram Coal Co., 4,500 tons Arley rough slack. 83. per ton. The engineer's report contained the following: —Netherley— Boring Contracts ;—The Contractor's workmen have been engaged for the greater part of the past month in fitting up the boring machine and fixing the tubes at the top of the well, The total depth now sunk is 37ft.,an1,as stated in last month's report,the rock was met with at 301 t. from the ground level, the tubes having been forced into the rock a distance of 51t.; and the whole of the space in the teniporary well at the back of the tubes is being filled with concrete, thus making a solid backing for the tubes from the rock to the ground level. A rough pebble bed was found on the surface of the rock, which occasioned some delay and difficulty in driving the tubes to the required depth. Boring with the machine has been commenced to-day. A certificate for the sum of £lOO on account of his contract is sub- mitted. Sulphate Plant :—The lead lining the saturator which was put in last season, has proved to be of infer- ior quality, necessitating frequent repairs. A new satu- rator and stand is under course of preparation. This plant has worked 21 days during the past month,4 cwts. have been sold, present stock gtons, The rainfail for the month has been :—Gas yard Guage. 3.905 inches; Pex Hill Gnaw!, 3.050 inches: mean 3.477 inches. Water in stock, July 1, 1891- 10,214,463 gallons.—On the motion of Mr. Brown the minutes were adopted.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE
div.p: THE HIGHWAY COMMITTEE

This Committee's minutes contained the following : Letter, June sth, from Peter Balmer, stating that he had made an error of £lOO in the pricing out of No. 3 contract and asking to be allowed to amend his tender accord• ingly, read. Resolved that the paragraphs'of the recom- mendation, passed at last meeting, relating to contracts Nos. 4 and 3 be withdrawn, and that instead thereof, it be recommended that the following tenders be accepted, viz. : Contract No. 4 : Railway-street and two streets off Victcria-street, and passages on the East side of Ann- street, Peter Balmer, £1,036 103. ; contract No. 3: Sut- ton's-lane and passages on West side of Ann-street West, Peter Balmer, £1,496 10s. Letters, 29th June, from (1) Cowburn and Harris, stating that in consequence of their having dissolved partnership they wished to withdraw their tenders for street works, and that they were agreeable that such tenders should be transferred to S. Cowburn and Sons, of Hindley, near Wigan. (2) S. Cowburn and Sens intimating their willingness to take over such tenders and to undertake the work at the prices named therein read and considered. Recom- mended that the resolution of the Local Board, passed on the 9th ult., so far as it relates to the accept- ance of Cowburn and Harris's tenders be rescinded, and that instead thereof it be recommended that the tenders of Cowburn and Sons for the same work at the same prices as stated in Cow- burn and Harris's tendeis be accepted, subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board, also that the question of the adoption of this recommendation be one of emergency.—The Surveyor's report read as follows: —Steam Roller: During the past month the roller has been engaged in rolling. public roads 191 days, private work 1± days, and has been used in the yard nine daYs. Workmen: Repairs have been made to gas and water trenches, flag footways, &c. Slag macadam has been put on Lowerhouse-lane, the sewer trench at the Moss Bank sewer has been banked up with earth, and the ditch at Oakes's barn, Crow Wood, has been piped. Liebee-st. has been sewered with 12in pipes, and a ins'- hole built. built. The 15in. pipe sewer and manholes ie Deacon-road are being proceeded with and will be com- pleted this week. The repairs to the paving of Lugsdale- road and Albert-road railway bridges are completed. Birchfield-road railway bridge is now beingrepaved. I have received an order from Mr. F. Neil to kerb and flag Gossage-st, co-extensive with his premises. The flagging at Mr. W. Smith's property, Mill Brow, is being pro- ceeded with. Lugsdale-road improvement has been set out. Public Lighting : The Gas Engineer has completed the fixing of three lamps in Moorfield-road. Ann-st. Sewer Outlet: Messrs. Muspratt's length of sewer has been examined and found clear. I have served notice upon the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company and the London and North-Western Railway Company to clear their portion. Sewerage Works: I have prepared details of flushing tanks and ventilating shafts, and suggest that tenders be invited from contractors for the next Committee meeting. Contracts for Materials: I wrote to Messrs. Hargreaves and Bolton refusing flags not in accordance with the specification; they are now supplying materials in accordance with their contract. Derby-road Bridge Approaches: I have taken levels and find that the average gradient of the road to Bold from crown of bridge is 1 in 24, and to crown of bridge to foot of slope 1 in 2160. Private Improvement Works: Plans, sections, and estimates are now submitted for the sewering, paving, &c., of streets and passages, Moss Bank district. Lowerhouse-lane Sewer: Plans, sec- tions, and estimates are now submitted fgs sewering from Little Briton to Birchfield-rd. and for street making from Little Briton to Milton-road and from Steward's- lane to Birchfield - road. The Committee recom- mended that legal. proceedings be instituted against James Walter Davies, the Secretary to the Widnes Athle- tic Sports Committee, for having allowed astand to be used on the occasion of the recent sports without such stand having been constructed to the satisfaction of the Surveyor. The Surveyor submitted plans, sections, and estimates for the making and sewering of the following streets and passages, viz. :—Brown-st., Moss-st., Mary- at.: street between Nos. 40 and 42, Brown-st., street between No. 9, Moss-st. and the Wesleyan Chapel. street running parallel with the street last described and oppo- site to No. 50, Moss-st., Little Mary-St., the whole of the passages situate between Mass-st., Mary-st., Moss Bank- rd ~and Brown-st.,passage between Nos. 10 and.l2,Miry- st., passage in rear of premises Nos. 2 to 10 inclusive, Mary-st., and 59 and 61, Moss Bank-road, passage bet- ween premises Nos. 22 and 24, Mary-St., passage in rear

of Nos. 12 and 26 inclusive, Mary-st., passages in rear of Nos. 4 and 52 inclusive, Brown-st. and 3 and 9 inclu- sive, Moss-st., passage in rear of the Wesleyan Chapel and adjoining houses in Moss-st. Recommended that notices be given under section 150 of the Public Health Act, 1875, requiring the owners or occupiers of the pre- mises fronting, adjoining, and abutting on such streets and passages within one month from the service of such notices to sewer, level, pave, metal, flag, channel, or make good and to provide proper means of lighting the said streets and passages as shown upon the said plans, sections, and estimates. Plans for the following sub- mitted by the Surveyor :—Alterations to 10, Mersey-rd., for D. Lewis, approved; alterations to 66, Victoria-rd., for D. Lewis, approved; wooden shed, 10. Frederick-st., for S.Joynson, disapproved ; wooden shed, 16,Frederick- st., for H. Hughes, disapproved ; office in Salisbury-st., for W. Smith, approved ; house in Cross-st., for Runcorn Co-operative Society, approved; shop in Albert-road, for Runcorn Co-operative Society, approved ; additions to 65, Halton-view, for M. Wilcock, approved; Wesleyan Chapel, in Derby/road, Farnworth, disapproved; Villa, Marsh Hall Pad, for J. Palmer, approved ; house in Oak- land-st. for J. Hedley, approved.—Mr. Sadler moved the confirmation of the minutes, and, referring to that

recommending the summoning of the secretary of the athletic sports said the Committee thought that if Mr. Davies tendered an ample apology they would withdraw the summons. This Mr. Davies had done, and therefore he wished to withdraw the minute.—The Clerk read the apology which had been received from Mr. Davies. It stated that the defects in the stand had been due to the contractor not carrying out instructions, and, after thanking the Board for allowing the proceedings.to drop, Mr. Davies added that, so far as he was concerned, he should take care the Board had no cause for complaint against him.—The Chairman thought the letter was a satisfactory one, and he thought it must also be satis- factory to the Board to know that the Committee had taken notice of that matter in the interests of the pub- lic.—Mr. Sadler said the stand had been erected in such a way that it was a wonder there had not been an acci- dent.—Mr. Hayes asked if the Surveyor had a micro- scope with which he saw the repairs at Birchfield-road railway bridge for he himself could see none.—Mr. Sad- ler thought it was Mr. Hayes who needed a microscope and not the Surveyor.—The minutes were then con- firmed as proposed.

THE HEALTH COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained the following : Letter, July Ist, from Miss R. Brew, resigning her office. as Matron, read ; recommended that the resignation be accepted, and that thq Clerk advertise forthwith for a successor to Miss Brew at a salary commencing at £3O per annum. The following report of the medical officer submitted and read :—Births 108, equal to 41.8 per 1,000; deaths (total) 71, equal to 27.48 per 1,000. Recommended that the followhig tenders be accepted for the period ending June, 1892, viz. :—James Fletcher, for supply of butcher's meat to Fever and Accident Hospi- tals at 80. per lb.; William Wilson, for supply of milk to Fever and Accident Hospitals at 3d. per quart. Recom- mended that notices Le issued requesting that all litter or rubbish to be removed from any premises be removed direct to the Local Board's depot, and that upon notice being given the scavenging carts will call for and remove such litter free of cost, also that eve-ry person found guilty of throwing or laying any dirt, litter, or ashes, or nightsoil, or any carrion, fish, offal, or rubbish on any street, is liable to a penalty not exceeding forty shillings for each offence. Market receipts for the month £lB 03d., being a decrease of £6 Os. Id. as compared with .Thne, 1890, caused by loss of hawkers' tolls £2 16s. 6d., and remainder on fair ground account. The following plans were submitted by the Surveyor and approved: Temporary office, Salisbury-st., for Mr. W. Smith; shop, Albert-road, for Runcorn Co-operative Society; house, , Cioss-st., for Runcorn Co-operative Society; alterations at 10. Mersey-road, for Mr. David Lewis; alterations at 56. Victoria-road, for Mr. David Lewis; addition to 65. ; Halton View, for Mrs. Mary Wilcock; house, Oakland- st., fer Mr. John Hedley ; villa, Farnworth, for Mr. John I Palmer.—Mr. Wright, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the efficient service as matron of I Miss Brew.—The minutes were confirmed.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.

This Committee recomrnended that the salaries of the following officials in the accountant's department be in- creased as follows :—Charles Whitfield, collector, from £llO to £l2O per annum; Thos. H. Wilson, chief clerk, £lOO to £llO per annum ; J. Heyes, clerk, £9O to £lOO per annum ; Isaac Sankey, assistant collector,£7s to £9O per annum.—Dr.O'Keeffe moved the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. Cook, in seconding, said he thought they ought they ought to pay an efficient servant a proper salary, and he mentioned that the collector had been in the office something like 12 or 13 years,and Mr. Wilson 13 or 14 years. It smnqcl to him tint 4 chid clerk cought to be paid as much as the collector.—Mtaidwood moved that the paragraph referring to the increase of salaries should not be adopted. One of the staff, he said, was really not worth the salary he was already getting, and with regard to the cther three, he thought they ought to wait a little longer, and, in fact, when the town was in- corporated, rates that were collected from that office would be handed over to the overseers.—Mr. Sadler se- conded Mr. Midwood's ameodment.—ln answer to Mr. Taylor' the Clerk said that only a small part of the rates would have tobe collected by the overseers.—Mr. Hayes said Mr. Wilson acted as assistant overseer for a neigh- bouring township, and got paid for it.—Mr. Houghton said Mr. Wilson did not borrow any of the Board's time to do that work.—The Chairman thought they had no right to take the matter mentioned by Mr. Hayes into consideration. There was no doubt Mr. Wilson was an efficient servant.—For Mr. Midwood's amendment there voted only three members ,viz. : Messrs.Midwood,Sadler, and Hayes.
