div.head: HOME RULE MEEtING AT WIDNES.
div.p: HOME RULE MEEtING AT WIDNES.
SPEECH OF THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

Under the auspices of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League, a public meeting was held in the Drill Hall. on Saturday night, in support of Home Rule. There was a good attendance and Dr. Olieeffe presided. On the platform were Messrs. E, F. Vesey Knox, M.P., (County Cavan), Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., Liberal candidate for Widnes Division, Councillor G. J. Lynskey (Liverpool), Messrs. D. Boyle (Manchester), J. Randle, J. How- lin, P. Hartland, Delaney (secretary), and others Letters apologising for non-attendance and wish- ing the meeting success had been received from ' Messrs. T. Logan, M.P., Quinn, M.P., J. Duncan, M. P., W. R. Kennedy (Liberal candidate for St. Helens), T. Snape (Liberal candidate for Heywood), ER. Russell, E. K. Muspratt,liajor J. W. Wareing, and others. Mr. Herbert Gladstone M.P. wrote: I Finch re- gret that owing to my engagements, it is out of my power to accept the invitation you are good enough to send me to attend your meeting on the 11th. lam obliged to you for your kind inquiries about my father who is rapidly regaining his health and strength." The following letter had been received from Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P.--" Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, 10th July, 1891.—Dear Mr. Delaney,—l should have been very glad to attend your meeting on Saturday night had it been possible, but the many calls upon my time unfortunately put it out of my power. A visit to Widnes revives so many pleaspnt recollections, and pro- cures for me so many kindly greetings from old friends, that I should always welcome such an opportunity as your invitation affords. Especially should Ibe glad to support the candidature of Mr. Deacon, from whose father I received many valuable political lessons in the days when both Widnes and I were young. He would make an unexceptionable member, whom I should be heartily glad to see taking his seat in the House of Com- mons. Please convey to the meeting my cordial con- gratulations on the magnificent result of the Carlow elec- tion. It is a triumphant proof that the vast majority of the Irish people are convinced,thoroughly and profoundly convinced, of the sincerity and heartiness of the Liberal party in Great Britain. The English alliance was the test question at Carlow, and the election of Mr. Ham- mond is a definite ratification of that alliance. Day after day, throughout the contest, from its doubtful be- ginning to its glorious end, Mr. Healy urged the men of Carlow to trust Mr. Gladstone and his followers. A further result of this election, and to us Liberals a great satisfaction, is the utter discomfiture of Lord Salisbury, In his attempts to compete with Captain Coe as a sport- ing prophet. We may now confidentally trust the Tories nevez again to put their money on Parnell. A word in conclusion as to my personal position. A "Freeman's Journal," founding its mis-statement upon a garbled quotation from a speech of mine delivered last autumn in the Wirral Division of Cheshire, classed me at the time as a supporter of My. Parnell. No one who read the re- port of that speech in the Liverpool papers of the follow- ing dt!y could have been misled,but I have observed that the trick has Imposed upon some Irishmen in Widnes. What I then said was that Mr. Parnell's past services to Ireland had been so great that I had no word of blame to utter for the generous-hearted men who in committee- room N 0.15 had.stood up for him so stoutly.' I though I them greatly mistaken, and said so most clearly. think so still, and believe that most of them, if not all o them, are now of the same opinion.—Yours, faithfully, Jour; T. BRUNNER." The reading of this letter was fre- quently interrupted by cheering. The Chairman having opened the proceedings in a brief speech, Councillor Lynskey proposed That we hereby in public meeting assembled, pledge ourselves never to rest satisfied until we have won back for the people of Ireland the right to govern themselves in accordance with the wishes of the people." (Cheers.) Mr. Deacon,whohad a mast cordial reeeption,seconded the resolution, and said in the Widnes division they hap a hard fight before them if they were to win the victory, and it was the duty of every man who took an interest

in political questions of the day not only to attend public meetings but to take care that his name was upon the register of voters. Not only would they have a hard fight in their own division: it would be the same all over Lancashire, for this county sent to Parliament 43 Conservatives and only 15 Liberals. They hoped that at the next election that proportion would be reversed. (Cheers.) He hoped that at all events they in Widnes would do their best to reverse it. (Cheers.) That meeting was called under the auspices of the Widnes branch of Irish National League and the majority of those present were Irishmen. Under these circum. stances—though he was an Englishman and was not ashamed to own it—it seemed to him wise that he should mention some of the reasons that had convinced him as an Englishman and not only as a Liberal, that the pre- sent Government in Ireland was wrong, and that for it must be substituted one that was in harmony with the wishes of the people. (Cheers.) If the Union which was effected some 90 years ago had been successful they would see Irishmen satisfied with the present system of Government; they would see an equal measure of free- dom in Ireland to what existed in England, and they would see the Irish people as happy, as contented, and as prosperous as we in England. (Cheers.) Tested by these tests had the results of the Union been success- ful. He said not. From the very time of the forma- tion of thwUnion, Irishmen had protested against it. With regard to the matter of freedom, let them compare it as it existed in England with freedom as it existed in Ireland in respect to the right of public meeting and the administration of the law as regarded combination and conspiracy (Cheers.) Outrage in Ireland was some- times spoken of. He did not uphold outrage, but it was only right that as the minds of Englishmen were calcu- lated to be affected through the stories of outrage and crime in Ireland, it was only right that they should remember the constant irritation and the feelings of bitterness and soreness that filled the minds of Irishmen and the constant repression to which their national in- stinct had been subjected. (Cheers.) One thing that was wanted was to sweep away the irritating and absurd anachronism that was known as Dublin Castle. (theers.) He would give just one selfish reason that had influ- enced him. It was this; that he desired to see Parlia- ment strong, free, and well up to its work. He was anxious by an arrangement for Home Rule in Ireland to relieve Parliament of a large amount of work so that the English as well as the Irish might be able to govern themselves as they desired. (Cheers.) He was full or hope for the future. He trusted, with their help, that Widnes would return a Literal at the next election. (Cheers.) There, publicly, he once again pledged him- self to vote for Irish Home Rule and to support Mr. Gladstone (cheers) if ever he had the honour to be returned to Parliament. It was growing more and more evident day by day that the moral and political sins of one man had not weakened the ties that were formed. between the Liberal and Irish parties but that they would continue to work together side by side to bring about the consummation of the noble policy of reconci- liation that had been the crowning point in the long life of their great leader to have conceived. (Loud cheers.) Mr. T. Delaney moved and Mr. J. Randles seconded the following motion :—" That we enter on record our firm coviction that no settlement of the Irish land ques- tion which does not recognise the right ef the tenants on the plan of campaign estates in Ireland to return to the farms from which they have been most unjustly evicted. will ever be accepted by the Irish plople as a final or satisfactory one." (Cheers.) Mr. Knox, M.P., supported the resolution in a vigor- ous speech, in which he defended the action of the Irish party in regard to the evictions and the plan of cam- paign. They were not going to pick up crumbs which fell from Cabinet Ministers in the shape of light rail- ways, but would continue to work for the one great end of Home Rule for Ireland. Mr. Deacon was well worthy of the support of the Irishmen of Widnes, and after hear- ing the pledges sif Mr. Deacon on home Rule be felt that they would be able to gnin the same lobby in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) In cenclusion Mr. Knox re- pelled the charges of "Clerical dictation " in Ireland. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. Boyle proposed "That we, the Nationalists and Liberals of Widnes, tender our heartfelt sympathy to Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone in their sad bereavement at the loss of one whom they loved dearly. We earnestly trait that the Giver of all good gifts will console the Grand Old Man in this his hour of grief and sorrow by giving. to him renewed health and strength to accomplish the heart-felt wish of his lattersday life." Mr. F. Hartland seconded the motion which was car- ried with enthusiasm, and the meeting afterwards ter" minated.

div.head: GASSED AT A RUNCORN C EMIC.A.It
div.p: GASSED AT A RUNCORN C EMIC.A.It
WORKS'. INTO TIIE JAWS OF DEATH.

The Coroner for the Honour of Efaltoa (Mr. J. J. Wors)ey), on Saturday afternoon, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court on the body of Peter Faulk.- ner, chemical labourer, of 7, Parker-it., Runcorn, who died on Friday evening, under circumstances detailed below. Margaret Faulkner, widow of the deceased, said her husband was :a labourer, and had worked at Messrs. Hazlehurst and Sons, chemical works. He came home at 5,30 on Thursday-and told her he had been gassed in a chamber. She gave him some tea, bub as he became worse she sent for Dr. Robinson who attended him. He died next evening. Before he died he said he would not have been where he was if he had not gone into the nitrate chamber. Deceased had beea at the w.)rks for 36 years and had filled bottles with muriatie acid for 22 years. He had been several times " gassed" but she could not tell whether it was going into the chamber or not. He was sent into the chamber by his foreman James Williamson. Joseph Bate, Spring-st., an employe at the works for 38 years, said he had known_the deceased all his life. When deceased had no acid bottles to fill he laboured at various kinds of work. On Thursday afternoon witness with the deceased and other men were engaged in cleaning out a vitriol chamber. Deceased had done similar work on several occasions. Some men objected to the work and would go home before they would do it. In order that the gas mieht escape from the chamber ventilation holes were made, but after the chamber was considered fit to enter, gas always arose from the refuse in the clean- ing process, and nothing could be done to prevent thiS. There were now two men at home ill from the effects of - the gas. They had never had a fatal accident before. There was no other way of cleaning the chamber.—By a Juryman: The chamber had been empty since the pre- vious Saturday. The gas which overpowered deceased-: was created by stirring the refuse.—James Williams in,. foreman over the vitriol department, who had known decease .1 25 years, said deceased had done thesaine kind • of work before and did not refuse to go into the cham- ber. It was gas from the refuse which caused the in in to he ill. There were no directions given as to the lenrh of time the men should stay in the chamber. By a Jury- man: Cleaning operations had been stopped sines-, deceased was gassed and there was probably less gas in the chambei• now.—By Mr. Pope (manager of the works) : He did not compel any man to go into the chambers. He himself often went into the chambers w hen being cleaned, but never felt ill. He usually drank tea, while the men drank spirits and it was the tea in his • opinion, which enabled him to stand the gas better than the men. The men only stayed in the chamber five orten minutes at a time and came outside for about 15 minutes to get fresh air.—Dr. Robinson said the cause of death was asphyxia,, caused by an irritating gas. He con- sidered deceased a strong man. Had deceased recovered from being gassed very probably bronchites would have set in, as was the case with other men.—Sanmel Pope said he had been manager of the works for 20 rears. The chamber had not been opened since 1875, and last Saturday afternoon' owing to the weight of the deposits from the action of sulphuric acid on the lead, a prtion • of the floor 16ft. by 12Ft. fell out. To repair this it was necessary to clean the chamber, and large holes were made to allow the gas to escape. Cleaning operations were not commenced until Wednesday. He did not con- sider the work dangerous when care was taken. The only directions given to the men was not to stop in too long.—ln summing up the Coroner said it was clear that the deceased had been long enough in the works and knew the effects of gas to thomughlr appreciate what he was going to do when he undertook this werk ; it WAS also clear that the work formed part of his employment and therefore he (the Coroner) did not think they could. find that any criminality rested with the owners of the works for the death of the deceased. At the same time while he was sure the works had endeavoured to do everything for the workmen, and with the most humane - intentions, yet it was a pity that more supervision was not exercised in the case of men who went abut the most dangerous anti hazardous undertakings. There ought to be some directions given when the work wag- commenced and coverings for the mouth and nostrils ought not to be left optional to the men. Then again the men ought not to stop in the chambers more than a few minutes. As far as lie could see there was nothing to prevent a stranger going into the works and running headlong into the jaws of death. He submitted that men should not undertake any work of this kind with- out every possible precaution being taken for their safety.--The jury returned a verdict "that deceased died from asphyxia caused by inhaling acid gas, such death being caused accidentally and not otherwise.". Mr. Pope remarked that the fullest attention should be given to the Coroner's observations.
A London Novelist named Formes lies in a hopeless rondition at Folkstone, his maehine having run away with him while de.eending a steep hill, icanying him (mora cliff nearly 200 feet high.

LICENSING BUSINESS. At the Magistrates' Court, on Monday, licenses at tha following places were transferred as follows :—To Sarah Ford in place of her late father, Charles George Ford, Green Dragon Inn, Bridge-st. To Martha Guy, in place of the late Wm. Hough, Millstone Inn. Sankey, fit. To James Lee---on the application ot Mr. Jenkins, *iolicitor—from John Shepherd, Red Lion Inn, Winwick- road. ToMary Ellen Lee in place of her late father, out- door license at 1 and 3 Jones's Buildings off Winwick-et. To George Si rncock from Philip Rathbone,Farmers' Arms, Dallam-lane. From Wm. Martin to John Derbyshire off license, Boar's Head, Hill-st. Temporary authority to sell at the Coach and Horses was granted to Margaret Hill, and the like authority was granted to Harriet Johnson, at the off-licensed premises,3B, Pinner's Brow, in place of her brother-in-law, Andrew Johnson. Tem- liorary authority was also granted to Ellen Maria Brun- dritt to sell at the General Wolfe in place of the late Mr, Brundritt. A GIPSY TRAVELLING WITHOUT A TICEET. •

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday morning, Ann Finney, a gipsy, was charged with travelling on Saturday last between Frodsham and Warrington, and also between Manchester and Warrington on the London and North-Western Railway Company's line, without having a ticket. She had told one railway official at Ordsall-lane That she had lost'it and her pocket too, and another that she had given up her ticket from Frodsham to Warrins,,ton,and pi oceeded on to Manchester; and she then paid her fare and obtained an excess receipt. On her return jeurnev she had to change at-Warrington,and she there tendered no ticket and took a ticket for Dun- ham Hill. She was folhwed there and taxed with not having paid her fare to Warrington, and could not give a satisfactory explanation. She was then given into custody. She was now fined 20s. and costs, in default a waonth's hard labour, and cautioned that if convicted again of such an offence she would be sent to jail without the option of a fine. —.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE. At the Magistrates' Court, yesterday, John Thomas Lea, 37, Cartwright-st., Sankey Bridges, was charged with cruelly treating a horse while in an unfit state, on the 30th ult., and Samuel Silcock, coal dealer, of the same place, was charged with causing the animal to be worked.—P.C. Dean said he was on duty in Rose and Crown-st., on the day in question, and saw Lea working the horse, which he found had a wound under the saddle the size of a two-shilling piece and another under the collar as large as a five-shilling piece. Inspector Dowty deposed to seeing the wounds, and that Silcock came to him and said he had been from home and did not know .t he horse had the wounds.—Lea was fined the costs and .Silcock 20s. and costs. GROSS 017TRAGE BY A MARRIED WOMAN. eemily Narroway, married woman. of 24, Hoyle-street, 'was charged with assaulting Ellen Wycherley, wife of Benjamin Wycherley, 50, Catherine-street, on the 7th inst. Ellen Wycherley and Jane Elizabeth France, mar- ried women, of 3, Refuge Square, charged each other with assault. Mr. Jenkins appeared for Wycherley. It appeared that Mrs. France and her husband had been lodging at Mrs. Wycherley's, and owed Bs. for rent and Is. for coal. They were leaving in accordance with a notice from Mrs. Wycherley, and the quarrel arose through their attempting to remove a wringing machine, which she desired to keep as security for the sum due. Mrs. France was locked in the scullery to prevent her taking the machine away, and the keys of the front door were handed through the window to Mrs. Narroway who came in and saying" I will show you how to manage this thing," came as was stated intathe kitchen, "knocked them all alibut like skittles right and left," and held Mrs. Wycherley down an the sofa, pushed her against the boiler, and slapped her face and hit a little girl who was in the house.—Mrs. Fiance admitted being in Mrs. Wycherley's debt, and said she held Mrs. Wycherley on the sofa because she struck her on the face. They were both holding each ether down. Mrs. France stated that Mrs. Wycherley struck her, and pulled her away from the machine. Mrs. Narroway denied that she held Mrs. France down but said Mrs. France held her, and seized her by the throat. Narroway was fined 40s. and costs, the Chairman, Alder- man Harrison, characterising her conduct in going into another's house and doing what she did as a gross out- rage.—The case against Wycherley was dismissed, and ,the other defendants were bound over to keep the peace for six months. ANOTITER WOMEN'S QUARREL. James Floyd,Alice Floyd, and Ann Floyd, of the neigh- bourhood of Warburton-St., were charged with assault- ing Elizabeth Harrison, an elderly married woman, on the 13th inst. The dispute it appeared commenced about some pigeons and it was alleged that one of the women threw a kitten at her and James Floyd got over the wall and struck her in the eye causing it to bleed; the two other defendants also striking her. It was stated for the defence that the complainant used most provoking language, indeed that cited was of a most horrible character, and described by Alderman Harri- son as a disgrace to civilisation. It was also stated that Mrs. Harrison struck the women with a prop, and dressed a mop up and said that was the rotten mother and brother. Mrs. Harrison's windows were smashed in the row. Ann Floyd, the elder woman was dismissed, and the other defendants were bound over to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs.

div.head: MINOR. CASES.
div.p: MINOR. CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and L. Voisey,

WIFE ASSAULT.—James Appleton, fitter, Baxter-st., was brought up in custody on a charge of assaulting his wife, Elizabeth, on the 3rd inst.—According to the com- plainant, her husband came /home drunk on the day in question, and without any provocation, beat her.— Defendant said his wife gave him asgood as he gave her. —The Bench bound the defendant Jiver in two sureties of £l.O to be of good behaviour for six months. Dauwx.—Winifred Jennings, was charged with being drunk and incapable on the previous night.—She was discharged on promising to sign the pledge. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor and Alderman Harrison. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Martin Lyons, 30th appear- ance, drunk and disorderly in the Market on Saturday afternoon, was discharged with promising to keep sober for the future.—John Rooney and John Morris, in Bridge-st. on Saturday night. Rooney 10s. and costs or 14 days; l‘lorris 10s. including costs, or seven days.— John Vickers, in Church-st., the same night, 10s. or seven days.—William Brown and Joseph Ray, drunk and disorderly and fighting at Bridge-foot on Saturday night. Brown 2s. 6d. and Ray ls.—Wm. Hill, drunk and disorderly in Bakehouse-yard, on Saturday night, 54.— Elizabeth Russell, in Irlam-st., that night, ss.—Catherine Ryan, in Wilderspool-road, the same night; It was stated that the defendant was a tramp.—Alderman Harrison: The bulk of these people are not Warrington people but people passing through the town, 'and then the town gets the stigma of having drunken people in it. 55.—John Rohan, in Bank-st., on Saturday night.—The i Mayor said the defendant had paid £26 4s. n fines, and spent three years and five weeks in prison.—Michael Dow, in Friar's Green, on Saturday night, 2s. 6d.—Mary Jane Woolstencroft in Bridge-st., at 1.40 on Sunday morning, 14 days imprisonment with hard labour.— Patrick- Casey, in Denny-st., on, Sunday night, dis- missed.—John Raiby, in Tanner's-lane, on Sunday night,
dismissed.—Margaret Gibbons, in St. James's-st., on the Ist. inst. ss.

DM:WK.—Hannah Holmes, from Wales, in Robinson's Yard, off Fennel-st., on Sunday morning, dismissed with a caution.—Samuel Healy, in Buttermarket-st„ on Sun- day night, who was found creeping about on his hands and knees, dismissed. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE AND CART.—George Townsend, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Sankey-st. on the 22nd ult. Inspec- tor Spinks said the defendant fell out of the cart, and sustained severe injuries to the head, having to have it dressed at the Infirmary, and still being ill from the effects of his fall. He was fined 10s. and costs, 18s. 6d, in all. • _ _

PITCH AND Toss.—Richard Wilcock, John Barker, Thomas Hanlon, jun., James Burgess, George Crozier, and William Ball, jun., were charged with playing at pitch and toss on Sunday. the sth be. The defence was they were tossing for "pop" p.nernot for money. The Mayor said it was all the same thing. They were fined ss. each. _

OFFENSIVE OUTBUILDINGS.—Edward Hill and Eliza- beth Thomas for having outbuildings at 3 and 4 Knowles's Yard, in an offensive condition, on the 7th inst and were fined 2s. 6d. each. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett, (chairman), E. M.

Crosfield, and E. J. Guest. DarsK AND DISORDERLY.—George Wicks, drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on Saturday last; also with as- saulting P.C. Newey, on Saturday. The defendant was standing on the footpath with sone other men, and the constable asked them to leave. AU of them did except the defendant, who refused to go, and suddenly jumped up and" tupped " the officer with his head, and struck him and knocked him down.—He was fined ss. and costs.—Tnomas Glavin, for being drunk and disor- derly in Bank-st., and obstructing P.C. Newey, while in execution of his duty, on Monday night, was sent to jail for 14 days' hard labour.—John Shiel, drunk and disor- derly in Buttermarket-st., and assaulting P.C.'s Barlow and Bothwell, on Monday night, was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days.—John Conway, 20th appearance, drunk and disorderly in Dial Court, on Monday night, was fined ss. including costs. ASS-kJ:MT.—Patrick Reedy of Latchbrd was charged with assaulting Mary Kilkade in Dial's Court, on the 11th inst. Mr. P. Davies defended. It appeared that the complainant had been running at a little boy,the defend- ant's nephew, to strike him, and the defendant came, and as was asserted for the prOsecution struck her twice, the complainant falling on receiving the second blow. The complainant's husband came out and took her away. Dr. Peacock proved that the complainant had sustained a bruise on the arm. For the defence it was alleged that the complainant hit the defendant five or six times, and he struck her back with his open hand only, when she fell to the "floor."—Peter Hackney, a retired fitter, gave the defendant an excellent character. He was fined 10s. and costs. . _
WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (chairman)
and Mr. J. Fairclough.

CHARGE OF Assauvr.---Ann Donlan, married woman, of 24, Silverst., was charred on a warrant with assault- ing Ann Foley, married woman, on the 11th inst. The case was dismissed, but the defendant had to pay for tha warrant. Dianur.—Bodelia Smith, 18th appearance, drunk in Winwick-st.; on Tuesday night, was fined ss. ARMY DESERTION.—Wm. Lambert and Charles Pi. charged with deserting, on the 12th inst.. H.M. 9th Lancers, stationed at Dundalk,were sent to Strangeways jail to await an escort. TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton.

DESERTION F-110M nitE ARMY.—Henry Ridebalgh was charged with being a deserter from her Majesty's 2nd Lancashire regiment stationed at Curragh Camp, and was sent to Strangewa.ys jail to await an escort. Drumnr.—Michael Melia, bricksetter's labourer, drunk in Dial Court on the 25th of May, was fined 10s. includ- in et costs. . _ _
Before Alderman_ tiarrison (chairman), Dr.

• Gornall, &c. DAMAGE TO WlNDows.—George Hill and Robert Newell, boys, were charged with breaking four windows the property of James Stephenson, on the 30th ult. The prosecutor said he had had from 40 to 50 windows broken by boys.—The damage was proved by two lads, one of whom said the defendants were throwing stones at him and hit the windows.—The boys after being detained in court a considerable time for the magistrates' decision, were dismissed, on promising never to offend again, but had to pay costs, 3s. 6d. each.

WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Captain Withington and Mr. , James Tinsley. Frcurritto.—Patrick Dillon, for fighting at Burtonwoodf on the sth inst., was bound over to keep the peace for three months. - HIGHWAY OFFENCES.—John Thompson, for being asleep on his cart at Poulton, on the 30th ult., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.—James Cottam, for using a cart with- out having his name painted thereon, on the 30th ult., was fined is. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Henry Beach, drunk and disorderly at Poulton, on the 4th inst., was tined 2s. 6d. BREACH OF THE GAME LAWS. George Woods was charged that he on being searched by rdice-Sergeant Barnes, on the sth inst., on suspicion of ha-sing been on land, the property of William Robinson, for the purpose of taking game, was found in possession of agun.—Mr. Percy Davies defended.--Sergeant Barnes said on Sun- day morning the sth inst. he met the defendiunt on the towing path by the side of the Mersey, at Poulton carrying the gun produced, both barrels of which were loaded, and haring a dog with him. Witness, noticed that his socks and trousers were wet and coved with grass seeds, also that the dog was very wet. 17.'e asked the defendant to give an account of himself, and he said he had come out to empty the gun. Witness traced his clog marks into Mr. Robinson's field, where there was game—both pheasants, partridges, and hares.—Mr. Davies for the defence said theland in question had been sold by his father to its present owner, and he (Mr. P. Davies) could not remember there being any game upon it. The defendant had a right. to shoot crows on,the• farmer's land, near to it, and the police could not say that the gun had ever been discharged.—The case was dismissed.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Mr H. Gaskell jun._(chairman) and
Lieutenant.:Colonel Gaskeli.

_ DRUNKENNESS.—John Hayes, Ellison-st., and John Conley, 20, Ellis-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night. They were each fined ss. and costs. SLEEPING IN CHEMICAL WORKS.—James Riley and John Walsh, of no fixed abode, were charged with being found asleep in a shed at Messrs. Golding, Davis, and Company's chemical works, on Sunday night.—They were each committed to gaol for seven days with hard labour. ABSENCE WITHOUT LBAVE.—Thomas Murphy, David, Jones, Robert Price, Michael O'Neil were each charged with being abSent from Orford Barracks, Warrington, on Saturday, without leave.—They were remanded in custody to await an escort. THEFT OF CABBAGES.—George Cank, of 57, Kent-st., was charged with stealing a number of cabbages, valued at Bd., from the garden of John Abbot, market gardener, Farnworth.—He pleaded guilty, and was fined ss. and 14s. costs.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. F. Stapleton Bretherton and Mr.

A. R. Gladstone. MISCELLANEOUS.—For being drunk Anthony Gragher, Duke-street, Ditton, and John Noon, Wellington-street, were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs and Patrick Butler, Pleasant-street, was fined ss. and costs.—James Mc Donald and James Watson were summoned for commit- ting a breach of the peace in Beaumont-street, and they were each bound over to keep the peace for three mouths John Griffiths, of Widnes-road,was ordered to pay 7s. 6d. for playing at pitch and toss.—Agnes Constantine, of no fixed abode, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk in the Alexandra Hotel and refusing to quit when requested. ASSAULT.—Kate Harrison, of Walmsloy-street, was summoned for assaulting Winifred Carney, a married woman from the same locality. It was alleged that Mrs. Harrison struck and kicked the complainant and threatened violence with a brick. A fine of 10s. and costs 14s. was imposed.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst. DRINICERS.—PhiIip Taylor was summoned for being drunk on the licensed premises of the Castle Hotel on the first inst.—P.S. Costello, P.C. Brew, and P.C. Fryer gave evidence as to the drunkenness and the defendant called Dr. Dr. Carruthers, who said defendant had had something to drink, was not drunk, but was not fit to be served with any more.—A fine of 28.6 d. and costs was im- posed.—For being drunk at Frodsham Bridge, Frederick Ellams, of Water-st., Frodsham was fined 2s. ed. and costs 6d.—Edward Foulkes, Smith,Catherine Hynes, and Patrick Carrot, were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. GAME LICENSES.—Mary Brimelow, of Bridge-st. and Mary B. Hardley, of Devonshire square, were granted licenses to sell drink. _

VERY NICE BlRDS.—Henry Forshaw Canal-st., was summoned for having been in possession of two thrushes and a blackbird on the 23rd June.—lnspector Dowty, R.s.p.C.A., said the birds had been recently taken.— The defendant said he knew nothing about the close season. The birds were given him by a boatman, and very nice ones they were too. (Laughter.) He was ordered to pay costs, 4s. 6d. ASSAULTS AND THREATS.—Martin Rafferty, a young man, was summoned for assaulting Lizzie Jones. She alleged that when walking along the street the defend- ant placed his arm round her neck, and when she pushed him away he struck her.—The defendant, who -said he only "shoved" her, was fined ss. and costs.—A labourer named William Whittle was charged with using threats to Emma Walker. It was allerd that he threatened to split her head wlth a hammer.—The case was dismissed. —Maggie Foster and Catherine Palin charged each other with using threats, and they were both bound over to be of good behaviour far six months. •

Murray and Lang placed a different complexion on the game from their predecessors, and to those batsmen do Cheetham Hill undoubtedly owe their victory. Runs were put on rapidly,Lang espacially playing fine cricket. At 41 a double change of bowling was tried, Crosfield relieving Captain Adam,whilst Bell went on in the place of Smith. In attempting a short run Murray fell to a smart piece of work by England and Bell, the partner- ship having realized 38 runs. Bell bowled in grand form, and out of his first five overs, four were maidens, with wicket included in them, and at 49 Pennington fell to a brilliant catch by Lee. With 60 on the board, Captain Adam and Smith again resumed, and swallow was soon bowled, half the wickets being down for 61. Lang, however, continued to hit brilliantly, scoring freely off Crosfield. Bothwell placed one in the safe hands of Podmore when he had made 10, but on Oats joining Lang, a stand, which decided the fortunes of the day, was made. Oates apparently thought he was out from the first ball he received, but the home umpire, (Wag- staffe) decided in his favour. With this slice of luck, he commenced to hit in all directions, and runs came freely from both ends. Bell resumed at 120, and in his first over got Oates caught low down, whilst two balls later E. Holt was clean bowled. Duck was res- ponsible for the score being rapidly augmented, but, being a trifle too eager, lost his wicket owing to the cleverness of Clark, the wicket-keeper. Orford, after making five, was caught by Voisey, and Lang thus car- ried out his bat for an admirable 70, included in which were eight fours, five threes, and eight twos. Scores : WAARINGTON. Whether he haa " found the use of his legs again "or not, Shrewsbury has been playing aplendicrly, and he Gunn have quite maintained the reputation of the Notts v. Sussex matchea for heavy scoring. The two men put on 312 runs for the second wicket; in the second innings, last year, at Trent Bridge, against Sussex, they pnt on 398 runs. Admirable as, their performance was, however, we should, considering the difference in the quality of the bowling..class it below the display given by Bean,the importation from 115ottnigham. To score 237 runs for once out against the Nottinglram bowling was a splendid achievement.

Some. cricketers may remember that Beam played a fineinnings of 100 runs against the Piustralians for Sll3-, sex last year. This season, he has Iplayed very finely. Marlow,. another importation. also scored heavily; and. altogether Sussex, although,defeated,was not disgraced. No fewer than 1,137 runs were scored,. and of these only 10, weroextras! Sherwin was keeping-wicket for Notts and Blatt for Sussex, and in point of ability there was little to choose between them. Notts, tried a "colt" named Btiggaley, and he met with the success which new bowlers so often meet with. Bowlers, however,. are not exactly what the county requires.

An unkind critic has whispered that Shrewsbury's "return to form" synchronises with a "freer use of his legs" instopping the ball ; but that, no doubt is a calumny At the same timer it is to be heped that a 'Ong time will pass before the alteration in thelaw will compel men, no matter where the ball pitches, to,defend the stumps with. the bat only.

WARRINGTON V. OELRETRAM HILL. —This, match took place at Arpley on Saturday, before a fair number of spectators. The afternoon cricket's was, certainly dis- appointing to the home supporters, for winning the toss- and on a good wicket the Warringtonians only managed to score 87, whilst Cheetham Hill put together the res- pectable score of 161. Mr. S. M. Cros.geld was away at Bristol with the Lancashire team, and the captaincy was in the hands of• Mr. J. J. Crosfield. The latter with Lee occupied the wickets first, Pennington and Murray being the bowlers. The first-named was depatched for three in his first over, but Lee showed a partiality for Murray, and after knocking six off his first two balls, the first hit being a grand drive, he failed to get proper hold of one to leg, and fell to an easy catch .at the wicket,, one being 'dvn for nine. With Clarke in runs came but slowly, and after eight had been added Crosteld was bowled. Voisey placed one in the hands of Cadman, after making two, whilst Bell was run out after making a grand cut to near the boundary; which only realized one run. A similar fate befell E. England when he had made seven, and it was disappointing indeed to see the match literally thrown away, and all for the want of a little judgment in the matter of running. Clarke falling to a good catch by Swallow,retired at 52, but the junior 1 professional made an unexpected stand. Changes were ' made to separate Smith and Clarke with a poor result, and it was only after 26 runs had been added that Pen- nington beat Smith, the latter having been., a long time for 6. Captain Adam failed to score, and then Clarke began to hit out. A couple of fours were placed to his credit in quick time, but Murray, relieving Swallow, got Clark cought at mid-on, the latter having played fine cricket for his 21. Pennington also accounted for Pod- more, and the venture closed for 87. The prospects of Cheetham Hill reaching this total were certainly not bright when they commenced, for without a run on the

The English foot-ball team on Saturday played their second match against a fifteen representing the Western. Province and again scored a second victory, winning by two goal, to nil; The game was sharply contested throughout, and the home team, though overmatched, made a gallant resistnince. A high wind prevailed dur- ing the match, which was witnessed by. a very large number of spectators. The English team are in.splendid form.

At an athletic meeting held in Manchester, on Wed- nesday night, Messrs. Gary and Remington, the Ameri- can athletes, in the course of the programme, endeav- oured to beat the English records for 100 yards and the quarter-mile, the first of.which is held by A. Wharton, with the time of 10Secs.,.the holder ofithe quarter-mile being H. C. ILTindall, and the time 49tsecs. There would be 5,000 Spectators present, and Cary, runving in the final of the sprints, could only finish second to Hal- loeke, a fellow clubman, Cary's time being returned at 10 1-ssecs., the same as he accomplished in the English championships. while Remington, though winning the quarter-mile easily, failed to touch the record, doing the distance in 50s. Gary's display was disappointing, whilst Remington would certainly have been nearer Tindall's time but for the fact that he was not pushed,. and towards the finish seemed to ease up atit.

.Undoubtedly the most Important Lancashire fixture on Saturday, was that of the-far-famed Blackburn Rbvers ; and their attractive prospectus commanded a capital entry, a strong contingent of Glasgow athletes putting in an appearance. The two miles scratch race was tha first event in the programme, its position being due to the fact that the management committee wished to consult the convenience of Parry and Morton, who had to get away to Eccles to compete in the Harriers' race there. Kibblewhite made most of the running, and drawing• right away round the last bend 'won gallantly from Parry, who defeated Morton by a bare yard. The half-mile bicyole race proved a triumph for the handicapper, as Baylis and Campbell (Glasgow} could not bedivided, and Douglas Johnson was only half a, wheel's length behind them, with G. Hawley right on his shoulder: In the ran off Campbell won easily. J. W. Schofield, the Southport rider,won the mile handicap with-the greatest ease,and his powers do not yet seem to have been successfully gauged by the allotter of starts. B. Blargerison, of Bradford, had a very succesf ul afternoon. He secured first honours in the 220, and ran second to R.' W. Whalbn in the sprint.

Saturday was perhaps the busiest- 'day, so-far, of the pres9nt season. Athletic meetings were• hekl north, south, east, and west, with the result that one or two notable performances have to be recorded. Earlier in the week at a London evening meeting Queckburner, the " pocket Hercules" of the Manhattan team; accomp- lished his heart's desire by creating a new English hammer-throwing record, as at Taffnell Park he suc- ceeded in covering 132 ft. 7-in., which is 2ft. nin. better than Barry's English record, although lft. 21in. worse than the American figures. Most of the Manhattan athletes were competing at the Landon Athletic Club meeting, with, however, one very notable exception, viz. Cary, who had gone to Gateshead to take part in the 100 yards Northern Counties -Championship. His presence, of course, put the ultimate issue of this event beyond doubt, and the local sprinters were much chagrined at his appearance. setting away well, he rapidly forged ahead, and won easlly by three yards in time equal to a yard worse than, tm seconds: Beswick was second, having defeated Steavenson after a good race.

WARRINGTON V. LIVERPOOL.—A grand afternoon's cricket was witnessed on Wednesday, at the prettily laid ground' of the Liverpool club at Aigburth, when the above clubs met in their return engagement. The first match had resulted in a win for the seaport team, and the chances of Warrington reversing the first verdict were indeed forlorn when it was found that several of their most prominent players were absent. Winning the toss, the visitors opened the defence with Messrs. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield. The start was indeed disastrous, as not a run had been totalled before the Warrington cap- tain skied one to short leg. With only a run on J. J. Crosfield was bowled all over hia wickets, and two good men were thus down for one run, Whitehead being credited with the pair. Lee and George Clarke dis- played remarkable patience in their opening strokes, but at length both hit out brilliantly, the professional scoring much the' faster. With the score at 45, Eccles relieved Gregory, and with eight runs added, White- head reached Clarke's wicket with a beauty. Yonge hit a four—a grand drive—and was bowled,the board read- ing as 63-5-4. The two Warrington professionals were now together, and although Clark did not hit so heavily, as his co-partner-rills play was marked by some pretty strokes. A fine drive by Lew reached his 50* and runs coming at a still- more rapid pace,. Harrison relieved Eccles at 107: With his third ball he got Clark to an exceptionally fine catch by Bright, the partnership hav- ing realized 46,rues A fine place of fielding ran Hindley out, and then another stand was made by Podmore and Lee, the latter scaring freely off the amateur bowling, whilst Podmore contented himself with singles. At 147 Podmore was bowled, whilst 1& runs later Captain Adam was sent back by Gregory, who had relieved O'Dwyer. Adamson and Lee augmented the score rapidly, and the professional completed his IGO amid loud cheers. The century, however' .proved fatal to him, for Whitehead a with grand ballbeat him, the total now standing at 168. Lee had batted magnificently for his, runs sever giving a chance. His gereral command of the bat was marked, and his strokes' whether cutting or driving, were brilliant. 'winded in his 100 were 12. fours, 4 threes, 6 twos. THE SUDDEN DEATH OF AN, AGED
IVONA.L

Mr. C. 11. Yates, coroner, beld an inquest at the Golden Lion Inn, Latchford,lon Monday, on the body of Ann Suthern,'widow, , aged 76 years, who resided with her married son in Grove-st., Latchford, and died suddenly on the 10th inst. The deceased's son said she had lived with him and his wife for some years, and had 'never 'complained of anything ailing her except thatshetaapains which , she attributed to rheumatism in her back. She had dinner svith them on,Friday the lOth inst., and seemed all right, and just before be went out she put her arms , round his neck and kissed him in honour of his birthday. When he next heard of her she Naas dead.—The wife of the previous witness said that the deceased seemed all • right except that she complained of pains-near her heart. Witness went out of the home at five • minutes to one o'clock, and five minutes later was called back by a, neighbour, who found the deceased sitting dead in a, chair.—Mary Elizabeth Chorley, , the neighbour, said a, lad had thrown a stone at a grandsona the deceased. and witness took him into his lather'n- house in order to, tell Mrs. Suthern, jun., and when she got in she found therold lady sitting upright in the chair,apparently dead;. Witness brought a neighbour in, and: they found that she was no more. She had a calm and placid expressions I Mrs. Suthern mentioned that deceased had lived with, her for seven years, and during thattinae had not had a 1 single day's illness in bed.—The jury returned a verdibt that death was caused by heart disease.
NEW VEHICULAR BRIDGE: ACROSS 'PJTE MERSEY.

Some months ago the members of the Widnes Local Board were requestettby the Runcorn,Cona- missioners to co-operate with, them in bringing before the councils of their respective countieS a scheme for erecting a bridge across the Mersey for vehicular traffic. The proposal was rather, coldly received by the Widnes. Local Board, as, is was believed that the effect of making easier the com- munication with ehe,Che,slaire side of the river .would be to induce many residents in Widnes to take- up their aboda,in and outside of, Run.corn. The Runcorn Com- missioners, however, have nellallowed the matter to rest herci, and have endeavoure&p push forward the scheme, at least until it was considered by the County Councils of Lancashire and. Cheshire. With this view plans have been prepared by Sin Douglas Fox of a bridge 140 which is to, cost :S„.000. If the proposal is carried out, the bridge will run parallel with the wsent structure which carries the L. & N.-W. Railway across the Mersey. One plan shows the bridge taking its riseon the Widnes side at the point where Church-st., joins Viaduct-st., and. thus running upon land in the possession of the London and North- Western Railway Company. This scheme willnecessit- ate the purchase of a considerable number of houses which here adjein the viaduct, and as ibis understood, tnat the railway company do not favour the proposed bridge, some difficulty will very likely be experienced in, the purchase of their property hereabouts in case thig` plan is approved. The alternative- plan is to make the bridge a continuation of Viaduerst. with, of course, the necessary alteration in the levels. This will avoid the Londc,n and North-Western Railway (ampany's property, and Neill only necessitate the purchase of a much smaller portion of land, (in this case nearly wholly vacant), than contemplatedi by the first-named plan. The rise in either case will be, one foot in thirty„ which will carry the bridge to the level of the present railway and foot bridge alongside which it will run, on the east or Warrington side. Thepresent bridge seevesas a model forthat pro- posed to be constructed. The main portion of the river will be spanned by three girder bridge supported on four piers of 301 t each, the approaches on either side be- ing carried on arches, each, of 60ft. Each of the central spans will be 305 ft. long,. and the height of the bridge will be exactly the same, as that of the London and North Western Railway, namely, 75ft. above high water mark. On the Runcorn side the gradient to Ashridges- st. will be also one in thirty, and will include a bridge of 150,ft. over Lord-st. and Ashridge-st. It is in the neighbourhood of" "Seville, that the oramges best suited for " " marmalade making are grown. A recent" "frost, (the like of wh'eh has not been ex-" " perienced for ten years, hasnlayed havoc" "with the fruit, and, although though the" " full extent of the damage is not yet" • ' known, it is believed that fully one half " "the orange crop has been destroyed." "Luckily one shipment has been made to" " Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" " SS " Zurburan," which has just arrived." "The Liverpool firm of %V. H. WALKING DAY BANDS.

• • ----- - iir,—Referring to the letter of your corresponpent "A Lover of Fair Play" in your last Saturday's issue, in which he states that I, as conductor of the League of the Cross Band, played a second or third cornet, which was not suitable to lead a band with, I beg to inform your readers that his statement is untrue, as I played first cornit. Those of your readers who understand music will be aware that a conductor may suitably play any instrument in his band according to where, in his judgment, his band is weakest, or he may not play at all.—Yours, &c., J. 'MULLINS.

Warrington, 15th July, 1891. We are glad to receive Mr. Mullins' correction, and re- gret that "A Lover of Fair Play" should have made use of our columns for circulating an inaccurate state- ment, which was calculated to injure Mr. Mullins in his professional capacity.—En. Ex.

div.head: HALTON LADIES CLUB. •
div.p: HALTON LADIES CLUB. •

The 7411 anniversary of this club was celebrated on Monday afternoon in the customary manner. The members assembled at the Parochial Schools at 12 o'clock and after transacting some business,they formed in processional order, and headed by the Runcorn Volunteer band, walked three times round the Green of the Castle Hotel,and then went to the Parish Church. here the Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, preached a sermon from the text " God is faithful." Service over, the members who num- bered over 200 marched through the village, return- ing to the Castle Hotel, *here a large marquee had been erected on the Green. Lady Brooke the Lady Patroness presided at the head of the centre table, and amongst those who supported her were Mrs. Henry Reynolds, high stewardess; Miss Kathleen Rey- nolds, Miss Thomas, Miss Blaine, Mr. C. Reynolds. J.P., and Mr. J. H. Gamon, trustees; Mr. Thomas Wright, secretary : Mr. Carruthers, Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar of Halton, Mr. Cecil Reynolds, and Mr. Lightwood. A sub- stantial tea was provided and much enjoyed. Subse- quently Lady Brook delivered an address in which she said the past year had been one which had given many of them cause to rejoice that there was such a club in the village for not often inhe recollection of most of them had there been a year in which sickness had been so prevalent. The terrible epidemic of influenza, which had ravaged other parts of England had been severely felt in Balton. and had seemed to at- tack all alike, the young and strong, as well as the aged and weakly. It was at such a time that they saw what a blessing such a club as theirs was. The money help that they received from the club was no doubt a great thing, but there was something higher and better, and thatiwas the:sympathy and kindly feeling which it sought to promote amongst them. Many changes had passed over Halton since the club was founded for the benefit of the women of Halton 70 or 80 years ago. From a small beginning had grown that large society as it existed to-day, and whatever time might have in store for them in the future, OP trusted that nothing might weaken or destroy the bond of friendship and fellow-feel- ing which existed between the members, and that the club would continue to prosper and carry on its good and useful work. (Applause.)—Mr. C. Reynolds sub- mitted the financial statement, which showed that on December 31st, 1873, there werA 149 members, and the funds amounted to £777 12s. sd. Now they had 260 members, and the funds stood at £1,345 18s. 4d. (Ap- plause.) He thought that the result of the fast 17 or 18 years' working had, been most satisfactory, and they had every reason to congratulate themselves, because as Lady Brooke had truly said, it was a friendly society inevery sense of the word because it helped others to help themselves and that was the truest sort of help they could render in this world. He mentioned that the name of Carruthers had been associated with the Club for sixty years and he was sorry to state that Dr. Carruthers had resigned his position as medical officer.—Mr. Reynolds tendered the thanks of the members to Lady Brooke for her presence and to the Rev. H. B. Blagg for his sermon.—Mr. Blagg having made a few observations, cheers were given for Lady Brook, Dr. Carruthers Dr. Robinson, Mr. G. J. Knight, Rev. H. B. Blogg, Rev. G. D. Wray, Mr. Thomas Wright, Mr. C. Reynolds, and Mr. J. H. Gamon. Dancing was indulged in on the green during the evening to the strains of the Volunteer band.
Messrs. Povey and Co.'s extensive forage 0-ores in Tanner-street, Bermondst_T, were destroyed by fire early on Friday morning. - -
, • Intelligence has been received from two distinct sources of an important naval victory by the Chilian in- surgents, two of the Presidential warships being almost destroyed.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUA

Mr. Brandreth presided over the fortnightly meet- ing held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Edwards, Taylor, Aaron, Lewis, Kirkham, J. Bate, P. Speakman C.C., J. Ashton (clerk.) THE COUNTY RATE.—REPLIES FROM MR. POTTS.

The following letter was read in reply to a resolution passed on the motion of Mr. S. Taylor a month ago : "Cheshire County Council, Clerk Office, Chester, 6th July, 1891. Dear Sir,—County rate. I duly received your letter on the 23rd ult., and which in consequence of Quarter Sessions and other pressing County business I have not been able to answer before. While anxious to give your board information respecting the general county expenditure Jam afraid I cannot in the compass of a letter give you in detail the various causes for the in- crease of the County Rate since the County Council came into power, and I do not think I can do better than re- fer you to the annual abstract of the County accounts which you or your predecessor will no doubt have re- ceived. The necessity for increasing the County Rate in 1889 mainly arose by the Council having to pay to the Highway Authorities one moiety of the cost of main roads for the year endiug 31st March, 1889, and for which Quarter i.e. January to March they did not levy any rate and also by the whole cost of the main roads being thrown upon the county in addition to which the surplus revenue of the River Weaver Trust has since fallen off. A comparison of the County accounts for different years will no doubt give you any further in- formation you may require. I am,yourstruly, Reginald Potts. John Ashton, Esq." The Clerk said he had received from the representa-

tives of the late Clerk a bundle of county accounts, but he could find none since Lady Day, 1889. He had writ- ten to Mr. Potts asking for copies to be sent him since that date. When those arrived the matter could be , further considered.—The Clerk had written to the Clerk of the County Council,stating that at the last meeting of the Board, attention was called to a report of the pro- ceedings of the Birkenhead Guardians, from which it seemed that the call on the county rate for this half-year was £2,617 9s. 91., as against £2,600 at the same date last year, being an increase of £l7 9s. 9d. He was re- quested to ask for an explanation why the call now made on the Runcorn Union was so much in excess of that of the corresponding period of last year, being now £3,292 10s., whereas in May last it was £2,670- 13s. 5d., an increase of £621 16s. 7d. Was it, he asked, that the call now made was the whole call for the half-year or would there be another call made in August next, as was the case last year, and if the present call was for the whole half-year could one half be paid now and the other half in August P—Mr. Potts replied as follows ; " 7th July 1891. Dear Sir,—County Rate. In reply to your letter of the 4th inst., the statement made by one of your Guardians that the county rate levied by the Council on the Birkenhead Union for the first half of the past financial year was £2,600 is incorrect as the actual amount so levied was £2006 14s. Bd. The present call of £3,292 10s. on the Runcorn Union is for the current half year and should have been paid on the day named in the precept. The Council will no doubt levy a further rate in November." Yours truly, Reginald Potts." Mr. Aaron said the statement was made in the" Liver- pool Courier." At a late period of the proceedings Mr. Brandreth as chairman of the Finance Committee moved the passing of accounts amounting to £2,183 Bs. 2d. in- cluding £1,646 ss. half the Ccunty call.—Mr. Aaron ob- jected to the County rates being paid. The Clerk had to supply them every half year with a financial statement of the affairs of the Union and the Board formerly re- ceived one from the County magistrates but siuce the Comity Council was formed they had not received any statement of County affairs. He objected strongly to paving over £3OOO until he knew what it was for.— The Clerk said he thought the abstract of accounts had been sent, but he could not find them. Mr. Potts would now send them on.—Mr. Aaron said he could not recollect one being produced at the Board since the Council was formed.—The Chairman said he had seen them produced at this Board.—Mr. Aaron: Why should we pay until we know what it is for ?—The Chairman: We are keeping one half now.— Mr. Aaron: I propose that not one farthing be sent.— Mr. Edwards seconded the Motion.—The Clerk said the Council could compel them to pay.—Mr. Speakman said if Mr. Aaron would just consider a moment he would withdraw this proposition. He for one had a very great respect for that Board, and he did not want the members to look ridiculous before the public. Any information he could give relating to County Council matters he had given, and there was not the slightest doubt in his mind that the statement Mr. Aaron wished for had been sent. If, through the death of the late Clerk, this had not come to the bands of the Clerk that was not the fault of the County Council. He did not like this continued ridicule that came from Mr. Aaron on the County Coun- cil. If there wan any sense in it he could under- stand it, but he was bound to say it was a piece of ridi- cule from one end to the other, without any sense or reason about it.—Mr. Aaron said he was much obliged to Mr. Speakman. There was no ridicule about it. Were they as representatives of the ratepayers to pay £3,000 and not know what it was for? He would not withdraw it.—The Chairman: We do know what it is for.—For the amendment Mr. Aaron and Dr. Gastaldi voted, and the original motion was carried by a large majority.
A QUESTION ON FREE EDUCATION.

Dr. Gesteldi asked a question with regard to Free Education. Religious schools, he said, would not accept the Free Education Act; it was left to the discretion of schools to accept it or not. He asked would those schools which did not accept free education continue to receive school fees for poor children from the guardians. —Mr. Taylor pointed out that the Board only paid 3d. per head and the Free Education grant was 3d. per head, so that the Guardians would not pay fees if the Act were passed.—The Clerk said he did not read Acts of Parliament until they were passed as there were usually so many alterations made.—Mr. Lewis said the question was premature.
EXTRAORDINARY FXPLOSION AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS.

An explosion of an extraordinary nature took place at the works of Messrs. Sullivan and Co.,Moss Bank, Widnes, on Monday morning. About live o'clock two men named Bryan Gatley and James Lynch were engaged in conveying black ash balls from the furnaces by means of a bogie. and deposit- ing them before the vats. One of the balls resisted dislodgment from the bogie and the men only suc- ceeded in their object by pushing the truck with greater force than usual. Near the place was a pool of water, and one of the balls rolled into this and immediately exploded with a loud report, fragments flying in all directions. Lynch who was behind the bogie was thrown with great violence against a wall several yards distance, and killed instantly. Gatley received injuries to the left arm and leg, besides a severe shock to the system.—The inquest on Lynch was held by Mr. W. T. Husband, at the Golden Bowl, Moss Bank, on Wednesday. Mr. Richmond, - inspector under the Factories Act, was present and the United Alkali Company were represented by Mr. Thomas Minton, manager of the works.—Margaret Lynch, of 37, Moss Bank-road, said the deceased was her son and 19 years of age.—Bernard Gately, who was with the deceased at the time of the accident said the black ash balls were red hot. The black ash ball that exploded was difficult to move from the bogie, and when they had thrown it to the ground it exploded. He was of opinion that the ball was not set properly. It was drawn at 3.30. As an experienced furnacenian he knew that a hot black ash ball would ex- plode if thrown into water.—Edward Kaye, vat runner, said he heard the explosion, and running to the spot found deceased lying on the ground with his clothes on fire. He put out the flames and found that he was dead. Gately was sitting on one of the black ash balls, and ap- peared to be injured. One end of the bogie was in a pool of water in front of the vats. The water was waste out of a pipe used to carry water out of the vats. He had warned Gately that there was water where he was go- ing to tip. Water had been seen there before, and it was not an unusual practice to tip balls into it.—Thos. Roughsedge, foreman said the balls, if soft, would ex- plode when thrown into the water: if they were pro- perly set they would not burst. Be had tipped into water himself, but he would not do so if the black ash ball was not set. In this case it appeared that the ball had broken, and the inside of it being soft had flowed into the water and exploded.—The Coroner said it would be much safer if the ground was made level so that water could not collect, and probably Mr. Minton would see this done. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and added a rider that the firm be requested to take measures to prevent the lodgment of water in the place where the balls are tipped.—Major Wareing, the foreman, said the evidence showed that there was an utter disregard on the part of some of the men for their own personal safety or that of others, and -they must be protected against themselves.
RtNCORN FREE LIBRA RY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on VV ednesday afternoon, Rev. Canon Wood pre- sided,and,there were present Messrs. H. J. Grice,W. Handley,W. Hankinson,and J. D. Jones (Librarian) The Librarian reported that the number of books issued from the lending department was 923. The re- ceipts for the month amounted to El. 6s. 2d. Mr. Once suggested,in face of the progress we were making in edu- cation especially having regard to the Technical Educa- tion Act, that it] would be advisable to obtain a few works of literature in Fernch and German. —Mr. Handley said a few dictionaries would be very use- ful.—Mr. Grice moved and Mr. Handley seconded a motion that it be an instruction to the Rook Selection Committee to secure several standard works in French and other foreign languages.—The motion was carried. A discussion ensued on a suggestion made by Mr. Handley, and at the request of the Chairman he drafted the following resolution which was unanimously passed: —" That with a view to furthering technical instruction in Runcorn district it was resolved that the members of • the School Board be invited to confer with the Library Committee at an early day in order to see if joint action cannot be taken under the provisions of the Act."
THINGS HEARD AND, SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDIMT.

The inquiry of the Runcorn Guardians with refer- ence to the expenditure of the County Council has met with the answer I predicted. Mr. Potts, the clerk, refers them to the annual budget ; but inci- dentally he mentions the payments to highway Authorities and the loss of revenue from the River Weaver Trust as the two chief causes of the in- creased rate. Mr. Aaron was not satisfied with this explanation, and, with his usual persistency, on Tuesday he asked for a bill of particulars and moved a resolution objecting to pay the County call until this demand waS met. Mr. Edwards who seconded this motion deserted his colleague when the voting came, and Mr. Aaron was only joined by Dr. Gastaldi in his protest against County extravagance.

Mr. Speakman who was present waxed indignant over Mr. Aaron's attitude towards the Council. He declared that Mr. Aaron spoke without sense or reason, and made the Board ridiculous before the public. Mr. Aaron retorted that he acted as he thought best for the interests of the ratepayers, and there the incident ended.
leas 1

I was not aware until a few days ago that Mr. Frith, the secretary and manager of Runcorn Gas Works was the inventor of an improved furnace for gas making. It seems the furnace is in use at Run- corn Works and at many works in the country, and at the present time the Manchester Corporation are having a number of the furnaces constructed under Mr. Frith's personal superintendence. Little Run- corn helping mighty Manchester seems a reversal of the usual order of things.

At last! Waterloo Bridge is beginning to wear a finished appearance. The footpath-. of granolithic pavement has been made, and very well; indeed does it look. Similar pavement has been laid down each side of Percival's-lane ; and Church-at. is the next locality where the pavement will be put down. In appearance granolithic is clearer and better than either flags or tiles, and it is. claimed that it will last a generation. Frost has been the ruin of the pavement in Greenway-road, but it is to be re-laid at the cost of the makers.. At any rate, the pavement will have a severe trial in Clurch-st., and if it bears the test, no doubt other thoroughfares will be dealt with..

Since Mr. W. H. Handley, of Runcorn, read his paper on the charities of the Northwich Parliamen- tary Division, several charities supposed to be lost have been brought to light and are now fulfilling the purposes intended by the founders. The last ex- ample has occurred at Sutton. The overseers ot this township have under their control .£2O which had been invested in Frodsham Savings Bank since 1822 and the interest of which is applied to the reduc- tion of the poor rate. How and why this money came there were questions which no one seemed able to answer,but the facts brought to light by Mr.Handley led the overseers and their assistant, Mr. Acton, to make a research, and they have discovered that the money is composed of the charities of Samuel Shaw, rector of Warrington, and the charity of John Hough ot Sutton. These charities are each of the value of £5, the former being bequeathed in 1739 and the latter in 1719, and both for the benefit of the poor of Sutton, and they have increased to £2O by the accumulation of interest during years when the charity was not distributed early in the century. Arrangements are being made to put the charities on a proper footing. Messrs. William Lowe Joseph Acton, and Denis Acton have been nomin- cted as trustees and in due time the :Charity Com- missioners will send down a scheme.

From the question asked by Dr. Gastildi, at Run- corn Board of Guardians,on Tuesday, there would appear to be some doubt as to the operation of the Free Education Act. That school:fees will be re- mitted to pauper children attending schools which are not free is beyond the bounds of possibility.

I was speaking this week to a gentleman who has not yet reached middle age, who attended Run- corn National School when the only fee charged was a penny, and even whole families were admitted for that small coin. The fees have, however, been gradually raised to the present rate, and the Free Education Bill is in such cases bringing the cost of education to the level it was some 20 or 30 years ago. The difference between the 103. grant and the fees will mean a loss to the Parish Church Schools of about £l7O, to Holy Trinity of about .CBO, the Wesleyan School of about .Cl4O, and the Board schools of about £3O. To the Catholic School the grant will mean a gain of about £l2. There appears, however, to be little doubt that all the schools in Runcorn will be declared tree.

In Widnes the fees are rather high, and there will be a loss all round. it has been computed at 2s. 6d. a head and that may be taken as a fair estimate. To the Board .Schools which find accommodation for half the children of the town the loss will be proportionate. The, deficiency might be made up by charging the Infants a halfpenny ar d other scholars a penny. but I am of opinion the ratepay- ers would prefer to have the schools entirely free. Before the School Board takes action in the matter they intend to confer with the managers of the denominational schools, and no decision can there- fore he arrived at for nearly two months. In this matter it was felt in some quarters that the School Board had better take an independent course and not be influenced by the opinions of denomina- tional managers.

Even without the aid of raffling, the Frodsham bazaar in aid of the Church Boys School was a great success. The comfortable sum of £5OO was realised, and there are sufficient materials left to raise a further .C2OO.

The Vicar of Runcorn evidently knows the art of advertising. The bill he issued announcing the school sermons would have warmed the heart of a showman. The way .in which the two chief lines were thrown up led some people, I hear, to believe there were two preachers engaged, one for the morning and another for the evening. I always read the small type, and se know that the Yen. Archdeacon would preach on both occasions. The collection was nearly £4 in ayance of last year.

Familiarity breeds contempt in other things than manners. It appears to lead to contempt of danger in chemical works. Within the last few days two lives have been lost that might have been saved by the exercise of the commonest care. At Widnes a man tips the black as ball into a pool of water with a result he knew might occur, and the explosion kills a young man of 19. At Runcorn a labourer ex- posed himself too long in a chamber that was being cleaned, he became gassed, and in 24 hours was dead: In the latter case the unbrtunate man leaves a. widow and ten children, and Dr. Robinson gener- ously gave her the guinea allowed for his attendance at the inquest; the coroner added a subscription, and the jurymen contributed their shillings.

Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, of Runcorn.h as been appointed registration agent for, the Liberal party in the Knutsford Division, and I congratulate him upon the fact. He is an ardent politician, a fluent speaker, and, being a lawyer, should know his way about. May he secure such a register that the present member will be Gusted and a better man take his place.

We are to have a thorough change of Wesleyan preachers in the town this autumn. Mr. Burson will be succeeded by the Rev. Thomas Wilk, chair- man of the Nottingham antl Derby district; Mr. Kendrew by the Rev. Wm. Arrowsmith of South Shields, and Mr. Judson by the Rev. (iv. Hanby of Worcester.
MR. MC KIN_LEY.

Mr. McXinley is now one of the most famous, at ost talk-of, men in the world, for he has given his name to a Tariff Act which has and will continue to have far-reaching consequences. Oue of the most immediate consequences of the passing. of the Act was an overwhelming and unex- pected defeat at the polls of the Republican party with

which Mr. McKinley is con- nected. Mr.. McKinleyr him- seii, author . the Bill,was defeated in Ohio and the Democrats made a gain of eight seats in that State. Altogether, the Democrats secured the im- mense majority in the next Congress of over 1150. The AlcKin)ey Act has, as may be expected,. been spoken of in very different ways by different peo- ple. On the one hand Mr. Blaine claimed that the Tariff would benefit the people of the ignited States at large and especially the farmers, but,. on. the other hand, ex-President Cleveland slrongly con- demned the " iniquitous " Act, which "not only enhanced the cost of the necessaries, of life, but fostered extortions, trists, and com- binations," but he added that it would "make certain the advent of free and better times, and the final ascendancy of the demo- cracy in New York." in England the Act did not ' meet with any commendation. Mr. Gladstone said that Article 105 proved too much for him,. but he warned the country against a policy of retaliation, as only aggravating the evil: The Marquis of Salis- bury, in his usual cynical way, said the prohibitive tariff had been instituted mainly because " Ameri- can pigs had not received'proper treatment at the hands of Europe." That Protection often has the very opposite effect to that which is sought is well known, and the working of the McKinley Act has afforded a few more instances of this. We have Just been told, for example, that "Jewellers and the manufacturers of silver vpare are chafing under the tariff in their trade. Much, of what is known, as silver tissue paper is used to protect articles from the air, and America has been making this article for 25 years, but it has never given satisfaction,and the English article has always been used. The M'Kuiley tariff imposes a duty of Sc. per pound and 25 per cent. ad valorem. This has sent up the im- ported article 45 per cent., or from idol. 25c. per ream to idol. 75c. The domestic article rose accord- ingly, but the largest silver ware merchants say they will simply pay the enhanced price. That is all they can do, for to use the domestic article would ruin their business. They must have the imported article, even if they pay sdols. a ream for it. The tariff does net affect th'e domestic article, but the price goes up 'all the same on this andsimilar manufactured goods of all kinds."
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY
AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Brandreth presided and there were also present, Messrs. Action,. Lewis, Edwards, Kiriham, J. Bate, J. Ashton (clerk) and J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).
VINANCE.
Accnunts amonnting to £34 Us. 10d. were pasmtd; for payrrmit. The Chairman stated that the balance ii the. treasurer's hands was £35955. 9d.
A COMPLAINT :FROM PRODSHAM.

Mr. Pdwards asked why the call for the Rural Simi- tary Authority made on Friday was not made previonslY. —The Clerk : We have adopted the course adopted'hy• the late cltrk.—Mr. Edwards said he thought it was usual to sand out the call for the poor rate and the saui--1 tary rate at the same time so that one collection would suffice. The call was for £230 to be paid by August 12t'a but there was-only a balance of £24 in the hands of the- overseers and'it could not be done.—Mr. Aaron said the' calls had always been raadein this way.—Mr. Edwards. said he did not find fault with the call—it was necessary; but he complained that so little time was suffered to elapse between the call and the demand for the money. —The Clerk sairlthe precept for the poor rate and for the School Attendanee rate was made by the late clerk, but there was nothing made out for the Sanitary Authority expenses when he took office. He could not see why the two precepts-should not be issued at the same time. He would see what could be done in future.—Mr. Edwards also pointed out that last year the call was £lBO, this year it was £23o.—The Assistant Clerk said there was a balance against the township and they wanted to get a balance in favour of the township.— The subject then ceased.
NUISANCES A'ND% DISEASE.

The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams) reported that a case of diptheria had occurred at a cottage next to Appleton Hall farm. A case of diptheria had also occurred at Stork House, Stretton.. He had investigated both cases and found no sanitary defects which would account for the disease. He also examined the cottage situated next to Twenty Step Bridge, Stockton Heath, Appleton. The drainage had recently been blocked, but at the time of his visit was running freely. The condition of the privy and ashpit was such as to constitute in his opinion a nuisance under the Public Health Act, both beinc, full and the privy overfldwing through the brickwork into the yard. This called for immediate abatement.—The Inspector was instructed to serve notices for the abate- ment of the nuisance complained of, and if not complied with to take further action.
