The Nuisance Inspector reported that the outfalls of the sewer at the Weston Chemical Works and of Mr. Hadfield's Bone Works into the river Weaver were about 2 ft. 6in, under water, as he understood that the level of the water now would be the level when the Ship Canal was finished.—The Cleric said it was the duty of Mr. Wells, the engineer of the authority to investigate these matters, and it was decided that the attention of Mr. Wells should be drawn to the matter.
MR. PARNELL AND cA,rrAIN O'SHEA'S COSTS._

Mr. Parnell has at length paid Captain O'Shea's costs in the divorce suit. The amount was something under a thousand pounds, Mt. Parnell paid when a final notice of ulterior proceedings was served on him by Captain O'Shea's solicitors. The divorce episode may now be declared as closed..

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE, AND CONSERVATIVE
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE, AND CONSERVATIVE
SY M PATH Y.

Mr. Gladstone, replying to, a letter of condolence written by a gentleman on behalf of some old colleagues at the CarltonZlub, says :—I thank you heartily, and I know that in thanking you. I thank many. In a great affliction, a most heavy loss, God has been most kind to us, and so has man. Be assured that I have never dreamed that barriers erected by the necessities of poli- tics would check the flow of human sympathy within your walls.

div.head: RETURN TO LOWESTOFT.
div.p: RETURN TO LOWESTOFT.

Mr. Gladstone on Thursday Left Hawarden Castle for Lowestoft, his beneficial sojourn at which was inter- rupted by the lamented death of his son, Mr. W. H. Gladstone. In passing through Wisbech Mr. Gladstone assured the Hon A. Brand,. Liberal candidate, that he would gladly have spoken in his behalf had he not been forbidden by his medical men to speak in the open air.
ALARMUiG RAILWAY COLLISION AT EART,ESTOWN.

On Thursday night a collision of a serious nature occurred on the London and North-Western Railway, on what is known as the Vulcan bank, at Earlestown. At 1050 the 9.15 p.m. fast goods train frorcWarrington to Liverpool, was passing, heavily loaded, Winwick Junction, at which point it is customary for trains with heavy loads, to whistle for the assistance of the bank engine. The usual signal was given, and the train which was travel- ling at the rate of about 30 miles an hour con- tinued on its way. The bank engine was standing in the siding at Winwick Junction, and when the goods train had passed, followed in its wake. It however, failed to overtake the train, and the driver of the bank engine increased his speed. By some means he appears to have misjudged the distance between his engine, and the goods train, and before he realised the position he had pitched violently into the brake van, smashing the buffers of the engine, damaging the brake van, and throwing several of the wagons across the up line, causing both the up and down lines to be blocked. The brakesman of the goods train (J. Wakefield) saw that the bank engine was coming at a good speed,and observing that a collision was imminent, he saved his life by jumping from the van, just as the impact took place, portions of the inonwork from the engine buffers, flying past his head. The driver and stoker of the bank engine remained at their posts, and escaped with a shaking. The- break-down gang were soon on the spot, and the Bine was cleared about two o'clock on Friday morn- ing.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A WOMAN
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A WOMAN

Harriet Collett, a respectably connected woman,. aged 51, residing at Mr. Forshaw's near the Common Locks, Earlestown, was charged at the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, with attempting to commit suicide by:drowning herself in the St. Helens and Sankey Canal, at Newton, on the 14th inst.— William Forshaw, labourer, of Earlestown, said the prisoner bad been in his employ, as his housekeeper, for three or four months his wife being Ord and feeble. She left his house on the night of the 13th inst., and he had not seen her since.—Peter Drown, of Newton Common Locks, said that on the 14th inst., in consequence of what he was told, he went outside his house and saw the prisoner struggling in the water. He ran across to the lockhouse, and wit a rake, and went to the canal side and pulled her out. She called out two or three times "'Don't save me."—Ellen Collett, a domestic servant, out of employ- ment, the prisoner's daughter, said her mother had been living apart from her husband about nine mouths. On Monday night when she was going to bed, she said " You won't have me to trouble you long." She had threatened several times to commit suicide. She had drunken bouts occasionally.—P.C. Bowes, stationed at Earlestown ,said he apprehended the prisoner on Tuesday night, and , charged her with attempting suicide, when she replied, "I admit it ; I don't deny it." The prisoner's husband was called, and in reply to the magistrates, said he was 43 years of age. He was not prepared to take care of his wife, as it would be impossible for him to do so. She had threatened many a time to commit suicide, and also to take the lives of her children.—The magistrates said the woman must go to the Workhouse,, and her husband would have to contribute to her maintenance.—The pri- soner's daughter here burst into tears, and appealed to her father to take care of her mother.—The Bench then again questioned him, and it appeared from his answers that he was a joiner, and earned 355. a week. He had formed a home for her several times, but she had always broken it up. She had a" husband "living besides him, and that was the cause of the bother.—A Poulton con- stable stated that the parties formerly !ived next door to him. It was said that the woman took drink, but he never saw her the worse for drink, although he had seen her husband in that state several times. —The prisoner's daughter promised to take care of her mother, and the Bench dismissed the case; advising her to take some steps to compel her husband to contribute to her support.—Her husband said he was willing to do that, and had offered to do so in the past, but she had refused to accept anything from him. It appears that no reason can be assigned for the attempt by Mrs. Collett on her life. It seems that on Tuesday she told Mr. Forshaw she would go and drown herself and walked down the garden and threw herself into the canal which flows past the garden. Mr. Forshaw raised an alarm, and Peter Brown then rescued her as above des- cribed. Several other men appeared on the scene, and with their fassistance the woman was hauled into the garden, and afterwards taken into the house and put to bed. The matter having got to the ears of the police, Sergeant Longworth and P.C. Bowes, arrested the woman and after charging her with the offence, which she admitted i placed her in one of the cells.

div.head: FAMSHAM.
div.p: FAMSHAM.

THE BAZAAR.—Yesterday week, the bazaar on behalf of the fund for restoring the boys' school in connection with the Parish Church. was opened by Mr. Heron,.of Manley Hall, who performed the ceremony in the un- avoidable absence of Mrs. Jayne. The visitors- were numerous, and when the.bazaar closed in the evening, it was found that the effort had realised upwards of £5OO.

_ FIVE CROSSES CuAnst..—Anniversary services were held in the Five Crosses Chapel. on Sunday, when the Rev. P. Pizey, of Frodsham, circuit minister, preached in the afternoon and evening to good congregations. At the latter, however, the chapel was crowded to excess. The choir rendered the special hymns and an anthem in a creditable manner. The collections amounted to £23 10s. 0/2-d.

div.head: LThIM.
div.p: LThIM.

GARDEN PXRTY—Mr. and Mrs. Dutton invited between 40 and 50:teachers of the Congregational Sunday School and members of the choir to a garden party at West View, on Monday evening. After tea games and music were enjoyed to the full, and afterwards fruit was served to the guests. It was a most pleasant social gathering.

SUDDEN. DEA-TH.—On Wednesday evening an old man named Abraham Tavlar died suddenly on the road at M!. Blinston's, Statham. He was a noted character in Lymm, having spent the latter days of his life about public-houses and the railway station begging for drink. He was. a joiner, fustian cutter, and we believe a gardener, all these rolled into one, but he did not like work of any kind. He was going to get in a load of coals for Mr. Blinston, and when about to start that gentleman noticed he did not look so well and brought him a glass of beer. He drank it and put a "cob" of coal in the barrow, and then the poor fellow sat down and died. The police were at once informed and the remains removed to his sister's.

A DROWNING MYSTERY.—About half-past twelve on Sunday morning, as a canal steamer was passing the Wash, near Oughtrington Bridge, the body of a man was seen to rise to the top of the water and then to sink. A boy named William Clare saw the body and ran to the Police Station and informed P.C. Howie of the occur, rence. The body was recovered from the water and conveyed to the Railway Hotel, Heatley. On Tuesday an inquest was held at the Railway Hotel, Heatley, by Mr. R. Dobson, jun., deputy coroner.—William Clare said that on Sunday morning he was on the canal bank, near Oughtringten Bridge, when he saw a body floating in the canal. He informed the police.—P.C. Howie said he received information from the witness Clare on Sun- day. and went to the canal. He found that the body had been drawn up to the side of the canal by a man named William Smith. He examined the body and dis- covered bruises on the chest, and the flesh under the armpits was torn.—Sarah Jane Marsden, Oughtrington. said on Wednesday afternoon she saw the deceased in her garden. She spoke to him, and he said that the police were after him because he had sold medals for food. On Thursday ,morning •she again saw the de- ceased from her bedroom window. He asked her to let him in as some navvies were going to cut his throat: Dr. Williamson said he had made a post-mortem examin- ation of the deceased, and was of opinion that he met with his death by drowning. There were no marks of violence on the body, which had been brought up to the top of the water by the propellers of a passing steamer. —The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before T. P. Norris (in the chair), C. Lister, W. P. Brabazon, and J. D. Dewhurst. THE EntrcAnosT ACT.—Dr. Thomas Hill,:of Partington, was summoned for neglecting to provide sufficient ele- mentary instruction for his son. A certificate of birth was then handed to the magistrates, which proved that the lad was 14 years of age. The case was at once dis- missed.—Mr. Hill was also summoned for a similar offence in respect of his two daughters, who were be- tween the ages of 5 and 13 years.—The defendant stated that his daughters had been:suffering from the measles and the case was adjourned for two months. Several other cases of a similar character were adjourned. ASSAULT ON A PourabAN.—H. Harrison, engineer, Pen- dleton, was summoned for being drunk and refusing to quit the licensed premises of the Saracen's Head, War- burton ;• and also for assaulting the landlord, Arthur Bath, on the Bth inst. Evidence 'laving been given, the defendant was fined 20s. and costs for the first offence, and 40s. and costs for the second, in all £4 15s.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

• The work in connection with the extension of the Wesleyan Chapel is being proceeded with, though not very quickly. During the past few weeks the foundations of the new vestries, which are to be built at the back of the chapel, have been laid, and the-walls built up to the ground level. The work of building the new foundations at the front of the chapel is being proceeded with. It is expected the alterations w.ll be completed by the end of October.

THE YOUNG MEN'S .CHRISTIAN A SSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the above association was held last evening week at Bethany House,the resid- ence of Mrs. Coop. Amongst those present were Messrs. C. E. Parker, A. H. Robinson,W. J. Wigfield, and T. Gandy. There was a good attendance. The first business to dispose of was the election of officers. This was at once proceeded with. Mrs. Coop was unanimously re-elected president • vice- presidents: Rev. T. E. Winder, Messrs. C. E. Parker, W. J. Wigfield, R. E. Garnett, and H. S. Jones. Mr. A. Tucker was unanimously re-elected treasurer. and Mr. J. T. Budden, secretary. Mr. W. B. Moston was elected gymnasium instructor, assisted by Mr. E. Webster. After some discussion it was decided that the association should continue under the old name. In cennection with the gymnasium it was decided that a building in which to practise should be either built or hired. The treasurer's report was read by Mr. A. Tucker, which, after meeting all demands, showed a balance to the credit of the association of .211 105. sd. This was commented favourably upon, and ultimately passed. At the conclusion of the meeting refreshments, kindly provided by Mrs. Coop, was partaken of by those present.
The report of an apprehended famine in North- Western India has been confirmed. In Madras there has been no rain for some days, and the heat is very great.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF A WIDNES GENTLEMAN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF A WIDNES GENTLEMAN.

On Wednesdey there took place at the Queen-st. Con- gregational Chapel,Burslem, Staffordshire, the marriage of Mr. Thomas Simmons Lawley,,of Haltwhistle, North- umberland, only son of Mr. William Lawley, of Widnes, with Miss Alice Hodson Derry, youngest daughter of Mr. Thomas Derry, postmaster and auctioneer, Burslem. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. T. Hartley. The bride was attired in a beautifully rich dress of em- broidered chinese silk, the material a present from her brother-in-law and sister Mr. and Mrs. Barnett, of Pen- ang. The bridesmaids were Miss Counsel, of London, and Miss Ireland of Widnes. The weddiug was a quiet one, and only members of the family were present. At the conclusion of the ceremony MT. and Mrs. Lawley drove to Longport Station, from whence they departed to Bettys-y-Coed, .where the honeymoon will be spent, The presents were numerous and costly.

div.head: THEFT OF ,'lO FROM A P ÜBLICHOUSE.
div.p: THEFT OF ,'lO FROM A P ÜBLIC- HOUSE.

At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, George Clarke, bricksetter, Hollins Green, was charged on remand with stealing, some time bet- ween 11.15 and 11.50 a.m., on the Bth inst.' a print bag and £lO its contents, the property of Martha Guy, widow,landlady of the Millstone Inn, Sankey- at. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle prosecuted. It appeared from the evidpnce now and previously adduced, that about 8.30 a.m., on the /Bth inst. the prisoner went to the inn and remained there till about 11

o'clock. Mrs. Guy went into the kitchen for a short time,leaving him at the bar smoking his pipe, and she left thelbag containing the .ElO in gold and silver in an unlocked drawer in the bar. A little girl came into the bar and found that the prisoner had moved a form from the wall up against the counter and was standing on the form looking over the bar. Mrs. Guy had left him standing at the bar, smoking his pipe, with his arms on the counter. She 'was absent about four minutes, and on her return the bag and its contents and the prisoner had disappeared. She saw marks of his clothes on the counter. She had saved the money to pay her brewers, and the loss had put her about a great deal. On the first day on which the prisoner was brought up (Monday) the Mayor re- buked Mrs. Guy for leaving her money in such a dangerous place.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said in reply to the Chairman (Alderman Harrison) the prisoner had bought a new suit of clothes and a watch and chain with the money. Nothing bad been recovered but the clothes, and it was supposed he had pawned the watch and chain in Manchester, where he had been.—The prisoner, who ))leaded guilty, was, after a severe denunciation of him by Alderman Harrison, for his heartless ramatity, sent to gaol for six months with hard labour,

FATAL FALL FROM A TRAPEZE. NEW YORK, TGESDAY.—A dispatch from Lyons, lowa, states that William Hanlon, one of the brothers who have become famous as trapezists, was killed while going through his performance at the Circus there yesterday, Owing to the breaking of the bar of the trapeze, he was thrown to the ground, a distance of 30 feet, and broke his neck, dying instantly. PRINCE GEORGE GEORGE AND HIS WATCH. Prince George of Wales sailed from Halifax on Mcnday for England. On Sunday evening the crew were ordered on deck, and informed that the Prince's cabin had been entered and his watch stolen. Every man declared him- self innocent, and offered to be searched. The watch ' was not found, and the police are trying to trace it on shore. IN INTERESTING MARRIAGE • POSTPONED. • t A London correspondent, referring, it is understood, to Lord Hartington says :—Ever since Easter the political and social world have been on the look out for a marriage, interesting in both spheres. A high political personage was, it was reported, about to change his estate, marry- ing a recently widowed duchess. I hear that the cere- mony is postponed, and will certainly not take place this year. MURDER OF OF A PARAMOUR. At the Durham Assizes, on Wednesday, Mr.. Justice Day sentenced Harriet Harledge, 30, widow, to 20 years' penal servitude for the murder of her paramour' George , Dixon. The parties quarrelled, and the accused stabbed the deceased in the heart and then assisted him into the house and ran for a doctor, but the man died almost immediately. The prisoner and the deceased were about to be married.

RAILWAY ACCIDENT: BRAVE RESCUE. Shortly after seven o'clock on Monday night, Ellen Hyland, eight years of age, residing with her parents at 102, Canal-bank, Greenbank, met with an accident on the railway in the yard of the Greenbank Alkali Company, St. Helens. Deceased and another girl named Catherine Hardy were play- ing inside the gates, and, apparently not noticing their danger,ran across the lines of the siding as an approach- ing engine was but a few feet away. Both were in inv. minent peril, but, with remarkable presence of mind, a man named Michael Gaffney, who was just at the spot,. dragged Hardy to one side, while aryther man name& James Slater, rushed across the lines, seized the girl HY- land, and attempted to save himself and the girl bY grasping the buffer of the engine. He escaped unhurt,. and dragged the girl's body away,but her right arm, WaS badly smashed by the locomotive. P.C. Donegan was on duty in the vicinity, and, as a successful in.eraber_A of the St. John's Ambulance Association, bandage" the broken limb, and removed the girl on an ambulance to the Providence Hospital

THE ARCHBISHOP OF YORM, The-ceremony of electing Dr. Maclagan to the arch- bishopric of York was performed yesterday. in York Minster. HANES& OF THE BISHOP OF CHESTER. Dr.- Jayne,. Bishop of Chester, is suffering from a. severe attack of influenza' and has been compelled to. cancel labis engagements. THE SHARES FORGERY. At MA,nohester Assizes yesterday afternoon;- Ernest Le Poer Pdwerwas sentenced to five years's penal servi- tude for forgery relating to shares valued £25',0001.' A SELF-ACCUSED MURDERER. William Fisher, leather dresser, was remanded at Greenwich-o.yesterday, charged on his own confessioni witn murdering a lad named Collins in 1881, . THE, WISBECH DIVISION ELECTION: Mr. Duncan (Conservative) and the Hon. Mr. Brand. (Gladstonian). were yesterday nominated as candidates- for the Paehamentary representation of the • Wisbech- division. Tbelpolling takes place on July 23rd. A' MURDER NINE YEARS AGO. At Berwick, yesterday, William Burke was.charged.on remand with murdering John Burns. butcher's' appren, tice, in 18d2d. The prosecuting counsel said a mar:named Armstrong would depose to seeing Burke throw Burns- into the Tweed. MR. SPURGEON. A bu letin issued on Thursday morning states that Mt. Spurgeon iselot worse. The delirium is rather less, and his strength-is maintained. Yesterday's bulletin states that Mr. Spurgeon passed a. better night, and had a little quiet sleep. His strength. has also somewhat improved. THE LABOUR COMMISSION. Lord Derby presided at the resumed sitting of the. Royal Commission on Labour on Thursday.—Mr. Hub- bard, of the London and India Docks Joint Committee, said 9,000 'men were employed at the docks.- The labourers' full weekly pay averaged 28s. Notwithstand- ing precautions, nine fatal and 100 minor accidents oc- curred at the docks last year. FATAL BOILER EXPLOSION. The Press Association's West Bromwich correspondent' telegraphs that a boiler exploded yesterday morning at the foundry. of Messrs. W. Cross and Sons, wrecking the building and killing a man named Price and a boy named. Taylor. Portions of the boiler fell through the roofs of several houses fifty yards distant,without.hew,• ever, injuring any of the occupants. SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT. An accident happened yesterday, at Bullingluigi ,on the Highland Railway, to the down London nightmail. Four carriages left the rails and were smashed. Miss Hardinge, one of the passengers, had two ribs.broken and her spine injured. Several others sustained minor injuries, and the Whole have miraculously escaped from death by the accident, apparently caused by the snapp- ing of a loop rail. YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENL HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-pasb four. A QUESTIONABLE PICTURE.—Lord STANLEY of Alderley,. asked a question relating to the purchase, by trustees of Chantrey bequest. of Calderon's picture ef the Renuncia- tion of Saint Eliiabeth which he said was a gross libel on the Catholic faith. The Marquis of Samsnuny expressed the beliefthat the artist had no intention of outraging religious feeling and the purchase by the Chantrey trus- tees he could not interfere with. The Public Health (Scotland) Bill was read acecond time. After a division the House adjourned at twenty minutes to eight. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. THE 'MCKINLEY TARIF.— Sir J. CAIN asked if the attention of the piesident of the Local Government Board had been directed to the fact that 25,000'then had been thrown out of employment owing to the increased duties- now levied by United States. Sir Michael Hick Beach understood that, though these increased duties had prejudicallv affected them, the Government saw no reason to take special steps to meet probable consequent misery. EDUCATION IN IRELAND.—The CHIEF SECRETARY said the Irish members would have an opportunity early next session of discussift the allocation of that grant to be- land corresponding to the grant to England for the aboti tion of school fees. GOLD MINING IN WALES.—The House went into Com- mittee of supply. On the vote for the office of woods and forests, Mr. PRITCHARD MORGAN complained of the discouragement by the Governaient of gold milling in Wales. The gold which they raised wastof itself of no vane, and it was only because it was treated with first class machinery that it had gained any value: All he wanted to do was to set up a new industry,. Sir WM. HARCOURT urged treatment in a more liberal manner in regard to Reyalties of the industry referred to. Mr. W. Arnow said that the matter had received careful consi- deration, and he did not think that the scale imposed erred on the side of severity. The proposal to reduce the vote was negatived by 136 to 89. Mr. Lloyd George next objected to the amount of royalties.
